lectures.title: Esophagus
key: Esophagus C6–T11, 18–26 cm; no serosa → early lymphatic spread; Killian triangle → Zenker
Esophageal syndrome = dysphagia, regurgitation, pain, sialorrhea (NOT vomiting)
Paradoxical dysphagia (liquids > solids) = achalasia; rapidly progressive dysphagia + weight loss = cancer
GERD: most frequent symptom heartburn; best exam 24 h pH-metry; manometry before surgery
Achalasia: bird's beak → sock-like (advanced); Heller myotomy + anti-reflux valve
Zenker: cricopharyngeal myotomy mandatory
Cancer: biopsy at esophagoscopy = diagnosis; staging CT + EUS + PET-CT; Gavriliu esophagoplasty = greater curvature tube
traps: Vomiting does NOT belong to the esophageal syndrome
'Niche' is a gastric-ulcer sign – not a typical esophageal radiological aspect (stop, stenosis, filling defect, diverticulum are)
Rolling (para-esophageal) hernia: GEJ stays BELOW the diaphragm; sliding: GEJ ABOVE
Epiphrenic and Zenker are PULSION diverticula; parabronchial = traction (post-TB)
Reflux esophagitis is the starting point of Barrett – the old key treats achalasia as the classic pre-neoplastic answer
Anti-reflux surgery does NOT suture the cardia to the left crus; it restores intra-abdominal esophagus (2–4 cm), His angle, LES pressure
Savary-Miller II = confluent NON-circular erosions
gloss: esophagoplasty with reversed greater-curvature gastric tube

lectures.title: Stomach & duodenum (ulcer, cancer)
key: Most frequent cause of UGI bleeding = duodenal ulcer; most frequent gastric ulcer site = lesser curvature
Johnson I lesser curvature, II gastric + duodenal, III prepyloric, IV juxtacardial, V NSAIDs anywhere
Main diagnostic method = upper endoscopy with biopsy of every gastric ulcer; DD = gastric cancer
Perforation: sudden epigastric pain, board-like abdomen, pneumoperitoneum; fever is NOT a cardinal sign; treatment = suture + omental patch + lavage
Pyloric stenosis: Darrow syndrome = hypokalaemia, hypochloraemia, hyponatraemia, metabolic alkalosis; correct first, then resect
Early gastric cancer = mucosa/submucosa, regardless of nodes; radical = gastrectomy + D2
Truncal vagotomy needs a drainage procedure; highly selective does not
traps: Duodenal ulcer pain is RELIEVED by milk/alkali; it wakes the patient at night
Copious saline irrigation is part of the SURGICAL procedure – it is 'never indicated' as emergency (pre-hospital) treatment
Blumberg sign is not found in initial pyloric stenosis; Bouveret, clapotage, Kussmaul are
Darrow syndrome does NOT include hypocalcaemia
Finsterer exclusion-resection = post-bulbar (difficult) duodenal ulcer
Forrest Ib = continuous slow (oozing) bleeding
gloss: hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis of pyloric stenosis
gastro-duodenal / gastro-jejunal anastomosis after distal gastrectomy

lectures.title: Small intestine
key: Meckel: rule of 2; painless bleeding in children; Tc-99m scan
Crohn: transmural, skip lesions, ileum; surgery only for complications, bowel-sparing (strictureplasty)
Mesenteric ischaemia: pain out of proportion; AF/cardioversion; CT angiography; revascularise + resect + second look
Short bowel: worse without colon, without ileocaecal valve, after ileal resection (B12 + bile salts)
traps: Short bowel malabsorption is LESS severe when the colon is present
Ileal resection → bile salt + vit. B12 malabsorption (not calcium/folate)
Childhood short bowel: atresia, volvulus, necrotizing enterocolitis
Crohn surgery is palliative; conservatism is the main principle

lectures.title: Colon (cancer, IBD, diverticular disease)
key: Right colon cancer: anaemia, mass, fever; left: bowel habit change, obstruction, rectorrhagia
Colonoscopy + biopsy = gold standard; CT staging; CEA follow-up
Not pre-neoplastic: diverticulosis, sigmoid volvulus, melanosis coli
UC: mucosa only, rectum + continuous; cure = proctocolectomy; risk of cancer ↑ with duration, extent, early onset
Diverticulitis: CT = preferred test; Hinchey I–IV; Hartmann for III–IV
Volvulus: coffee-bean; endoscopic detorsion then elective sigmoidectomy
traps: Hinchey has 4 stages – there is no stage V
Contrast enema in diverticulitis must use WATER-SOLUBLE contrast
UC occurs more in NON-smokers and has inflammatory pseudopolyps; cobblestones = Crohn
Colon cancer complications: diastatic perforation, intussusception, stenosis, colo-vesical fistula – not diverticulitis
Massive haemorrhage with shock is NOT usual in UC
gloss: resection + end colostomy + closed rectal stump

lectures.title: Rectum & anal canal
key: Internal haemorrhoids above dentate line – painless bleeding; band ligation only for internal
Longo stapled hemorrhoidopexy = grade III; Milligan-Morgan for IV
Fissure: posterior midline; GTN/diltiazem → lateral internal sphincterotomy
Abscess = incision & drainage; fistula: fistulotomy, fistulectomy, seton; MRI for complex
Rectal cancer: DRE + pelvic MRI; neoadjuvant CRT; TME; APR if sphincter invaded / no tone
traps: Rubber-band ligation is NOT for external haemorrhoids
A rectal tumour can cause secondary haemorrhoids
Fistulotomy = laying open from one end to the other; fistulectomy removes the tract
APR indications: external sphincter invasion, lack of sphincter tone (low T1/T2 near the anal verge per the old key)

lectures.title: Gallbladder & bile ducts
key: Risk factors: female, obesity, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, rapid weight loss
US = first-line; lap cholecystectomy = standard
Acute cholecystitis: Murphy sign, US wall thickening; surgery in first 24–72 h
Charcot triad = pain + fever + jaundice; Reynolds = + shock + confusion
Cholangitis = obstruction + infection → ERCP decompression
Aerobilia: after ERCP/sphincterotomy, stents, bilio-enteric fistulas, gas-forming infection
Courvoisier-Terrier: palpable painless gallbladder + jaundice = malignant distal obstruction
traps: Charcot triad does NOT include hypotension or altered mental status (those are Reynolds)
Veganism and high-fibre diet are NOT risk factors for gallstones
Transabdominal US shows stones and duct dilatation – not 'biliary stasis' or CBD fibrosis
ALT rise is NOT part of the cholestatic syndrome
Prehepatic jaundice = haemolysis (spherocytosis, sickle cell, thalassaemia)
gloss: two structures to gallbladder before clipping

lectures.title: Liver
key: 8 Couinaud segments; Cantlie line = surgical right/left division; falciform = anatomical
Hydatid cyst: Echinococcus; Gharbi I–V (V calcified, inactive); albendazole, PAIR, pericystectomy (Lagrot unroofing most frequent)
Pyogenic abscess: biliary route most frequent; percutaneous drainage + antibiotics; amoebic = metronidazole
Surgery even if asymptomatic: adenoma, biliary cyst(adenoma), hydatid cyst; NOT FNH, haemangioma
HCC: AFP; radical = resection, transplant, ablation; Milan criteria
Portal hypertension bleeding: banding, vasoactives, balloon tamponade, TIPSS
traps: Liver blood supply is NOT only the hepatic artery (portal vein ~75%)
Segment I (caudate) is not seen on the anterior surface
Needle liver biopsy is the invasive study
No biopsy in haemangioma (bleeding); HCC biopsy risks seeding
Treatment of adult polycystic disease: unroofing + fenestration
RFA/sorafenib are not 'radical' in the old key (radical = resection, transplant)

lectures.title: Acute appendicitis
key: Most common abdominal surgical emergency
Pain migration epigastrium → RIF, then nausea/vomiting, then low fever
Signs: McBurney, Blumberg, Rovsing, psoas, obturator, Grassmann-Mendel (bell)
US (children/pregnancy), CT adults
Treatment: (laparoscopic) appendectomy; mass → antibiotics; abscess → drainage
Most frequent post-op complication: wound infection
traps: High fever is NOT always present
Nausea/vomiting is a symptom, not a physical-exam finding
In children local signs are LESS obvious; toxic forms frequent
Complications include portal pyaemia – not melena or intraperitoneal haemorrhage
Right colectomy is not an option for simple appendicitis

lectures.title: GI bleeding
key: UGIB: proximal to Treitz; top 3 causes: duodenal ulcer, haemorrhagic gastritis, varices
Resuscitate: O2, 2 large IV lines, Ringer, urinary catheter; endoscopy after stabilisation
Forrest Ia spurting, Ib oozing, IIa visible vessel, IIb clot, IIc black spot, III clean base
Surgery: Forrest Ia/IIa failures, massive bleeding not responding, rebleeding, >2 L loss
Varices: banding, sclerotherapy, balloon tamponade, IV somatostatin/terlipressin
Mallory-Weiss: tear at GEJ, alcoholics; endoscopy (not barium) for diagnosis
traps: Melena alone is not an indication for EMERGENCY endoscopy
Abdominal US and CT are not routinely used to find the UGI source
Arteriography cannot find the site if bleeding is slow (<0.5–1 mL/min)
Ulcerative colitis is NOT a cause of upper GI bleeding
Esophagectomy is not a treatment of variceal bleeding

lectures.title: Spleen
key: Spleen = most frequently injured solid organ in blunt trauma
Kehr sign = left shoulder pain; signs of hypovolaemia: tachycardia, hypotension
Stable → CT → non-operative ± embolisation; unstable → splenectomy
CT: laceration, haematoma (intraparenchymal, subcapsular, perisplenic), haemoperitoneum, contrast blush
Vaccinate (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib) – OPSI
Absolute splenectomy: ruptured splenic aneurysm, unstable splenic trauma bleeding
traps: Bradycardia is NOT a sign of splenic rupture
Hereditary spherocytosis is a classic elective (not absolute/vital) indication
Surgery for splenic trauma is for hypovolaemic shock, not for stopped bleeding

lectures.title: Pancreas
key: Acute pancreatitis: gallstones + alcohol = top causes; trypsin = central role
Atlanta: 2 of 3 – pain, enzymes >3×, imaging
Ranson admission: age >55, WBC >16 000, glucose >200, LDH >350, AST >250; 48 h: Hct ↓10%, BUN ↑5, Ca <8, PaO2 <60, base deficit >4, fluids >6 L
CT = most accurate morphology; Balthazar = CT score
Morphine contraindicated (Oddi spasm)
Necrosectomy postponed ≥4 weeks; edematous pancreatitis is never surgical
Pseudocyst: no epithelial lining, >4 weeks; best = Roux-en-Y cysto-jejunostomy
Cancer: ductal adenocarcinoma, CA 19-9, Courvoisier; Whipple for head; liver mets, carcinomatosis, SMA = unresectable
traps: Hyperamylasaemia is NOT a Ranson criterion
Hypocalcaemia is a consequence, NOT a cause – hypercalcaemia is a cause
Pain is the most constant sign; vomiting does not relieve it
Infected necrosis is an indication, not a contraindication, for intervention
Pseudocyst does NOT have its own (epithelial) wall – a 'false' statement trap
Courvoisier sign appears in cancer of the head – not tail/body

lectures.title: Acute bowel obstruction
key: Most frequent cause: adhesions (~40%), then malignancy (~20%), hernias (~15%)
Four cardinal signs: pain, vomiting, distension, stop of stool/gas
X-ray: air–fluid levels; CT = best; Gastrografin is diagnostic + therapeutic
Rebalance + NGT; surgery if strangulation, hernia, closed loop, failure
Colonic obstruction with right-flexure tumour → right hemicolectomy with ileo-transverse anastomosis
traps: Intramural lesions causing obstruction: tumours, intramural haematoma, Crohn
Strangulation: continuous pain, fever, tachycardia, peritoneal signs, raised lactate
Sentinel loop belongs to acute pancreatitis, not colonic obstruction

lectures.title: Abdominal trauma
key: Closed (blunt) 60–80% vs open (wounds); penetrating = peritoneum breached
ATLS ABCDE; FAST in emergency room
Unstable + FAST positive → laparotomy (damage control)
Stable → CT → non-operative management of solid organs
Lethal triad: hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy
traps: Penetrating trauma is not contusion, thermal damage or barotrauma – it is a wound (stab, gunshot)
Most affected viscus in abdominal trauma per the old key: spleen
gloss: focused assessment with sonography for trauma

lectures.title: Peritonitis
key: Primary (SBP), secondary (perforation – most frequent), tertiary
Wooden abdomen, Blumberg, silent abdomen, Douglas tenderness
Tachycardia from mediators, hypovolaemia, third-space losses
Principles: source control + lavage + drainage; percutaneous drainage for abscess
Laparoscopy is NOT contraindicated
traps: Free peritoneal air is the characteristic X-ray sign – not air–fluid levels
Intraperitoneal antibiotics are not a principle of treatment
Bacterial translocation and cardiac failure are not the main causes of tachycardia per the key

lectures.title: Acute abdomen
key: Syndromes: peritonitis, obstruction, haemorrhage, ischaemia, trauma
Topography: RUQ – cholecystitis, pancreatitis; LLQ – sigmoid diverticulitis, ovarian cysts; RLQ – appendicitis
Always: β-hCG in women, ECG in elderly (MI), urinalysis
traps: LLQ pain from ovarian cysts – not caecal carcinoma or gastric ulcer
LUQ pain workup: CT, amylase, CBC, urinalysis – not colonoscopy

lectures.title: Laparoscopic surgery
key: CO2 pneumoperitoneum 10–14 mmHg; Veress (closed) or Hasson (open)
Advantages: less pain, faster recovery, fewer wound problems
Complications: vascular/visceral injury, gas embolism, emphysema, port hernia
Conversion = safe decision, not failure
traps: Laparoscopy can be used in peritonitis and appendicitis

lectures.title: Bariatric surgery
key: Indication: BMI ≥40 or ≥35 + comorbidity, failed diets
Pre-op: cardio-respiratory, endoscopy, psychiatric, endocrine evaluation
Sleeve: Gastrografin at 24 h, LMWH ~10 days, PPI, liquids 10–14 days then purée
Early leak: tachycardia, fever, left pleural signs, hiccups → CT with oral contrast
traps: Psychological distress alone is NOT an obesity comorbidity indication
Abdominal MRI is not part of pre-op evaluation
Heredity is not a criterion

lectures.title: Organ transplantation
key: Autograft, isograft (identical twins), allograft (same species), xenograft
Liver: orthotopic (standard), heterotopic/auxiliary (liver), split, domino, living donor
Brain death after excluding hypothermia and depressant drugs
Complications: rejection, arterial thrombosis, biliary leak/stenosis, infection
traps: Auxiliary transplantation is used for the LIVER
Island is not a type of liver transplantation

lectures.title: Other exam topics
key: These appeared in old surgery papers: valve surgery, pneumothorax, burns, Z-plasty, soft tissue sarcoma
traps: Burn 2A: blisters with clear fluid, pink, very painful
Circumferential burns need admission and escharotomy

paths.def: Esophageal injury after ingestion of acids (coagulation necrosis) or bases (liquefaction necrosis – deeper, more dangerous). Evolution: necrosis → inflammation → granulation → scarring → stenosis.
sx: Intense retrosternal/oral pain, shock
Dysphagia, odynophagia, sialorrhea
Hoarseness, stridor, dyspnoea (laryngeal edema)
Later: fever, signs of mediastinitis/peritonitis (perforation)
ex: Subcutaneous emphysema, peritoneal irritation if perforated
img: Chest/abdominal X-ray → pneumomediastinum, free air
Early endoscopy (first 24–48 h) for grading – stop at necrotic area (perforation risk)
Iodine contrast if perforation suspected; barium only for late stenosis
tx: Acute: anti-shock measures, analgesia, antibiotics, nil per os
Corticotherapy for deep lesions / laryngeal edema (may mask mediastinitis)
Tracheostomy for laryngeal edema
Chronic stenosis: periodic dilation; esophagectomy + esophagoplasty (stomach/colon) in severe stenosis
oth: Never induce vomiting or neutralise
Bases are swallowed in larger amounts (less initial pain)

paths.def: Gastric content reflux exceeding physiologic limits causing symptoms ± mucosal injury. Main cause: transient LES relaxation / incompetent LES (<10 mmHg), often with hiatal hernia (sliding type I most common).
sx: Typical: heartburn (pyrosis) – most frequent symptom, acid regurgitation, postural (bending forward – 'shoelace sign', supine) and postprandial
Atypical: chronic cough, laryngitis/hoarseness, asthma, pneumonia, dental enamel erosion, non-cardiac chest pain
Alarm signs: dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, bleeding, anaemia
ex: Look for anaemia, signs of aspiration
lab: H. pylori testing in selected cases
img: Upper endoscopy + biopsy: esophagitis grade (Savary-Miller / Los Angeles), Barrett's
24 h pH-metry (± impedance) = gold standard for diagnosis of reflux, esp. without esophagitis
Manometry: LES pressure, peristalsis – mandatory before fundoplication
Barium swallow (Trendelenburg): type of hernia; chest X-ray: retrocardiac air bubble
tx: Lifestyle: weight loss, elevated head of bed, avoid late meals, coffee, alcohol, smoking
Drugs: PPIs (first line), H2 blockers, prokinetics, antacids

Surgery (refractory, complications, young patients, large/paraesophageal hernias): laparoscopic reduction of hernia + hiatal calibration (cruroplasty) + fundoplication – Nissen 360°, Toupet 270° posterior, Dor 180° anterior
Rolling/paraesophageal hernia: surgery even if asymptomatic (volvulus/strangulation risk)
cx: Erosive esophagitis, ulcer, bleeding, peptic stricture
oth: Savary-Miller: I isolated erosions, II confluent non-circular, III circular, IV ulcer/stricture, V Barrett
Hernia types: I sliding (GEJ above diaphragm), II rolling/paraesophageal (GEJ below), III mixed, IV other organs

paths.def: Sac-like outpouchings communicating with the lumen. Zenker (pharyngo-esophageal, pulsion, through Killian's triangle), parabronchial/midthoracic (traction, all layers – post-TB lymph nodes), epiphrenic (pulsion, above diaphragm, motility disorders).
sx: Zenker: elderly men >60; cervical dysphagia, gurgling on swallowing liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, nocturnal aspiration/cough, bitonal voice
Parabronchial: mostly asymptomatic; cough
Epiphrenic: dysphagia, intermittent regurgitation, epigastric pressure
ex: Zenker: left latero-cervical mass that gurgles on compression / after drinking water (Valsalva)
img: Barium swallow = key exam (sac, neck, level)
Esophagoscopy with caution (perforation risk) – biopsy, rule out cancer
Manometry for epiphrenic (associated achalasia)
tx: Zenker: surgery always indicated – diverticulectomy + two-layer suture + cricopharyngeal myotomy (mandatory, prevents recurrence); endoscopic diverticulotomy (stapler) alternative
Parabronchial: resection only if symptomatic/fistula
Epiphrenic: resection + myotomy ± antireflux procedure, treat associated achalasia/hiatal hernia
oth: Pulsion = Zenker + epiphrenic; traction = parabronchial

paths.def: Failure of LES relaxation + absent peristalsis due to degeneration of the Auerbach (myenteric) plexus.
sx: Dysphagia – earliest & most constant; intermittent then permanent; paradoxical (liquids worse than solids), worse with cold food
Regurgitation of undigested food, nocturnal (supine) → cough, aspiration
Sialorrhea, rare retrosternal pain
Long evolution with preserved nutritional status (vs cancer)
img: Barium swallow: dilated esophagus with 'bird's beak' tapering; advanced: sock-like/sigmoid esophagus; glucagon/nitrate test vs organic stenosis
Manometry = confirmation: incomplete LES relaxation, high LES pressure (>25–35 mmHg), aperistalsis
Endoscopy + biopsy mandatory to exclude pseudoachalasia (cardia cancer)
tx: Lifestyle: small meals, avoid very hot/cold food
Drugs: Ca-channel blockers, nitrates (poor results); botulinum toxin injection
Pneumatic dilation
Surgery of choice: laparoscopic Heller extramucosal esocardiomyotomy (6–8 cm) + antireflux procedure (Dor anterior or Toupet; Nissen in hypermotility per course)
POEM (peroral endoscopic myotomy)
End-stage megaesophagus: esophagectomy
oth: DD: esophageal cancer (rapid progression, weight loss), epiphrenic diverticulum, hiatal hernia, Chagas disease

paths.def: Squamous cell carcinoma (upper/middle third; smoking, alcohol, achalasia, caustic, Plummer-Vinson) or adenocarcinoma (distal third; GERD, Barrett, obesity). Spreads early via rich lymphatics (no serosa).
sx: Progressive dysphagia – solids then liquids, rapid evolution
Weight loss, anorexia, odynophagia
Regurgitation, sialorrhea
Advanced: hoarseness (recurrent nerve), cough on swallowing (eso-tracheal fistula), hematemesis, Horner
lab: Liver tests; tumour markers of limited value
img: Esophagoscopy + biopsy = positive diagnosis
Barium swallow: irregular stenosis, 'apple core', filling defect, niche
Staging: CT thorax/abdomen, endoscopic US (T and N), PET-CT (distant), bronchoscopy for upper/middle third
Laparoscopy for distal/GEJ tumours (peritoneal spread)
tx: Early (T1a): endoscopic resection (EMR/ESD)
Resectable: neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy then esophagectomy (Ivor-Lewis transthoracic, transhiatal, McKeown 3-field) + lymphadenectomy
Reconstruction: gastric tube (preferred), colon, jejunum; Gavriliu = reversed gastric tube from greater curvature
Cervical SCC: definitive chemoradiotherapy
Palliation: stent, laser/argon ablation, brachytherapy, feeding gastrostomy/jejunostomy
cx: Postop: anastomotic leak, chylothorax, recurrent nerve injury, pneumonia
oth: Pre-neoplastic: Barrett, achalasia, caustic stricture, Plummer-Vinson, tylosis, HPV

paths.def: Mucosal defect beyond muscularis mucosae. Main causes: H. pylori, NSAIDs. Duodenal ulcer – high acid output; gastric ulcer – mucosal barrier damage.
sx: Epigastric pain – rhythmic, periodic (seasonal)
Duodenal: pain 2–4 h after meals, nocturnal, relieved by food/milk/alkali ('painful hunger')
Gastric: pain soon after meals, aggravated by food, nausea, weight loss
Dyspepsia, heartburn
ex: Signs of complications: anaemia, peritonitis, gastric clapotage
lab: H. pylori testing (urea breath test, stool antigen, biopsy urease, serology)
CBC, gastrin if Zollinger-Ellison suspected (refractory, multiple, atypical ulcers + diarrhoea)
img: Upper GI endoscopy = main diagnostic method (+ biopsy of every gastric ulcer – exclude cancer)
Barium meal: niche (now rarely used)
tx: Medical: PPI, H2 blockers; H. pylori eradication (PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin/metronidazole); stop NSAIDs
Surgery for complications (perforation, bleeding, stenosis), intractability or suspicion of malignancy
Gastric ulcer: gastric resection including ulcer (Billroth I) ± vagotomy depending on Johnson type
Duodenal ulcer: vagotomy (truncal + drainage, selective, highly selective) or antrectomy + truncal vagotomy; Finsterer exclusion-resection for difficult post-bulbar ulcers
cx: Bleeding (most frequent cause of UGIB = duodenal ulcer)
oth: Johnson: I lesser curvature (most frequent, low acid), II gastric + duodenal, III prepyloric, IV juxtacardial (high on lesser curvature), V anywhere – NSAIDs
Truncal vagotomy → gastroparesis/pyloric spasm → needs drainage (pyloroplasty/gastroenterostomy); highly selective (supraselective) does not
DD: gastric cancer (essential), GERD, biliary lithiasis, pancreatitis

paths.def: Free perforation of a (mostly anterior duodenal) ulcer into the peritoneal cavity → chemical then bacterial generalized peritonitis.
sx: Sudden, violent epigastric 'dagger-like' pain, then generalized
Often history of ulcer (may be absent)
Vomiting, shoulder-tip pain
Fever is NOT an early sign (appears later with bacterial peritonitis)
ex: 'Board-like'/wooden abdomen (muscular contracture) – does not follow respiratory movements
Absent bowel sounds; Douglas pouch tenderness on rectal exam
lab: Amylase (DD pancreatitis), electrolytes, renal function, lactate
img: Erect chest/abdominal X-ray: pneumoperitoneum (free air under diaphragm) in ~75%
CT if doubt – free air, fluid; water-soluble contrast leak
No endoscopy / no barium
tx: Pre-op: nasogastric aspiration, IV fluids, PPI IV, broad-spectrum antibiotics, analgesia, urinary catheter, urgent transfer to surgery
Surgery (open or laparoscopic): closure of perforation with omental (Graham) patch + abundant peritoneal lavage + drainage
Excision/biopsy of gastric ulcer (cancer); definitive procedure (resection) only in selected stable patients
Conservative (Taylor) treatment only in sealed perforation, high-risk patient, without peritonitis
oth: Cardinal signs: pain, contracture/tenderness, ulcer history, pneumoperitoneum (Mondor triad: pain, contracture, ulcer history)

paths.def: Chronic complication of relapsing peri-pyloric/duodenal ulcers (scarring) – or antro-pyloric cancer. Leads to gastric dilation, vomiting and hypochloremic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (Darrow syndrome).
sx: Postprandial abundant vomiting of food ingested many hours/days earlier, without bile
Epigastric fullness, early satiety, belching (foul)
Weight loss, dehydration, oliguria
Stages: compensated (hyperkinetic) → decompensated (atonic)
ex: Visible peristalsis (Kussmaul sign) in early stages
lab: Hypochloremia, hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, metabolic alkalosis (Darrow syndrome) – NOT hypocalcaemia
img: Upper endoscopy + biopsy (benign vs malignant) after gastric lavage
Barium meal: dilated 'basin-shaped' stomach, delayed emptying, stenosis
Plain X-ray: large gastric air-fluid level
tx: Correction first: rehydration, K+, Cl–, nutrition, nasogastric aspiration/lavage – surgery is not an emergency
Endoscopic balloon dilation in high-risk patients
Surgery: gastric resection (Billroth I/II) ± vagotomy = optimal; gastro-enterostomy (bypass) in frail patients; feeding jejunostomy/gastrostomy in particular cases
oth: DD: antro-pyloric cancer (must be excluded by biopsy)

paths.def: Mostly adenocarcinoma (intestinal vs diffuse – Lauren). Risk factors: H. pylori, smoked/salted food, smoking, atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, adenomatous polyps, gastric stump, Ménétrier, pernicious anaemia, hereditary (CDH1, HNPCC).
sx: Early: asymptomatic or vague dyspepsia
Epigastric pain, loss of appetite (aversion to meat), weight loss, fatigue
Anaemia, melena/hematemesis
Dysphagia (cardia), vomiting (antral → outlet obstruction)
ex: Virchow node (left supraclavicular), Sister Mary Joseph (umbilical), Blumer shelf on rectal exam, Krukenberg (ovaries)
lab: Tumour markers CEA, CA 19-9, CA 72-4 (follow-up, not diagnosis)
img: Upper endoscopy + multiple biopsies = most accurate diagnosis
Staging: thoraco-abdominal CT, endoscopic US (T, N), staging laparoscopy (peritoneal spread), PET-CT selected
Barium meal: filling defect, rigidity, niche
tx: Early gastric cancer (mucosa/submucosa, no LN): EMR/ESD
Radical: subtotal (distal tumours) or total gastrectomy (proximal/diffuse) with D2 lymphadenectomy; Roux-en-Y reconstruction
Perioperative chemotherapy (FLOT) for ≥T2 or N+
Palliation: gastro-jejunostomy, stent, palliative resection for bleeding, chemotherapy
cx: Postgastrectomy: anastomotic leak, duodenal stump fistula, dumping, anaemia (B12)
oth: Early gastric cancer = adenocarcinoma confined to mucosa or submucosa regardless of lymph node status
Spread: lymphatic, haematogenous (liver), peritoneal, direct
Borrmann I–IV macroscopic classification; Siewert I–III for GEJ tumours

paths.def: Persistence of the vitello-intestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct – true diverticulum on antimesenteric border of ileum. 'Rule of 2': 2% population, 2 feet from ileocecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric, pancreatic), symptoms <2 years.
sx: Often asymptomatic
Painless lower GI bleeding in children (ectopic gastric mucosa → ulcer)
Mimics appendicitis (Meckel diverticulitis)
Intestinal obstruction (intussusception, volvulus around fibrous band)
img: 99mTc-pertechnetate scintigraphy (Meckel scan) – detects ectopic gastric mucosa
CT/ angiography in active bleeding
Often found at laparoscopy/laparotomy
tx: Symptomatic: diverticulectomy – wedge or segmental ileal resection (segmental if base is wide or ulcer in adjacent ileum)
Incidental: resection debated (young patients, narrow base, palpable ectopic tissue)
cx: Littre hernia (Meckel in a hernia sac)
oth: Most common congenital GI anomaly

paths.def: Chronic transmural granulomatous inflammation, any segment mouth→anus, discontinuous 'skip lesions'; terminal ileum most affected.
sx: Insidious onset; abdominal cramps, chronic (non-bloody) diarrhoea
Weight loss, fever, fatigue
Perianal disease: fistulas, fissures, abscesses, skin tags
Extra-intestinal: arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, PSC (less than UC)
lab: Faecal calprotectin, ASCA+, B12 deficiency (ileal disease)
img: Ileocolonoscopy + biopsies (non-caseating granulomas)
CT/MR enterography: wall thickening, 'string sign' of Kantor, fistulas, abscess
Cobblestone mucosa, aphthous ulcers
tx: Medical first: 5-ASA/sulfasalazine, corticosteroids, immunomodulators (azathioprine), anti-TNF biologics, antibiotics
Surgery only for complications – operative treatment is palliative, principle = conservatism (bowel-sparing)
Indications: obstruction/stricture, abscess, fistulas, perforation, bleeding, cancer, failure of medical therapy
Procedures: limited segmental resection (ileocecal resection/right hemicolectomy), strictureplasty (Heineke-Mikulicz, Finney), percutaneous abscess drainage; endoscopic stricture dilation
cx: Short bowel syndrome after repeated resections
oth: DD with UC: transmural vs mucosal, skip lesions vs continuous, ileum vs rectum always involved, fistulas, granulomas

paths.def: Abrupt suppression of intestinal blood flow: arterial embolism (SMA – AF, post-cardioversion), arterial thrombosis (atherosclerosis), venous thrombosis, non-occlusive (low-flow). Stages: apoplexy → infarction → gangrene.
sx: Severe diffuse abdominal pain out of proportion to clinical findings
Vomiting, diarrhoea (may be bloody), then ileus
Rapid deterioration, shock
Context: atrial fibrillation, recent cardioversion, MI, vascular disease, elderly
ex: Initially soft abdomen with little tenderness ('pain > signs')
Later distension, absent bowel sounds, peritonitis signs
lab: Marked leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis, high lactate
img: CT angiography = investigation of choice (vessel occlusion, bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas)
Plain X-ray: non-specific, late gasless abdomen/ileus
Mesenteric angiography (diagnostic + therapeutic)
tx: Rapid resuscitation, metabolic rebalancing, heparin, antibiotics
Emergency laparotomy: revascularisation (SMA embolectomy, bypass, endovascular) + resection of necrotic loops (enterectomy)
Second-look laparotomy at 24–48 h
Venous thrombosis: anticoagulation ± resection
cx: Sepsis, multiple organ failure; high mortality
oth: Stages: apoplexy (reversible) → infarction proper → gangrene (greenish-grey, limp, perforated loop)

paths.def: Malabsorption after extensive small bowel loss (<200 cm remaining). Causes – adults: mesenteric ischemia, Crohn's, volvulus, trauma; children: atresia, volvulus, necrotizing enterocolitis.
sx: Diarrhoea, steatorrhea, dehydration
Weight loss, malnutrition
Vitamin/mineral deficiencies
lab: B12 deficiency and bile-salt malabsorption after ileal resection
img: Contrast studies to assess remaining length
tx: Parenteral nutrition → progressive enteral feeding (intestinal adaptation)
Antidiarrhoeals, PPI, somatostatin analogues, GLP-2 analogue (teduglutide)
Surgery: bowel lengthening (Bianchi, STEP), intestinal transplantation
oth: More severe: absence of ileocecal valve, absence of colon, ileal resection

paths.def: Rare. Benign: adenomas, leiomyoma, lipoma, hamartomas (Peutz-Jeghers). Malignant: adenocarcinoma (duodenum), neuroendocrine/carcinoid (ileum), lymphoma, GIST.
sx: Vague pain, occult bleeding, anaemia
Intermittent obstruction / intussusception
Carcinoid syndrome (liver metastases): flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm, right heart valve disease
img: Capsule endoscopy, double-balloon enteroscopy
CT/MR enterography; octreotide/Ga-DOTATATE PET for NET
tx: Wide segmental resection with adjacent mesentery and lymph nodes (malignant)
Pancreatoduodenectomy for duodenal adenocarcinoma
Imatinib for GIST; somatostatin analogues for NET
oth: Intramural lesions causing obstruction: tumours, intramural haematoma, Crohn's

paths.def: Adenocarcinoma arising mostly from adenomatous polyps (adenoma–carcinoma sequence). Risk: age >50, FAP, Lynch (HNPCC), IBD (UC), personal/family history, red/processed meat, obesity.
sx: Right colon: anaemia (iron deficiency), fatigue, palpable mass, fever, weight loss – obstruction late
Left colon: change in bowel habits, constipation alternating with diarrhoea, pencil-thin stools, rectorrhagia/haematochezia, obstruction
Complications as first presentation: obstruction, perforation, bleeding
lab: CBC: microcytic anaemia; faecal occult blood
img: Colonoscopy + biopsy = gold standard (also detects synchronous lesions)
Staging: CT thorax-abdomen-pelvis; liver MRI if doubtful
CT colonography; barium enema: 'apple core' lesion
tx: Radical resection with en-bloc mesentery & lymphadenectomy (≥12 nodes): right hemicolectomy (caecum, ascending, hepatic flexure), extended right/transverse colectomy, left hemicolectomy, sigmoidectomy
Obstructing tumours: right – resection + primary ileo-transverse anastomosis; left – Hartmann procedure, stent as bridge to surgery, or resection with anastomosis ± protective stoma
Adjuvant chemotherapy (FOLFOX/CAPOX) for stage III (and high-risk II)
Liver/lung metastases: resection when possible
cx: Obstruction, perforation (tumoral or diastatic caecal), bleeding
oth: Not pre-neoplastic: diverticulosis, intermittent sigmoid volvulus, melanosis coli
Pre-neoplastic: adenomas, FAP, Lynch, UC, Crohn's colitis
TNM / Dukes staging

paths.def: Chronic idiopathic inflammation limited to mucosa/submucosa, starting in rectum and extending continuously proximally. More frequent in non-smokers.
sx: Bloody diarrhoea with mucus, rectal bleeding – most common symptoms
Tenesmus, urgency, crampy abdominal pain
Fever, weight loss in severe forms
Extra-intestinal: arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, primary sclerosing cholangitis
ex: Toxic megacolon: distension, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis
lab: p-ANCA +; stool cultures and C. difficile to exclude infection
img: Colonoscopy + biopsies: continuous lesions, ulcers, inflammatory pseudopolyps
Plain X-ray: toxic megacolon (transverse colon >6 cm)
Barium enema (not in acute phase): 'lead-pipe' colon
tx: Medical: 5-ASA/sulfasalazine, corticosteroids, azathioprine, cyclosporine, biologics (anti-TNF)
Surgery: total proctocolectomy – curative
Elective: restorative proctocolectomy with ileal J-pouch anal anastomosis (IPAA); or proctocolectomy + permanent ileostomy
Emergency (fulminant colitis, toxic megacolon, perforation, massive haemorrhage): subtotal colectomy + end ileostomy, rectal stump left
cx: Colorectal cancer – risk increases with duration, extent, early age at onset, PSC
oth: Surgical indications: failure of medical treatment, dysplasia/cancer, growth retardation in children, severe extra-intestinal manifestations, complications

paths.def: Diverticulosis = acquired false diverticula (mucosa herniating through weak points where vasa recta penetrate), mostly sigmoid; low-fibre diet, high intraluminal pressure. Diverticulitis = inflammation/micro-perforation.
sx: Diverticulosis: mostly asymptomatic; may bleed (painless lower GI bleeding)
Diverticulitis: LLQ pain ('left-sided appendicitis'), may radiate suprapubic
Fever, chills, change in bowel habits, urinary urgency/dysuria (bladder irritation)
Pneumaturia, fecaluria in colo-vesical fistula
img: CT with contrast = preferred test (wall thickening, abscess, free air) – Hinchey staging
Avoid colonoscopy and barium enema in acute phase; water-soluble contrast if needed
Colonoscopy 6–8 weeks after episode to exclude cancer
tx: Uncomplicated: fibre-rich diet, antibiotics (outpatient or IV), fluids
Abscess >4 cm: CT-guided percutaneous drainage
Hinchey III–IV: emergency surgery – Hartmann procedure (sigmoidectomy + end colostomy) or resection with primary anastomosis ± protective ileostomy; laparoscopic lavage in selected III
Elective sigmoid resection/left hemicolectomy after recurrent or complicated episodes, fistula, stricture
oth: Hinchey: I pericolic/mesenteric abscess, II walled-off pelvic/distant abscess, III generalized purulent peritonitis, IV generalized faecal peritonitis

paths.def: Torsion of a colonic segment around its mesentery – sigmoid (most frequent; elderly, constipation, long mesentery) or caecum.
sx: Sudden colicky pain, marked asymmetric distension
Absent stool and gas, late vomiting
ex: Huge tympanic distension, 'ovoid' asymmetric abdomen (von Wahl sign)
img: Plain X-ray: 'coffee bean'/'bent inner tube' sign
CT: whirl sign; contrast enema: 'bird's beak'
tx: Sigmoid without ischemia: endoscopic (sigmoidoscopic) detorsion + rectal tube, then elective sigmoidectomy
Gangrene/failure: emergency sigmoidectomy – Hartmann procedure
Caecal volvulus: right hemicolectomy
oth: Intermittent sigmoid volvulus is NOT pre-neoplastic

paths.def: Pathological enlargement/prolapse of anal vascular cushions (arteriovenous plexuses). Internal – above dentate line (painless); external – below dentate line. Secondary haemorrhoids: portal hypertension, rectal tumour.
sx: Painless bright red bleeding with defecation (on stool/paper)
Prolapse, itching, mucus discharge
Pain only if thrombosis (external) or strangulation
img: Anoscopy/rectoscopy; colonoscopy in >40–50 years or alarm signs to exclude cancer
tx: Grade I–II: diet (fibre, fluids), venotonic drugs, topical; rubber-band ligation (internal only), sclerotherapy, infrared coagulation
Grade III–IV: hemorrhoidectomy (Milligan-Morgan open, Ferguson closed), stapled hemorrhoidopexy (Longo – grade III), Doppler-guided ligation (HAL-RAR), ultrasonic/bipolar/laser
Thrombosed external: excision/incision under local anaesthesia (<72 h) or conservative
cx: Post-op: pain, urinary retention, bleeding, anal stenosis, incontinence
oth: Goligher grading: I no prolapse, II prolapse with spontaneous reduction, III manual reduction, IV irreducible
Rubber band ligation is NOT for external haemorrhoids (painful – somatic innervation)

paths.def: Radial tear in the anoderm below the dentate line, mostly posterior midline; driven by internal sphincter hypertonia. Chronic (>6 weeks): sentinel pile, hypertrophied papilla, exposed sphincter fibres.
sx: Severe sharp pain during and after defecation (lasting hours)
Small amount of bright red blood
Constipation (fear of defecation)
ex: Gentle separation of buttocks: posterior midline fissure, sentinel tag
Digital exam painful – avoid in acute phase / under anaesthesia
Off-midline fissures → think Crohn's, TB, HIV, syphilis, cancer
img: Anoscopy when tolerated; endoscopy for atypical fissures
tx: Conservative: fibre, stool softeners, sitz baths, topical nitroglycerin (GTN) or diltiazem, botulinum toxin
Surgery for chronic/refractory: lateral internal sphincterotomy (gold standard) ± fissurectomy

paths.def: Cryptoglandular infection (anal gland cryptitis) → abscess (acute phase) → fistula (chronic phase). Parks classification of fistulas: inter-, trans-, supra-, extrasphincteric.
sx: Abscess: constant throbbing perianal pain, swelling, fever
Fistula: chronic purulent/bloody discharge, perianal itching, recurring abscesses
ex: External opening; Goodsall's rule (posterior openings → curved tract to posterior midline; anterior → radial)
Digital exam: indurated tract, internal opening
img: MRI pelvis = study of choice for complex fistulas
Endoanal ultrasound, fistulography, probing under anaesthesia
tx: Abscess: urgent surgical incision & drainage (antibiotics alone insufficient)
Fistula: fistulotomy (laying open tract end-to-end – low/simple fistulas)
Fistulectomy – removal of entire fibrotic tract
Seton (cutting or draining loose seton, sequential ligatures) for high/trans-sphincteric fistulas
Sphincter-sparing: advancement flap, LIFT, fibrin glue/plug
oth: Abscess types: perianal, ischio-rectal, intersphincteric, supralevator

paths.def: Chronic inflammatory cavity in the sacrococcygeal cleft containing hair and debris; young hirsute men.
sx: Pain, swelling in natal cleft
Recurrent purulent discharge
ex: Midline pits in natal cleft, abscess or draining sinus
img: Not usually needed
tx: Acute abscess: incision and drainage (off-midline)
Chronic: excision left open to heal by secondary intention, or primary closure / off-midline flap (Karydakis, Limberg)

paths.def: Adenocarcinoma within 15 cm of the anal verge. Local staging (MRI) drives neoadjuvant therapy and choice of operation.
sx: Rectal bleeding (rectorrhagia), mucus
Tenesmus, sensation of incomplete evacuation, change in bowel habits, pencil-thin stools
Pain (sphincter/sacral invasion), weight loss, anaemia
ex: Digital rectal exam – palpable tumour, distance from anal verge, fixity
img: Colonoscopy/rigid rectoscopy + biopsy
Pelvic MRI (T, N, circumferential resection margin) – key
Endorectal ultrasound for early T1–T2
CT thorax/abdomen for metastases
tx: T1 (low risk): local excision (TEM/TAMIS)
Locally advanced (T3–4, N+): neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, then surgery
Total mesorectal excision (TME) via low anterior resection with colo-rectal/colo-anal anastomosis ± protective ileostomy
Abdominoperineal resection (Miles) with definitive colostomy: invasion of anal sphincters, very low tumour, poor sphincter tone
Hartmann procedure for frail/obstructed; adjuvant chemotherapy
cx: Post-op: anastomotic leak, LARS, urinary/sexual dysfunction (pelvic nerves)
oth: Rectal prolapse + anaemia + palpable tumour → cancer until proven otherwise

paths.def: Stones in the gallbladder – cholesterol (most), pigment (haemolysis), mixed. Risk factors: '5F' female, fat, forty, fertile, fair; pregnancy, oral contraceptives, rapid weight loss, haemolytic disease, ileal resection.
sx: Asymptomatic in most
Biliary colic: RUQ/epigastric pain after fatty meals, radiating to right scapula/shoulder, lasting <6 h, nausea, vomiting
Dyspepsia, bloating, fatty food intolerance
ex: RUQ tenderness during colic; Murphy sign negative between attacks
lab: Usually normal; LFTs, amylase/lipase, bilirubin to exclude complications
img: Transabdominal US = first-line (hyperechoic stones with acoustic shadow, mobile; bile duct diameter)
MRCP if CBD stones suspected; EUS
tx: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy = standard for symptomatic lithiasis
Critical view of safety; open conversion if needed
Asymptomatic: surgery in porcelain gallbladder, stones >3 cm, polyps >1 cm, haemolytic disease, before bariatric surgery/transplant, diabetics (selected)
cx: Acute cholecystitis, hydrops, empyema, gangrene, perforation
Bilio-digestive fistula, gallstone ileus (Bouveret), Mirizzi syndrome
oth: Cholecystectomy complications: bile duct injury (Strasberg), bile leak, bleeding, retained stones

paths.def: Acute inflammation of the gallbladder wall, >90% due to stone impacted in cystic duct (calculous); acalculous in ICU/critically ill patients.
sx: Persistent RUQ pain >6 h radiating to right shoulder
Fever, nausea, vomiting
Mild jaundice possible (oedema, Mirizzi)
ex: Murphy sign positive (inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation)
lab: Mild elevation of LFTs/bilirubin; amylase (associated pancreatitis)
img: US: thickened wall >3–4 mm (double contour), pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy, impacted stone
CT if complications/doubt; HIDA scan (non-filling) if US equivocal
tx: Nil per os, IV fluids, analgesia, antibiotics
Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy – ideally within 24–72 h (Tokyo Guidelines)
High-risk / severe: percutaneous cholecystostomy, then delayed cholecystectomy
cx: Empyema, gangrene, perforation → biliary peritonitis or pericholecystic abscess
oth: Tokyo grading: I mild, II moderate, III severe (organ dysfunction)

paths.def: Stones in the common bile duct (secondary from gallbladder or primary). Cholangitis = biliary obstruction + bacterial infection of the bile ducts.
sx: Biliary colic + obstructive jaundice (fluctuating), dark urine, pale stools, pruritus
Charcot's triad: RUQ pain, fever with chills, jaundice
Reynolds' pentad: + hypotension/shock + altered mental status (severe suppurative cholangitis)
ex: Non-palpable gallbladder usually (Courvoisier rule – a palpable painless gallbladder suggests malignancy)
lab: Cholestasis: raised direct bilirubin, ALP, GGT; ALT/AST mild
img: US: dilated CBD (>6–8 mm), stones
MRCP (non-invasive diagnostic), EUS
ERCP: diagnostic + therapeutic; PTC if ERCP fails; aerobilia may appear after ERCP/sphincterotomy, stents, bilio-enteric fistulas
tx: Cholangitis: resuscitation, IV antibiotics, urgent biliary decompression (ERCP with sphincterotomy & stone extraction / stent; PTBD if fails)
CBD stones: ERCP + endoscopic sphincterotomy, then laparoscopic cholecystectomy; or one-stage laparoscopic CBD exploration (transcystic or choledochotomy with T-tube)
Large/impacted stones: lithotripsy; bilio-digestive anastomosis (choledochoduodenostomy, hepaticojejunostomy) in selected cases
oth: Tokyo guidelines for cholangitis grading

paths.def: Cholangiocarcinoma – intrahepatic, perihilar (Klatskin – Bismuth-Corlette I–IV), distal. Gallbladder carcinoma – usually adenocarcinoma, associated with large stones, porcelain gallbladder, polyps >1 cm, anomalous pancreatico-biliary junction.
sx: Painless progressive obstructive jaundice, pruritus, weight loss
Gallbladder cancer: often incidental or RUQ pain, mass, change in usual biliary symptoms
ex: Courvoisier-Terrier sign (palpable non-tender gallbladder) in distal obstruction
img: US, CT, MRCP; ERCP/PTC with brushing/stenting
EUS ± FNA
tx: Distal CBD: cephalic duodenopancreatectomy (Whipple)
Hilar: bile duct resection + (extended) hepatectomy + lymphadenectomy; liver transplant in selected
Gallbladder cancer: radical/extended cholecystectomy (+ segments IVb–V, lymphadenectomy); re-resection if incidental ≥T1b
Palliation: endoscopic/percutaneous stents, bilio-digestive bypass, chemotherapy
cx: Gallbladder cancer frequently invades liver parenchyma

paths.def: Jaundice classified as prehepatic (haemolytic – spherocytosis, sickle cell, thalassaemia), hepatic (hepatocellular), and posthepatic/obstructive (stones, tumours, strictures).
sx: Obstructive: dark urine, acholic stools, pruritus
Painful + fever → stones/cholangitis; painless + weight loss → malignancy
lab: Prehepatic: unconjugated bilirubin, reticulocytes, LDH, low haptoglobin
Obstructive: high conjugated bilirubin, ALP, GGT, 5'-nucleotidase (ALT not part of cholestatic syndrome)
img: US first (dilated ducts?) → MRCP/CT → ERCP/EUS/PTC
tx: Treat the cause; biliary drainage for cholangitis or pre-operative in selected cases
oth: Cholestasis most commonly due to biliary tract obstruction

paths.def: Parasitic cyst caused by Echinococcus granulosus larva (dog = definitive host; humans/sheep intermediate). Liver most frequently affected (~70%), then lung. Wall: pericyst (host), ectocyst (laminated), endocyst (germinal).
sx: Long asymptomatic period
RUQ pain/heaviness, hepatomegaly, dyspepsia
Complications: jaundice/cholangitis, fever (infection), anaphylaxis (rupture)
ex: Jaundice if biliary rupture; peritonitis/shock if free rupture
img: US = first line – Gharbi classification
CT/MRI: daughter cysts, calcifications, biliary communication
ERCP for cysto-biliary fistula
tx: Albendazole (benzimidazole) peri-operatively / alone for small cysts
PAIR (puncture–aspiration–injection of scolicide–reaspiration) for Gharbi I–II
Surgery – conservative: partial pericystectomy/unroofing (Lagrot) – most frequent; radical: total pericystectomy or hepatectomy
Protect field with scolicidal-soaked pads; treat biliary fistulas
cx: Rupture into biliary tree (cholangitis, jaundice), free peritoneal rupture (anaphylactic shock, echinococcosis), into thorax/bronchi
oth: Gharbi: I pure fluid, II detached membrane (water-lily), III multivesicular/daughter cysts, IV heterogeneous solid, V calcified wall (inactive)
Biopsy/puncture forbidden without precautions (anaphylaxis, dissemination)

paths.def: Pyogenic: biliary route most frequent (cholangitis), portal (appendicitis, diverticulitis – pylephlebitis), arterial, direct, cryptogenic; E. coli, Klebsiella, anaerobes. Amoebic: Entamoeba histolytica via portal vein.
sx: Fever with chills, RUQ pain, malaise, weight loss
Jaundice in biliary cause
Amoebic: recent travel, dysentery history
ex: Tender hepatomegaly, pain on percussion of liver
img: US/CT: hypoechoic/hypodense lesion with rim enhancement, gas
Chest X-ray: elevated right hemidiaphragm
tx: Pyogenic: IV antibiotics + percutaneous US/CT-guided drainage; surgical drainage if multiloculated, rupture, failure; treat source
Amoebic: metronidazole (drainage rarely needed) + luminal agent
oth: Biliary mechanism is most frequent cause of pyogenic abscess

paths.def: Haemangioma (most common, vascular), focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH – central scar), hepatocellular adenoma (young women on OCP – risk of rupture/malignancy), simple cysts, biliary cystadenoma, adult polycystic liver disease (autosomal dominant).
sx: Mostly incidental
Large lesions: RUQ pain, fullness
Adenoma: acute pain/shock from haemorrhage
ex: Usually normal; hepatomegaly with large lesions
img: US first; contrast CT/MRI characterise: haemangioma – peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in; FNH – arterial enhancement + central scar; adenoma – heterogeneous, hepatobiliary-phase hypointense
tx: Haemangioma, FNH: observation (surgery only if symptomatic/complicated)
Adenoma: stop OCP; resection if >5 cm, men, growth, bleeding (surgery indicated even if asymptomatic)
Biliary cyst/cystadenoma: resection (malignant potential)
Simple/polycystic: laparoscopic unroofing + fenestration if symptomatic; transplant in severe PCLD
oth: No biopsy of haemangioma (bleeding); avoid biopsy of resectable HCC (needle-tract seeding)

paths.def: HCC: primary liver cancer on cirrhosis (HBV, HCV, alcohol, NASH, aflatoxin, haemochromatosis). Metastases (colorectal most frequent) are the commonest malignant liver lesions.
sx: Often asymptomatic (surveillance in cirrhosis)
RUQ pain, weight loss, decompensation of cirrhosis (ascites, jaundice)
Rupture → haemoperitoneum
img: US screening every 6 months in cirrhosis
Multiphase CT/MRI: arterial hyperenhancement with portal/delayed washout = diagnostic for HCC (biopsy often not needed)
Colorectal metastases: CT/MRI, PET-CT
tx: Radical (curative): liver resection (Child A, adequate remnant), liver transplantation (Milan criteria: 1 nodule ≤5 cm or ≤3 nodules ≤3 cm, no vascular invasion), ablation (RFA/microwave) for small tumours
Palliative: TACE, SIRT, systemic therapy (sorafenib, atezolizumab-bevacizumab)
Metastases: resection ± chemotherapy, ablation
cx: Rupture, portal vein thrombosis, liver failure
oth: Couinaud: 8 segments based on portal/hepatic artery branching; Cantlie line (gallbladder fossa–IVC) separates right and left liver (surgical); falciform ligament = anatomical division
Segment I (caudate) not visible on anterior surface

paths.def: Portal pressure gradient >5 mmHg (clinically significant ≥10); mostly due to cirrhosis (intrahepatic); pre-hepatic (portal vein thrombosis) and post-hepatic (Budd-Chiari).
sx: Haematemesis/melena from oesophageal/gastric varices
Ascites, encephalopathy, jaundice
Splenomegaly (hypersplenism)
ex: Stigmata of chronic liver disease: spider naevi, palmar erythema, caput medusae, gynaecomastia
img: Endoscopy: diagnosis and therapy of varices
Doppler US: portal flow, thrombosis; CT
tx: Acute bleeding: resuscitation (restrictive transfusion), vasoactive drugs (terlipressin, somatostatin/octreotide), antibiotic prophylaxis, PPI
Endoscopic band ligation (first line) or sclerotherapy
Balloon tamponade (Sengstaken-Blakemore) as bridge
TIPSS for refractory bleeding; surgical portosystemic shunts (selective – Warren distal splenorenal; non-selective) rarely
Prevention: non-selective beta-blockers + ligation; liver transplantation definitive

paths.def: Acute inflammatory process of the pancreas from premature intra-pancreatic activation of enzymes – trypsin plays the central role. Causes: gallstones (CBD migration) and alcohol (most frequent), hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroidism), ERCP, drugs, trauma, mumps, ascariasis, idiopathic.
sx: Pain – most constant symptom: severe epigastric, sudden onset, steady, 'belt-like', radiating to the back and both upper quadrants
Nausea, vomiting (not relieving pain)
Fever, shock in severe forms
ex: Grey-Turner (flank) and Cullen (periumbilical) signs – haemorrhagic forms
lab: CRP (>150 mg/L at 48 h → severe), WBC, Hct, BUN, glucose, calcium, LDH, triglycerides, LFTs (biliary cause)
img: US at admission: gallstones, CBD dilation
Contrast CT (after 72 h) – most accurate for necrosis and collections; Balthazar score (CT-based)
MRCP/EUS for occult biliary cause; X-ray: sentinel loop, colon cut-off
tx: Supportive: aggressive goal-directed fluid resuscitation, analgesia (avoid morphine – spasm of Oddi; use pethidine/metamizole/procaine), O2, early enteral nutrition
Antibiotics only for infected necrosis
Biliary pancreatitis with cholangitis/persistent obstruction: urgent ERCP + sphincterotomy; cholecystectomy in same admission (mild)
Step-up approach for infected necrosis: antibiotics → percutaneous/endoscopic drainage → minimally invasive/surgical necrosectomy, postponed ≥4 weeks (walled-off)
Edematous (interstitial) pancreatitis does not require surgery
cx: Local: acute peripancreatic fluid collection, pseudocyst (>4 weeks), acute necrotic collection, walled-off necrosis, infected necrosis, abscess, haemorrhage, splenic vein thrombosis
Systemic: SIRS, ARDS, renal failure, shock, MODS, hypocalcaemia
oth: Atlanta revised diagnosis: 2 of 3 – typical pain, enzymes >3× ULN, characteristic CT/MRI/US findings

Ranson criteria at admission: age >55, WBC >16 000, glucose >200 mg/dL, LDH >350, AST >250; at 48 h: Hct drop >10%, BUN rise >5, Ca <8 mg/dL, PaO2 <60 mmHg, base deficit >4, fluid sequestration >6 L – amylase is NOT part of Ranson
Severity: mild, moderately severe (transient organ failure <48 h / local cx), severe (persistent organ failure)
Surgical indications: infected necrosis/irreversible sepsis, failure of supportive treatment, abdominal compartment, perforation/doubtful diagnosis (perforated ulcer), abscess, haemorrhage

paths.def: Fluid collection with a well-defined wall of fibrous/granulation tissue without epithelial lining, persisting >4 weeks after acute (or in chronic) pancreatitis; usually communicates with pancreatic ducts and contains pancreatic juice.
sx: Persistent epigastric pain, fullness, early satiety
Nausea, vomiting (gastric compression), jaundice (biliary compression)
img: CT/MRI; EUS (drainage guidance, exclude cystic neoplasm)
tx: Asymptomatic: observation (many resolve)
Symptomatic/complicated (>6 weeks, mature wall): internal drainage – endoscopic transgastric/transduodenal (EUS-guided) first line
Surgical: cysto-gastrostomy, cysto-duodenostomy, cysto-jejunostomy on Roux-en-Y loop (best results)
External drainage only if infected/immature
oth: False: pseudocyst has its own epithelial wall

paths.def: Progressive irreversible fibrosis with loss of exocrine and endocrine function; alcohol is the most common cause (~70%); also obstructive, hereditary, tropical, autoimmune, idiopathic.
sx: Recurrent/chronic epigastric pain radiating to back
Steatorrhea, weight loss (exocrine insufficiency)
Diabetes mellitus (endocrine insufficiency)
lab: Faecal elastase low, glucose high; amylase may be normal
img: CT: pancreatic calcifications (typical), atrophy, dilated irregular Wirsung ('chain of lakes')
MRCP, EUS; plain X-ray calcifications
tx: Stop alcohol/smoking, analgesia, pancreatic enzyme replacement, insulin
Endoscopic: sphincterotomy, stone extraction/ESWL, stents
Surgery for intractable pain/complications: drainage – Partington-Rochelle/Puestow (longitudinal pancreatico-jejunostomy) for dilated duct; resection – Whipple, Beger, Frey (head-dominant)
cx: Pseudocyst, biliary/duodenal stenosis, splenic vein thrombosis

paths.def: Ductal adenocarcinoma (~90%), mostly head (60–70%). Risk: smoking, chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, obesity, hereditary syndromes, IPMN.
sx: Head: painless progressive obstructive jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools
Body/tail: epigastric pain radiating to back, late diagnosis
Weight loss, anorexia, new-onset diabetes, Trousseau migratory thrombophlebitis
ex: Courvoisier-Terrier sign: palpable, non-tender distended gallbladder with jaundice (head cancer, ampulla)
lab: CA 19-9 (marker), cholestasis enzymes, high conjugated bilirubin
img: Pancreatic-protocol contrast CT = staging & resectability
'Double duct sign' (dilated CBD + Wirsung) on CT, MRI/MRCP, ERCP
EUS + FNA for tissue; ERCP stenting for cholangitis
tx: Resectable head: cephalic duodenopancreatectomy (Whipple) – elective procedure; pylorus-preserving variant
Body/tail: distal (corporeo-caudal) splenopancreatectomy; total pancreatectomy when diffuse
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for borderline; adjuvant FOLFIRINOX/gemcitabine
Unresectable (liver metastases, peritoneal carcinomatosis, SMA/celiac encasement): palliation – biliary drainage (stent or hepatico-jejunostomy on Roux-en-Y), gastro-jejunostomy, celiac plexus block
cx: Post-Whipple: pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying, haemorrhage
oth: Invasion of portal/superior mesenteric vein may be resected; SMA invasion = contraindication

paths.def: Insulinoma (most common, usually benign – Whipple triad), gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison – gastrinoma triangle), glucagonoma, VIPoma, non-functioning; MEN 1 association.
sx: Insulinoma: fasting hypoglycaemia, neuroglycopenic symptoms relieved by glucose
Gastrinoma: refractory/multiple/atypical peptic ulcers (distal duodenum, jejunum), diarrhoea, recurrence after acid-reducing surgery
lab: Gastrinoma: high fasting gastrin, secretin test; chromogranin A
img: CT/MRI, EUS, Ga-DOTATATE PET
tx: Enucleation (insulinoma) or pancreatic resection; PPIs for gastrinoma; somatostatin analogues

paths.def: Spleen = most frequently injured solid organ in blunt abdominal trauma. AAST grades I–V.
sx: LUQ pain, left shoulder pain (Kehr sign – diaphragmatic irritation)
Signs of hypovolaemia: pallor, dyspnoea, tachycardia, hypotension
Delayed (two-time) rupture after subcapsular haematoma
ex: LUQ tenderness, abdominal distension, peritoneal signs
lab: Falling Hb/Hct, blood group & cross-match, lactate
img: FAST in emergency room (haemoperitoneum)
Contrast CT in stable patients: laceration, intraparenchymal/subcapsular/perisplenic haematoma, haemoperitoneum, active contrast extravasation (blush)
tx: Haemodynamically stable: non-operative management (ICU monitoring) ± angioembolisation
Unstable / hypovolaemic shock / failed NOM: emergency laparotomy – splenectomy or spleen-preserving surgery (splenorrhaphy, partial splenectomy, mesh wrap)
Post-splenectomy vaccination (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus)
cx: Thrombocytosis, subphrenic abscess, pancreatic tail injury
oth: Absolute vital indications for splenectomy: ruptured splenic artery aneurysm, intraperitoneal bleeding from splenic trauma with instability

paths.def: Spleen functions: filtration, immunity (opsonins, IgM), platelet storage (1/3). Hypersplenism = splenomegaly + cytopenias + bone-marrow compensation.
sx: Anaemia, bleeding (thrombocytopenia), infections
LUQ heaviness (splenomegaly)
lab: CBC, reticulocytes, peripheral smear, Coombs, osmotic fragility (spherocytosis)
img: US/CT spleen volume, accessory spleens; scintigraphy
tx: Indications: hereditary spherocytosis, ITP refractory to steroids/IVIG, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, thalassaemia, hypersplenism, splenic abscess, cysts (hydatid), tumours, splenic vein thrombosis
Laparoscopic splenectomy preferred; vaccinate ≥2 weeks before
oth: Prehepatic jaundice: spherocytosis, sickle-cell, thalassaemia

paths.def: Most common abdominal surgical emergency. Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen (faecolith, lymphoid hyperplasia) → distension, ischaemia, infection. Stages: catarrhal → phlegmonous → gangrenous → perforated.
sx: Pain starting periumbilical/epigastric, migrating to the right iliac fossa within hours (Murphy chronology: pain → nausea/vomiting → fever)
Anorexia, nausea, vomiting (after pain)
Low-grade fever (high fever is NOT the rule)
Atypical: retrocaecal (flank pain), pelvic (dysuria, diarrhoea, tenesmus), elderly (few signs), pregnancy (pain higher), children (rapid perforation, toxic forms, signs less obvious)
ex: Blumberg (rebound tenderness), Rovsing (pain in RIF on LIF pressure)
Psoas sign, obturator sign (pelvic), Grassmann-Mendel (percussion pain in RIF – 'bell sign')
Defence/guarding; rectal/vaginal exam: right Douglas tenderness
lab: Urinalysis (DD urinary), β-hCG in women of childbearing age
img: US: non-compressible appendix >6 mm, periappendiceal fluid (first line in children, pregnancy)
CT: most accurate in adults with doubtful diagnosis
Diagnostic laparoscopy if doubt
tx: Appendectomy – laparoscopic (preferred) or open (McBurney incision)
Pre-op antibiotics; continue in complicated cases
Appendicular mass (plastron): conservative (antibiotics) ± interval appendectomy; abscess: percutaneous drainage
Selected uncomplicated cases: antibiotics only (recurrence risk)
cx: Post-op: wound infection (most frequent), residual abscess, adhesions/obstruction, stump leak
oth: DD: mesenteric adenitis, Meckel diverticulitis, Crohn's, ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion/cyst rupture, salpingitis, right ureteric colic, pyelonephritis, cholecystitis, perforated ulcer

paths.def: Bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz. Causes: duodenal ulcer (most frequent), gastric ulcer, acute haemorrhagic gastritis/erosions, varices, Mallory-Weiss, tumours, Dieulafoy, angiodysplasia.
sx: Haematemesis (fresh or 'coffee-ground'), melena
Massive: haematochezia with shock
Syncope, dizziness, dyspnoea, pallor
ex: Haemodynamic assessment: HR, BP, shock index, capillary refill, urine output
lab: Hb/Hct (may be normal initially), blood group & cross-match, coagulation
img: Upper endoscopy within 24 h (urgent <12 h if unstable after resuscitation) – diagnostic + therapeutic, Forrest classification
CT angiography / angiography if endoscopy fails or massive bleeding (arteriography finds the site only if bleeding >0.5–1 mL/min)
US/CT not routinely used to find the source
tx: Resuscitation: O2, 2 large-bore IV lines, crystalloids (lactated Ringer), restrictive transfusion (Hb 7–8), urinary catheter, NGT
IV PPI bolus + continuous infusion
Endoscopic hemostasis: adrenaline injection + clips/thermal coagulation (combined therapy) for Forrest Ia, Ib, IIa (± IIb after clot removal)
Re-bleeding: repeat endoscopy; angiographic embolisation

Surgery: massive bleeding not responding to resuscitation, failure of endoscopic hemostasis / recurrence, >2 L loss; duodenal ulcer – duodenotomy + ligation of gastroduodenal artery ± vagotomy; gastric – excision/resection; unstable patient → operating room for intra-op diagnosis
cx: Re-bleeding (higher in Forrest Ia/Ib/IIa), myocardial ischaemia
oth: Forrest: Ia spurting (arterial jet), Ib oozing (continuous slow bleeding), IIa visible vessel, IIb adherent clot, IIc black/haematin spot, III clean base
Mallory-Weiss: mucosal tear at eso-gastric junction after vomiting (alcoholics); mostly stops spontaneously – endoscopic therapy; surgery rarely

paths.def: Bleeding distal to Treitz. Causes: diverticulosis (most frequent in elderly), angiodysplasia, colorectal cancer, polyps, IBD, ischaemic colitis, haemorrhoids/fissure, Meckel (young), intussusception (children).
sx: Haematochezia/rectorrhagia (bright red/maroon)
Anaemia symptoms; occult bleeding in right colon cancer
img: Exclude UGI source (NG aspirate/upper endoscopy) if massive
Colonoscopy after bowel prep (diagnostic + therapeutic)
CT angiography for active bleeding, angiography + embolisation; tagged RBC scintigraphy; capsule endoscopy for small bowel
tx: Resuscitation
Endoscopic hemostasis, angioembolisation
Surgery: segmental colectomy if source localized; subtotal colectomy if not localized and persistent

paths.def: Interruption of intestinal transit. Mechanical (obstruction by obturation, strangulation, compression) vs functional (paralytic ileus). Causes: adhesions (~40%, most frequent), malignant obstructions (~20%), external hernias (~15%), volvulus, intussusception, gallstone ileus, mesenteric ischaemia.
sx: Cardinal: colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, abdominal distension, cessation of stool and gas
High (small bowel): early, bilious vomiting, little distension
Low (colon): late, faeculent vomiting, marked distension
Strangulation: continuous pain, fever, tachycardia, peritoneal signs
ex: Inspection: scars (adhesions), visible peristalsis, distension; hernia orifices (always check!)
Auscultation: hyperactive metallic bowel sounds early, silent abdomen late
Percussion: tympany; rectal exam: empty ampulla, tumour, faecaloma, blood
img: Plain erect abdominal X-ray: air–fluid levels (small bowel: central, wider than high, valvulae conniventes; colon: peripheral, higher than wide, haustra); free air if perforation
CT with contrast = best: level, cause, signs of ischaemia (closed loop, whirl)
Water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) follow-through – diagnostic/therapeutic in adhesive obstruction
tx: Rebalancing: IV fluids, electrolytes, nasogastric decompression, urinary catheter, monitoring
Adhesive obstruction without strangulation: conservative 48–72 h
Surgery: strangulation, hernia, closed loop, failure of conservative tx – adhesiolysis, enterectomy of non-viable loops, hernia repair
Colonic tumour: right – resection + anastomosis; left – Hartmann, stent bridge, resection ± stoma; occlusion at right flexure → right hemicolectomy (ileo-transverse anastomosis)
oth: Mechanisms: obturation (tumour, gallstone, bezoar), strangulation (hernia, volvulus, intussusception), compression

paths.def: Inflammation of the peritoneum. Primary (spontaneous bacterial, monomicrobial, in cirrhotic ascites), secondary (perforation/visceral lesion – most frequent: ulcer, appendix, diverticulitis, anastomotic leak), tertiary (persistent after adequate therapy). Localized (abscess) vs generalized.
sx: Severe abdominal pain, worse with movement
Fever, vomiting, ileus
Septic shock in late stages; Hippocratic facies
ex: Abdominal wall contracture ('wooden abdomen'), guarding, Blumberg positive
Abdomen does not follow respiratory movements; absent bowel sounds
Douglas pouch tenderness on rectal exam
lab: Leukocytosis or leukopenia, CRP, procalcitonin, lactate
img: Erect X-ray: pneumoperitoneum (free peritoneal air) – characteristic of perforation
CT: free air, fluid, source, abscess
US: fluid collections
tx: Pre-op: resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, NGT, urinary catheter
Surgery: definitive source control (suture, resection, exteriorization) + abundant peritoneal lavage + drainage (open or laparoscopic – laparoscopy is NOT contraindicated)
Abscess: percutaneous drainage
Severe cases: damage control, open abdomen / planned relaparotomy
Primary peritonitis: antibiotics, no surgery
oth: Causes of peritoneal abscess: perforated viscus, gangrenous cholecystitis, perforated appendicitis/diverticulitis

paths.def: Closed (blunt – contusions, 60–80%: spleen most often injured, then liver) or open (wounds – stab/gunshot; penetrating = peritoneum breached). Management by ATLS principles.
sx: Abdominal pain, shoulder pain (Kehr)
Signs of haemorrhage: pallor, dyspnoea, tachycardia, hypotension
Peritonitis signs in hollow viscus injury
ex: ATLS primary survey ABCDE; log-roll; seat-belt sign
Lower rib fractures (liver/spleen), pelvic stability, rectal/urethral exam
lab: Hb/Hct serial, group & cross-match, lactate, amylase, urinalysis (haematuria)
img: FAST/eFAST in resuscitation room (haemoperitoneum, pericardium, pneumothorax)
Contrast CT in haemodynamically stable patients
Chest X-ray, pelvic X-ray; DPL rarely
tx: Unstable + positive FAST → emergency laparotomy (damage control surgery: haemorrhage control, contamination control, packing, temporary closure, ICU, re-look)
Stable: CT → non-operative management for solid organ injuries ± angioembolisation
Penetrating with peritonitis, evisceration or shock → laparotomy; stab wounds stable → local exploration/serial exams/laparoscopy
Liver: packing, Pringle manoeuvre, hepatorrhaphy, resection; spleen: splenectomy/preservation; stomach/bowel: suture or resection
cx: Abdominal compartment syndrome, missed injuries, delayed splenic rupture
oth: Haemothorax/pneumothorax after thoracoabdominal trauma: chest drain; tension pneumothorax → needle decompression

paths.def: Sudden severe abdominal pain needing rapid diagnosis and often emergency surgery. Syndromes: inflammatory/peritonitis, obstruction, haemorrhagic, ischaemic, traumatic.
sx: Pain onset, location, radiation, character
Vomiting, transit, fever, urinary/gynaecological symptoms
ex: Pain topography: RUQ – cholecystitis, pancreatitis, hepatitis; LLQ – sigmoid diverticulitis, ovarian cysts, ectopic pregnancy; RLQ – appendicitis
Peritoneal signs, hernia orifices, rectal exam
lab: CBC, CRP, amylase/lipase, LFTs, electrolytes, creatinine, lactate, urinalysis, β-hCG
img: Erect X-ray, US, CT; diagnostic laparoscopy
tx: Resuscitation, analgesia (does not mask diagnosis), treat cause; surgical vs non-surgical acute abdomen
oth: Most common abdominal emergency/most frequent emergency surgery: acute appendicitis
Non-surgical causes mimicking: MI, pneumonia, DKA, porphyria, pyelonephritis

paths.def: Minimally invasive surgery under CO2 pneumoperitoneum (10–14 mmHg) with video system and trocars.
sx: Advantages: less pain, smaller wounds, faster recovery, fewer wound infections/hernias, better cosmesis
ex: Patient selection: cardio-respiratory reserve (pneumoperitoneum ↓ venous return, ↑ CO2)
tx: Pneumoperitoneum: Veress needle (closed) or Hasson open technique
Trocar placement, diagnostic laparoscopy, dissection, hemostasis (bipolar, ultrasonic), clips, intracorporeal suture
Conversion to open surgery when needed (not a complication)
oth: Relative contraindications: severe cardio-pulmonary disease, uncorrected coagulopathy, massive distension

paths.def: Surgery for morbid obesity after failure of diet/lifestyle programmes. Restrictive (adjustable gastric band, sleeve gastrectomy), malabsorptive (biliopancreatic diversion), mixed (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass).
sx: Indications: BMI ≥40, or ≥35 with comorbidity (type 2 DM, obstructive sleep apnoea, hypertension, disabling osteoarthritis, dyslipidaemia), failure of supervised diets; age 18–65
lab: Endocrine evaluation (thyroid, cortisol), glucose/HbA1c, lipids, nutrition
img: Pre-op: upper endoscopy, abdominal US (gallstones), respiratory and cardiac evaluation, psychiatric/psychological evaluation
tx: Sleeve gastrectomy (most performed), RYGB (also anti-reflux), band (less used)
Post-op sleeve: Gastrografin swallow at 24–48 h, thromboprophylaxis with LMWH ~10 days, PPI, liquid diet 10–14 days then puréed diet
Lifelong vitamin/mineral supplementation (bypass), follow-up
cx: Early: staple-line leak/gastric fistula (tachycardia, fever, left pleural signs, hiccups – CT with oral contrast), bleeding, VTE
Late: stricture, GERD (sleeve), dumping, internal hernia (bypass), nutritional deficiencies, band slippage/erosion
oth: Tachycardia is the earliest sign of a leak

paths.def: Graft types: autograft (same individual), isograft (identical twins), allograft (different members of same species), xenograft (different species). Liver transplant: orthotopic (standard), heterotopic/auxiliary (liver only – acute failure), split, domino, living donor.
sx: Liver transplant indications: end-stage liver disease (cirrhosis), acute liver failure, HCC within Milan criteria, metabolic diseases
ex: Donor: brain death diagnosis after excluding hypothermia and neuro-depressant drugs
lab: ABO compatibility, HLA typing, cross-match; MELD for allocation
tx: Techniques: standard (caval replacement) or piggyback (cavo-caval preservation)
Immunosuppression: calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine), mycophenolate, steroids, mTOR inhibitors
cx: Vascular (hepatic artery thrombosis), biliary (leak, stenosis), infections, malignancy, drug toxicity

paths.n: Other exam topics (cardiac, thoracic, plastic, sarcoma)
paths.def: Miscellaneous items that appeared on old exams.
sx: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax: young (<45), tall, smokers; sudden onset without trigger; no underlying lung disease
ex: Burns: depth – 1st (epidermis), 2A superficial dermal (blisters with clear fluid, pink, very painful), 2B deep dermal (less pain, pale), 3rd full thickness (painless, leathery)
Rule of nines: lower limb 18%, upper limb 9%, anterior/posterior trunk 18% each, head 9%, perineum 1%
tx: Severe aortic stenosis + severe mitral regurgitation, normal coronaries → combined aortic + mitral valve replacement (biological prosthesis in elderly ≥65–70)
Burns: fluid resuscitation (Parkland 4 mL × kg × %TBSA) for >15–20% adults; circumferential burns → escharotomy; admit
Z-plasty: transposition of two triangular flaps – lengthens and reorients contracted scars
Soft tissue sarcoma: wide excision (essential), radiotherapy for local control, chemotherapy for distant spread

paths.def: Rare (<1% of esophageal tumours). Intramural (leiomyoma = most frequent, lipoma, fibroma, hemangioma, GIST) or intraluminal (fibrovascular polyp, papilloma).
sx: Mostly asymptomatic, found incidentally
Slowly progressive dysphagia, retrosternal discomfort
Regurgitation of a pedunculated polyp into the mouth (fibrovascular polyp) – risk of asphyxia
img: Barium swallow: smooth filling defect with intact mucosa, sharp angles
Endoscopy: smooth bulge under normal mucosa – do NOT biopsy a leiomyoma (makes enucleation harder)
Endoscopic US: layer of origin (muscularis propria = leiomyoma / GIST); CT
tx: Symptomatic or > 3–5 cm, growing, suspicious: surgical enucleation (thoracoscopic / open) preserving the mucosa
Intraluminal polyps: endoscopic resection
GIST: resection with clear margins (malignant potential)
oth: Leiomyoma = commonest benign esophageal tumour; distal 2/3 of the esophagus

paths.def: Polyp = lesion protruding into the lumen. Neoplastic (adenomas: tubular, tubulo-villous, villous – risk ↑ with size > 1–2 cm, villous component, high-grade dysplasia) vs non-neoplastic (hyperplastic, inflammatory, hamartomatous). Hereditary syndromes: FAP (APC gene), Lynch / HNPCC (mismatch-repair genes), Peutz-Jeghers, juvenile polyposis.
sx: Usually asymptomatic (screening)
Occult or overt bleeding, anaemia
Mucus discharge, hypokalaemia (large villous adenoma)
Intussusception (large polyps)
ex: Digital rectal exam for low rectal lesions
Peutz-Jeghers: mucocutaneous pigmentation of the lips
img: Colonoscopy = diagnosis + polypectomy + histology
CT colonography in incomplete colonoscopy
tx: Endoscopic polypectomy / mucosectomy; surgery if not removable endoscopically or invasive cancer
FAP: prophylactic (procto)colectomy (IPAA or ileorectal anastomosis) around 20–25 years
Lynch: colonoscopy every 1–2 years from 20–25 y; screening for endometrial / ovarian cancer
cx: FAP: 100% cancer risk by 40 y; desmoids, duodenal adenomas
oth: Amsterdam criteria (Lynch) '3-2-1': ≥ 3 relatives with CRC (one 1st-degree of the other two), ≥ 2 successive generations, ≥ 1 diagnosed < 50 y, FAP excluded
Not pre-neoplastic: hyperplastic polyps, diverticulosis, melanosis coli

paths.def: Classified by Duhamel and Hagel: 1) development abnormalities (agenesia, atresia, stenosis, duplications, persistence of embryonic elements – omphalo-mesenteric canal, Meckel), 2) position / rotation / joining abnormalities (absent, partial or inverse rotation – situs inversus), 3) extrinsic compression (annular pancreas), 4) histological abnormalities (nerves, epithelium). All manifest as occlusion.
sx: Neonatal bowel obstruction: bilious vomiting, distension, absence of meconium
Stenosis: may stay asymptomatic for a long time
Persistent omphalo-mesenteric canal: gas / meconium / ileal content through a pinpoint umbilical orifice
img: Plain X-ray: 'double bubble' (duodenal atresia / annular pancreas), air-fluid levels
Contrast study: malrotation (abnormal position of the duodeno-jejunal flexure)
US / CT for duplications
tx: Agenesia: usually fatal
Atresia: neonatal surgery (resection + anastomosis) – risk of malnutrition after loss of an important segment
Malrotation with volvulus: emergency Ladd procedure
Duplications (mostly ileum, tubular / cystic): resection

paths.def: Uncommon, increase with age (> 70), males. Acquired (primary) = false diverticula (mucosa + submucosa herniating through the muscle, mostly jejunal, associated with colonic diverticulosis and myenteric plexus dysfunction) vs congenital = true diverticula (full thickness; duodenum within 2 cm of the papilla of Vater, Meckel).
sx: 80% asymptomatic (incidentalomas)
Colicky periumbilical pain after meals
Weight loss, malabsorption (anaemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, hypoproteinaemia) – bacterial overgrowth
img: Upper endoscopy (duodenum), colonoscopy with terminal ileum
CT, barium small bowel follow-through, capsule endoscopy, enteroscopy (jejunum and ileum)
tx: Conservative: NSAIDs, antibiotics (bacterial overgrowth)
Surgery for complications: segmental small bowel resection with entero-enterostomy

paths.def: Intrahepatic stones: prevalent in East Asia, brown pigment stones (soft, friable) from bile stasis + infection + mucin (cysts, stenoses). Bile duct cysts: congenital dilatations (Todani), often with anomalous pancreato-biliary union (APBDU: long common channel, perpendicular confluence). Caroli disease = multiple intrahepatic cysts communicating with the bile ducts (± congenital hepatic fibrosis).
sx: Intrahepatic stones: RUQ pain (70%), jaundice + fever (30%), discomfort, vomiting; asymptomatic 16%
Bile duct cyst: jaundice, pain, abdominal mass (classic triad)
img: US, CT, MRCP (best for cysts), ERCP
Intrahepatic stones: PTC + drainage + cholangioscopy = best solution
tx: Intrahepatic stones: drainage of affected ducts, stone removal (percutaneous cholangioscopy with electrohydraulic / laser lithotripsy), treat stenosis; hepatic resection removes stones + cause
Bile duct cyst: complete cyst excision + Roux-en-Y hepatico-jejunostomy (risk of cancer → never simple drainage)
Caroli: hepatic resection if localized; liver transplant if diffuse
cx: Recurrent cholangitis (chronic proliferative / suppurative cholangitis), CBD stones, liver abscess

paths.def: Fibrosing, inflammatory obstruction of the bile ducts. Secondary (SSC: underlying cause) or primary (PSC: idiopathic, immune-mediated).
sx: Recurrent fever, RUQ pain, jaundice, pruritus
Late: steatorrhea, vitamin ADEK deficiency, portal hypertension
lab: ALP ↑ 2–3×, AST / ALT ↑, fluctuating bilirubin (a rise → stenosis, cancer, stones, cholangitis)
img: MRCP, ERCP, PTC: strictures at all levels alternating with ectasia – 'pruning' and 'beading' of the biliary tree
tx: Medical: almost ineffective (corticosteroids, UDCA)
Endoscopic: sphincterotomy, balloon dilatation, stents
SSC: resection + bilio-enteric anastomosis
Surgical biliary reconstruction; orthotopic liver transplantation (definitive for PSC)
cx: Liver failure – median survival ≈ 12 years after diagnosis
Acalculous cholecystitis, stones with cholangitis, cholangiocarcinoma
oth: SSC causes: formaldehyde injection of hydatid cyst, prior hepatobiliary surgery / trauma, ischaemic strictures, choledocholithiasis, intra-arterial floxuridine, bile duct carcinoma, AIDS (Cryptosporidium, CMV, microsporidium), autoimmune hepatitis
PSC diagnostic criteria: no previous biliary surgery, sclerosis of all / most extrahepatic ducts, exclusion of malignancy, no lithiasis
PSC associations: ulcerative colitis (main), Crohn's colitis, chronic pancreatitis, coeliac disease, sarcoidosis, glomerulonephritis

paths.def: Gallbladder diseases without stones: acute acalculous cholecystitis, adenomyomatosis, cholesterolosis (cholecystoses), polyps.
sx: Acalculous cholecystitis: like calculous cholecystitis but more severe, in critically ill patients
Adenomyomatosis / cholesterolosis: symptoms like gallbladder lithiasis
img: US: thick wall without stones (acalculous); intramural diverticula with 'comet-tail' artefacts (adenomyomatosis)
