tx: Acalculous cholecystitis: cholecystostomy in very ill patients, cholecystectomy when possible
Symptomatic cholecystoses / polyps > 1 cm: cholecystectomy
cx: Acalculous: fast and severe evolution – gangrene, perforation (wall ischaemia)
Cholesterolosis: loose cholesterol crystals act as stones → more prone to acute pancreatitis
oth: Acalculous cholecystitis settings: septicaemia, salmonellosis, severe burns, trauma, postoperative, post-chemotherapy, AIDS
Adenomyomatosis = mucosal + glandular hyperplasia with Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses reaching the serosa (Luschka glands), often in the fundus / infundibulum

paths.def: Aberrant connection between the extrahepatic bile ducts (gallbladder / CBD) and the digestive tract. Rare (< 5%); cholecysto-duodenal = 80%. Lithiasic origin 90%: large stone → recurrent cholecystitis → pressure, ischaemia, focal necrosis → adhesion block → stone erodes into the neighbouring viscus.
sx: Often asymptomatic (found at surgery)
Pain, nausea, vomiting, weight loss; diarrhoea (cholecysto-colic)
Cholangitis (digestive reflux), intermittent upper GI bleeding (melena)
Gallstone (biliary) ileus: sudden bowel obstruction – elderly women with 20–40 years of gallstones; stone 3–4 cm impacted in the terminal ileum (60%)
Bouveret syndrome: impaction in the duodenal bulb → proximal obstruction (frequent vomiting, electrolyte disorders)
img: Plain X-ray: RIGLER triad = small-bowel air-fluid levels + aerobilia + ectopic radio-opaque stone; Balthazar-Schechter sign = air in the gallbladder
US: aerobilia, scleroatrophic gallbladder; contrast CT (best), MRCP, ERCP
Gastroduodenoscopy shows the stone in Bouveret syndrome
tx: Fistula: (laparoscopic) cholecystectomy + suture of the duodenal / colonic orifice
Gallstone ileus: enterotomy proximal to the stone + extraction (enterolithotomy); cholecystectomy + fistula repair in the same or a later operation
Neoplastic fistulas: oncologic resection
oth: Other causes: chronic duodenal ulcer (2nd), trauma, Crohn's, iatrogenic, echinococcosis, neoplasms (CBD, ampulla, pancreas, duodenum, gallbladder, colon)

paths.n: Splenic abscess, cysts, hydatid cyst & tumours
paths.def: Abscess: haematogenous (endocarditis, sepsis), infarct superinfection, contiguity, trauma; immunosuppressed. Cysts: parasitic (hydatid) or non-parasitic (true epithelial / pseudocysts after trauma). Tumours: hemangioma (most common benign), lymphangioma, hamartoma; lymphoma (most common malignant), angiosarcoma, metastases.
sx: Abscess: fever, LUQ pain, left pleural effusion, splenomegaly
Cysts / tumours: often asymptomatic; LUQ heaviness, mass; rupture
lab: Leukocytosis, blood cultures; Echinococcus serology (ELISA); haematologic work-up
img: US / CT: hypodense collection ± gas (abscess); cyst wall, membranes, calcifications (hydatid)
tx: Abscess: antibiotics + percutaneous drainage; splenectomy if multiple / failure
Hydatid / large symptomatic cysts: splenectomy or partial splenectomy / unroofing (spleen-preserving when possible) + albendazole
Tumours: splenectomy (diagnostic and therapeutic)
oth: Absolute splenectomy indications include: ruptured aneurysm, trauma, abscess, hydatid cyst, sarcomas, benign tumours, splenic vein thrombosis with bleeding gastric varices, hereditary spherocytosis, CLL / CML (selected)
Relative: haemolytic anaemias, sickle cell, thalassaemia, elliptocytosis, ITP, Felty, rheumatoid arthritis, splenic neutropenia, lymphomas, Gaucher / Niemann-Pick, cirrhosis with hypersplenism
After splenectomy (desired): Howell-Jolly bodies, thrombocytosis; also target cells, acanthocytes, Heinz bodies, siderocytes, leukocytosis

paths.def: Obstruction with compromised blood supply of the bowel: strangulated external hernia (inguinal, femoral, umbilical, incisional), internal hernia, volvulus (sigmoid, caecal, small bowel), intussusception (children: idiopathic ileo-colic; adults: tumour as lead point), adhesive band.
sx: Sudden, continuous severe pain (not only colicky)
Early reflex vomiting
Irreducible, tense, painful hernia without cough impulse
lab: Leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis, raised lactate, CK
img: CT: closed loop, whirl sign, reduced wall enhancement, pneumatosis, free fluid
US: target / doughnut sign (intussusception)
X-ray: coffee-bean sign (sigmoid volvulus)
tx: Emergency surgery after rapid resuscitation
Reduce / release the strangulation, assess viability (colour, peristalsis, pulsations, warm saline) → resection of non-viable bowel + anastomosis or stoma
Hernia: repair (avoid mesh in contaminated field)
Paediatric intussusception: hydrostatic / pneumatic reduction under imaging if no peritonitis; adults: resection (tumour)
Sigmoid volvulus without ischaemia: endoscopic detorsion first
cx: Gangrene, perforation, peritonitis, sepsis – high mortality if delayed
oth: Simple (obturation) vs strangulation: strangulation = continuous pain + fever + tachycardia + peritonism + leukocytosis / lactate

paths.n: Organ injuries: liver, pancreas, duodenum, hollow viscera
paths.def: Liver = largest solid organ, often injured (penetrating); pancreas / duodenum injured in deceleration or epigastric blows (handlebar, seat-belt); hollow viscus injuries (stomach, small bowel, colon) cause peritonitis; aorta / IVC injuries are rapidly fatal.
sx: Liver: RUQ pain, haemorrhagic shock
Pancreas / duodenum: often delayed epigastric / back pain, retroperitoneal signs
Hollow viscus: progressive peritonitis
ex: Seat-belt sign, lower rib fractures, peritoneal signs
img: FAST; CT with contrast in stable patients (AAST grade, active blush, retroperitoneal air = duodenum, free air)
ERCP / MRCP for pancreatic duct injury
tx: Liver: stable → non-operative management ± angioembolisation; unstable → laparotomy: Pringle manoeuvre, packing (damage control), hepatorrhaphy, debridement / resection
Pancreas: drainage for contusion; distal pancreatectomy if duct transected left of the SMV; head injuries → drainage, rarely Whipple
Duodenum: primary repair ± pyloric exclusion / gastro-jejunostomy
Colon / rectum: primary repair or resection; stoma if heavy contamination / shock
Aorta / IVC: immediate control (damage control)
oth: Gunshot wounds: high-energy, unpredictable trajectory → laparotomy in most cases

questions.q: No biopsy is done in:

o.e: FNH has a typical imaging pattern; biopsy is possible if doubtful.
Adenoma can be biopsied when imaging is unclear (though usually resected).
Biliary cysts are not 'forbidden' for biopsy; diagnosis is by imaging.
Haemangioma: biopsy is forbidden – risk of major bleeding.
HCC: biopsy avoided when resectable – needle-tract seeding; imaging is diagnostic.

questions.note: Hemangioma: biopsy forbidden (bleeding). HCC: "maybe correct" – risk of needle-tract seeding. Key from the handwritten notes: D certain, E "maybe correct".

questions.q: Intramural lesions that can cause acute bowel obstruction:

o.e: Tumours (e.g. lymphoma, GIST, adenocarcinoma) narrow the lumen from the wall.
Crohn's transmural inflammation/stricture is an intramural cause.

questions.note: Options D and E were not recorded.

questions.q: A hydatid cyst appears completely calcified on imaging. Which (Gharbi) class is representative?

o.e: Gharbi V = completely calcified wall – inactive/dead cyst.
Gharbi III = multivesicular cyst with daughter cysts.
Gharbi II = detached floating membrane ('water lily').

questions.q: What corresponds to a Z-plasty?

o.e: Z-plasty = two triangular flaps transposed along a central limb.
Its main use: lengthen and reorient contracted scars.

o.t: Used to cover large wounds with exposed bone
o.e: Large wounds with exposed bone need flaps/grafts, not Z-plasty.

questions.q: Correct definition of an allograft:

o.t: Graft between different members of the same species
o.e: Allograft = between genetically different members of the same species.

o.e: EUS impossible/limited with an obstructing tumour (grade 4 dysphagia) – key did not choose it.
Bronchoscopy: tumour at 22 cm is near the trachea/carina – check airway invasion.

o.e: Major mutilating surgery – not first line.

AngioCT to highlight the source of bleeding

questions.q: A 28-year-old male patient presents with colicky abdominal pain occurring every 15-20 minutes accompanied by vomiting. The symptoms began suddenly approximately 18 hours ago. o.t: Acute intestinal obstruction. Obstruction due to post-appendectomy adhesions
o.e: Young patient, previous appendectomy, colicky pain + vomiting → adhesive obstruction.
Hernia would be visible on exam.

questions.q: An 87-year-old male patient, undergoing chronic anticoagulant treatment due to multiple heart conditions, obese, presents to the emergency department complaining of sudden and painful abdominal distension; multiple vomiting; suffering facies; intense and continuous abdominal pain; he had experienced similar episodes before, which usually stopped spontaneously, but not this time. o.t: Emergency laparotomy for suspected enteromesenteric infarction.
Emergency laparotomy, as an internal strangulated hernia is suspected
Oxygen and analgesics, followed by exploratory laparotomy
Emergency colonoscopy and endoscopic devolution of the sigmoid colon
o.e: Sigmoid volvulus without ischaemia → endoscopic detorsion.

Systemic heparin – first measure in mesenteric embolism.

o.t: Early oral feeding to stimulate bowel elongation
Revascularisation of the superior mesenteric artery and celiac trunk
o.e: Revascularisation depends on imaging – key chose C.

questions.q: A patient known to have Crohn's disease under medical treatment, with a history of appendicitis, is present in the emergency department with persistent pain in the right iliac fossa and umbilical area, vomiting, lack of bowel movements and change in general condition, with onset approximately 24 hours ago. A diagnosis of acute surgical abdomen is made. Exploratory laparoscopy is performed, revealing inflammatory changes in the intestine and mesentery in an ileal segment with 10 cm stenosis and dilated small intestine above the ileal stenosis. No intestinal perforation. No other pathological abdominal changes. What do you do next?

o.e: Drainage alone does not treat the obstruction.
Right hemicolectomy not needed if colon is spared.

A diagnostic laparoscopy is decided upon, which reveals inflammatory changes in the intestine and mesentery in a 20 cm segment of the ileum. No intestinal perforation. The appendix appears normal. No other pathological abdominal changes. What do you do next?

o.e: Appendectomy (appendicitis in a Crohn patient with normal caecal base).

questions.q: A 40-year-old female patient presents at the surgical clinic outpatient department with pain in her flank and right iliac fossa, which began several hours ago. CT – diagnoses ureteric stone vs appendicitis.

o.t: Cystoscopy, retrograde ureteroscopy and ureteral stent placement

Over the last two days, he has experienced chills and evening fever ("around 380C"), persistent abdominal pain, constipation and anorexia. He is undergoing antibiotic treatment with Ampicillin 500 mg every 6 hours, Algocalmin and laxative tea, without any improvement in symptoms. Physical examination reveals an imprecisely defined tumour in the right iliac fossa, approximately 10 cm in diameter and sensitive to deep palpation. Leukocytes 18,000/mm³with left shift of the leukocyte formula. The ultrasound examination reveals a visceral conglomerate in the right iliac fossa with a transonic area of 5/3 cm, sensitive under the transducer; the appendix cannot be visualised. Abdominal CT is not available. What do you do next?

o.t: Medical treatment with antibiotics, painkillers and hydro-electrolytic and nutritional rebalancing
o.e: Medical treatment alone – inadequate for abscess.
Percutaneous drainage of the appendicular abscess.
Laparoscopy is risky in a phlegmon.

o.e: Iron does not find the cause.
Colonoscopy at 78 to exclude caecal cancer.

o.e: Mesenteric adenitis – treat at home and monitor.

o.e: CT not needed in a child.

o.t: Probably mesenteric lymphadenitis. Laparoscopy is required for confirmation

The medical examination reveals pain in the right iliac fossa and positive Blumberg and psoas signs. Fever, 38.10C; Leukocytes 12,000/mm3. questions.q: Consult a 17-year-old patient, a family friend, who has been undergoing antibiotic treatment for three days for pain in the right iliac fossa. questions.q: A 60-year-old female patient presents to the emergency department with pain in her left flank and left iliac fossa, which began 48 hours ago, accompanied by changes in bowel habits: initially several episodes of diarrhoea, followed by constipation, but with preserved gas passage. Acute diverticulitis (left flank/LIF pain, fever, bowel change, 60 y).

questions.q: You are called to the specialist's office for a consultation with a 49-year-old retired patient. For about 7 weeks, he has had 3-4 bowel movements per day, with stools that are more liquid/soft than usual, but without blood. Sometimes he has episodes of constipation (2-3 days) followed by soft, diarrhoeic stools. He also sometimes reports painful colicky episodes in the epigastrium and left hypochondrium. He has lost about 1 kg in the last 3 months. His medical history includes a right femoral neck fracture operated on 9 years ago and an appendectomy at the age of 20. His mother had ulcerative colitis. He is an active person and plays golf. Physical examination reveals: temperature 36.50C; pulse 69 beats/min; BP: 150/85 mmHg; abdomen is soft and without palpable masses or organomegaly; rectal examination without pathological changes. Laboratory tests: Hb: 14.2 g/dl; L:4,100/mm³; Tr: 220,000/mm³; Na: 141 mmol/l; K: 4.6 mmol/l; Serum urea: 16 mg/dl; CRP: 1 mg/l; ACE: 550 ng/ml. Rigid rectosigmoidoscopy up to 25 cm reveals no pathological changes. What conditions are relevant for the differential diagnosis?

o.e: Left colon cancer – possible at 49 with new bowel habit.
Right colon cancer – anaemia, not change of habit.

questions.stem: You are called to the specialist's office for a consultation with a 49-year-old retired patient. Sometimes he has episodes of constipation (2-3 days) followed by soft, diarrhoeic stools. He also sometimes reports painful colicky episodes in the epigastrium and left hypochondrium. He has lost about 1 kg in the last 3 months. His medical history includes a right femoral neck fracture operated on 9 years ago and an appendectomy at the age of 20. His mother had ulcerative colitis. He is an active person and plays golf. Physical examination reveals: temperature 36.50C; pulse 69 beats/min; BP: 150/85 mmHg; abdomen is soft and without palpable masses or organomegaly; rectal examination without pathological changes. Laboratory tests: Hb: 14.2 g/dl; L:4,100/mm³; Tr: 220,000/mm³; Na: 141 mmol/l; K: 4.6 mmol/l; Serum urea: 16 mg/dl; CRP: 1 mg/l; ACE: 550 ng/ml. Rigid rectosigmoidoscopy up to 25 cm reveals no pathological changes. What conditions are relevant for the differential diagnosis?

questions.q: P.D. is a 59-year-old diabetic patient, a radiologist by profession, weighing 156 kg and measuring 1.83 m in height, resulting in an elevated BMI. Both his parents were obese, and he developed obesity as a child, progressively gaining weight with each passing decade. He followed various self-imposed diets and even participated in an institutional nutrition and cognitive-behavioural therapy programme, but he "regained the lost weight" within a few months. P.D. eats three meals a day, the most important being dinner at 7:30 p.m. He has a snack sometimes in the afternoon and frequently in the evening to prevent hypoglycaemia. His alcohol consumption is limited to one glass of wine on weekends, but no more than four times a month. He admits to one episode of binge eating per month, during which he compulsively eats a packet of biscuits or a plate of sandwiches, even though he is not hungry. His current medication includes NPH insulin (30-0-70 units), metformin 2x850 mg/day, atorvastatin, lisinopril, nifedipine, cardio aspirin and vitamin B12 supplements. He suffers from sleep apnoea, but does not use his CPAP machine very often. His fasting blood glucose levels are 100-130 mg/dL, HbA1c 6.1%, and triglycerides 201 mg/dL. P.D. is aware that he needs to lose weight but is afraid of bariatric surgery because, as a radiologist, he has seen a number of complications associated with it. What are the criteria on which you would recommend bariatric surgery for this patient?

o.e: Dyslipidaemia – comorbidity, but key chose A, C.

questions.q: The CT examination of a patient with acute pancreatitis shows inflammation of the pancreas and peripancreatic fat, without any peripancreatic fluid collections and pancreatic necrosis of less than 30%. What is the CT severity index based on the Balthazar score?

o.t: Low degree, due to the limited pancreatic necrosis
o.e: The degree is not decided by necrosis alone: it is the SUM of the Balthazar grade and the necrosis score.

o.t: Middle degree, having a score of 4 points
o.e: Grade C (pancreatic + peripancreatic fat inflammation) = 2 points + necrosis < 30% = 2 points → CTSI = 4 → moderate (4–6).

o.t: High degree, due to the inflamed peripancreatic fat
o.e: Fat inflammation is grade C (2 points); a high (severe) CTSI needs 7–10 points.

o.t: Middle degree, due to the absence of infection signs
o.e: Infection is not part of the CTSI.

o.t: Low degree, having a Balthazar score of 5 points
o.e: Wrong count, and 5 points would already be moderate.

questions.note: CTSI = Balthazar grade (A 0, B 1, C 2, D 3, E 4) + necrosis (0% → 0, < 30% → 2, 30–50% → 4, > 50% → 6). 0–3 mild · 4–6 moderate · 7–10 severe.

cases.title: Epigastric and retrosternal burning, acid reflux, hoarseness and dry cough
kp: Endoscopy first; pH-metry; manometry before surgery
PPI + lifestyle; laparoscopic fundoplication if refractory
cases.presentation: AG, a 44-year-old patient, presents to her family doctor with retrosternal burning that has been evolving for about 4 months. The sensation is stronger after eating and when lying down, and is only partially influenced by self-administered treatment with proton pump inhibitors (PPIs). The current illness began insidiously, about 4 months ago, with a strictly epigastric burning sensation, initially of low intensity and short duration, occurring immediately after eating. Subsequently, retrosternal radiation occurs both after eating and in the supine position or when bending forward (e.g. to tie shoelaces). The patient also describes the fairly rapid onset of exertional dyspnoea during normal physical activity. More recently, these symptoms have been associated with a hoarse voice upon waking in the morning, sometimes a dry cough and transient acid regurgitation. On her own initiative, the patient began treatment with PPIs, followed by a decrease in the intensity of the symptoms, but without their complete disappearance. On physical examination, the patient is slightly overweight with a body mass index (BMI = weight/height2 ) of 27.4, afebrile. Examination of the respiratory system reveals no abnormalities. The abdomen participates in respiratory movements, with no tenderness on palpation. Laboratory tests show haemoglobin and haematocrit at the lower limit of normal.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics Gastroesophageal reflux Heartburn and regurgitation are the most typical symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD); they are postural in nature, being triggered or aggravated by body position (supine or anteflexion, shoelace sign) and/or eating.

Gastro-duodenal ulcer Duodenal ulcer Gastroduodenal ulcer typically causes epigastric pain, usually triggered by eating and relieved by antacids, especially PPIs; the presence of heartburn indicates concomitant acid reflux.

Eosinophilic oesophagitis It is the result of eosinophil accumulation in the oesophageal mucosa, as a reaction to food, allergens or acid reflux, which can inflame or damage the oesophageal tissue. Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic disease of the immune system. The symptoms of eosinophilic oesophagitis do not respond to antacids and include: dysphagia, chest pain, persistent heartburn, epigastric pain, regurgitation.

Achalasia The clinical picture is dominated by dysphagia or possibly odynophagia (pain when swallowing). Regurgitation of food and saliva is quite common, occurring several hours after eating, but diminishes over time as the oesophagus dilates. At night, regurgitation can trigger coughing and dyspnoea. Manometry confirms the spasm of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LES), and barium transit reveals the characteristic "bird's beak" appearance.

Esophageal motility disorders Oesophageal spasms are strong but synchronous contractions of the oesophageal muscles, which prevent the progression of the food bolus. The diagnosis is suggested by chest pain and dysphagia, typically presenting as a stack of overlapping plates during barium transit. Manometry confirms the diagnosis by showing normal LES tone and oesophageal pressure waves that do not propagate along the organ.

Metabolic or degenerative disorders Scleroderma alters oesophageal motility due to fibrosis and atrophy of the smooth muscle, the so-called "glass oesophagus". Diabetes mellitus has the same effect by reducing peristaltic movements and increasing LES tone, sometimes leading to dysphagia or reduced regurgitation.
Drug-induced oesophagitis This is caused by damage to the oesophageal mucosa through prolonged contact with a drug. The main drugs responsible for this damage are:
– Tetracyclines – Bisphosphonates – Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs – Potassium chloride
Dysphagia is constant from onset and does not significantly affect nutritional status. It is sometimes associated with regurgitation and retrosternal pain.

Oesophageal diverticula These are relatively rare, the most common being Zenker's diverticulum, which causes regurgitation of undigested food, high dysphagia, foul breath (halitosis), and a palpable, depressible formation located on the left side of the neck.
Acute or chronic gastritis The clinical symptoms are non-specific and overlap with those of non-ulcer dyspepsia. Epigastric pain, sometimes with a burning sensation, nausea and vomiting may occur.
Cardiovascular disorders (ischaemic heart disease, pericarditis)
Retrosternal pain, sometimes with contracture. Sometimes there is also nausea, dyspnoea, ECG changes that remit after specific medication, without being influenced by PPI treatment.
Infectious oesophagitis (Candida, herpes simplex)

Occurs in the context of an immunocompromised state and is mainly favoured by infections with Candida albicans, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex. The diagnosis is supported by the infectious clinical context, usually painful dysphagia and characteristic endoscopic appearance: whitish deposits in candidal infection or oesophageal ulcerations specific to a viral infection.
Gallstones This causes a dyspeptic syndrome often manifested by epigastric discomfort, sometimes regurgitation, and a bitter taste in the morning.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: Assess the effects of gastric acid reflux on the oesophageal mucosa, namely the presence and severity of oesophagitis, as well as identify any associated digestive pathologies, namely hiatal hernia (HH) and gastric lesions (pyloric stenosis). The therapeutic strategy will be determined based on these elements.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: BRGE is a very common condition. The severity of the disease is determined by the severity of oesophagitis (assessed endoscopically), any morphological changes in the oesophageal mucosa (intestinal metaplasia = endobrachiesophagus or Barrett's oesophagus, precancerous lesion) and associated complications, mainly respiratory (infections) or possibly cardiac (rhythm disorders due to compression caused by a large hiatal hernia).

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Initial treatment is medication, represented by PPIs, depending on the presence and degree of oesophagitis. The existence of morphological causes, especially HH, may require surgical resolution. Surgical treatment should also be considered in cases of incomplete response or intolerance to medical treatment.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: The disappearance of symptoms, especially heartburn, are indicators of the effectiveness of treatment. In the case of oesophagitis, effectiveness is demonstrated by the healing of inflammatory lesions of the oesophageal mucosa.

cases.title: Dysphagia and food regurgitation
kp: Long history of dysphagia + regurgitation without weight loss
Barium 'bird's beak'; manometry confirms; endoscopy excludes cancer
Pneumatic dilation or Heller myotomy + anti-reflux valve
cases.presentation: A 22-year-old male medical student presents to the specialist outpatient clinic for dysphagia and food regurgitation. The symptoms began insidiously about 6 years ago, without weight loss. The patient has no other pathologies and no previous surgical interventions. He consumes alcohol occasionally and is a non-smoker. On physical examination, he is slightly underweight. No pathological changes are detected on cardiorespiratory and abdominal examination. On barium swallow, the terminal oesophagus shows symmetrical narrowing, comparable to a "shell".

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics Gastric Gastric Weight loss, epigastric pain, dysphagia – the proximal stomach is involved. Gastric emptying failure in antro-pyloric cancer, presence of a palpable tumour mass. Upper digestive endoscopy is mandatory for a correct diagnosis and is far superior to barium swallow, which can give false negative results.

Esophageal cancer esophageal Main symptoms: dysphagia and regurgitation are progressive. Regurgitation of saliva or food without gastric secretions. Aspiration pneumonia is rare. The diagnosis of oesophageal cancer requires histological examination of biopsy material obtained from upper digestive endoscopy.
Oesophageal Peptic strictures occur late, as complications of gastroesophageal reflux. A rare cause is radiotherapy to the chest or upper abdomen.

Esophageal motility disorders Motility disorders can vary. As a general rule, if upper digestive endoscopy with biopsy and Ba-passage are normal, oesophageal manometry will describe the type of disorder.
Scleroderma Thickening and hardening of the skin affects multiple subcutaneous areas. Extracutaneous manifestations and specific antibodies are present.
Schatzki ring Intermittent dysphagia for solids that may be associated with iron deficiency.
Infectious oesophagitis Herpes simplex, cytomegalovirus and Candida Sp.
Pseudoachalasia Dysphagia is caused by malignant tumours of the oesophagus or stomach, tumours that compress the distal oesophagus, or surgery on the distal oesophagus or cardia.
Eosinophilic oesophagitis A variable percentage of patients with dysphagia have eosinophilic oesophagitis. Biopsy and endoscopy are the main methods of diagnosis.
Functional dysphagia Defined as an abnormal sensation after swallowing, without organic oesophageal disease, GERD or major oesophageal motility disorder.
Drug-induced oesophagitis Occurs after ingesting tablets without water in the supine position. Mucosal lesions can be detected on EDS.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Achalasia.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: Oesophageal manometry.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: Depending on the Ba-passage and manometry. If it is dilated and pleated, without motility, the condition is advanced and the results of treatment will be poor due to the lack of contractility of the oesophagus.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: POEM - PerOralEndoscopicMiotomy After incising the oesophageal mucosa, the endoscope is passed through the mucosal breach into the oesophageal submucosa, and a submucosal tunnel is created by blunt dissection up to the cardia. A triangular electrode is used to section the circular layer of the lower oesophageal sphincter.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Disappearance of symptoms and barium passage with improvement of bolus passage at the esophageal junction.

cases.title: Progressive dysphagia and weight loss
kp: Progressive dysphagia + weight loss = cancer until proven otherwise
Endoscopy + biopsy; staging CT, EUS, PET-CT, bronchoscopy
Neoadjuvant CRT + esophagectomy or palliation (stent, gastrostomy)
cases.presentation: The patient, PD, aged 64, a civil servant, presents to the doctor with progressive dysphagia for solid foods, sialorrhea, regurgitation and weight loss of 10 kg in the last 5 months. The current illness began insidiously, approximately 5 months before presentation to the doctor, with progressive dysphagia for solid foods, sialorrhea, regurgitation, and weight loss of 10 kilograms. He currently weighs 75 kilograms and is 160 cm tall. He has no significant family history. From his personal history, we note that the patient suffered accidental ingestion of a caustic substance at the age of 5. He cannot specify what type of caustic substance he ingested. The ingestion was followed by difficulty swallowing, for which he underwent oesophageal dilation sessions at 6-month intervals for several years, with gradual improvement of dysphagia until it disappeared. Until 5 months ago, he had no significant difficulty swallowing. The patient is a smoker (approx. 30 cigarettes/day) and consumes alcohol daily (50-100 ml of alcohol). The clinical examination did not reveal anything significant. Biochemically, mild anaemia was identified. A CT scan performed by the patient on his own initiative revealed a thickening of the lower thoracic oesophagus. Esophagoscopy reveals a scarred esophagus, with a vegetative, friable formation 35 cm from the dental arch, partially occupying the esophageal lumen and extending over a length of 3 cm. Echoendoscopy reveals adventitial invasion, but without extension to adjacent structures, and two lymph nodes adjacent to the oesophageal wall, from which biopsies are taken. Biopsies from the tumour and lymph nodes identify a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, G1, metastasised to the two lymph nodes.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Although the diagnosis is confirmed by the results of paraclinical investigations and histological examination, the symptoms presented by the patient can also be found in achalasia and peptic oesophageal stenosis. Diagnosis

Diagnostic elements / differential diagnosis Achalasia Acalasia may clinically suggest neoplastic involvement of the lower oesophagus through regurgitation and dysphagia. Clinically, it is difficult to obtain a definitive diagnosis. The differential diagnosis is made by Ba passage (bird's beak appearance of the esophagogastric junction), esophagoscopy with biopsies from "suspicious" mucosal areas to rule out pseudoachalasia, which could mask a neoplastic process, and esophageal manometry.

Oesophageal peptic stenosis A complication of gastroesophageal reflux disease, oesophageal peptic stenosis induces oesophageal stenosis in 70-80% of cases. Clinically, it manifests as dysphagia and heartburn. Oesophagoscopy and biopsy of the stenosis area confirm the diagnosis. If a malignant process is histologically evident, the diagnosis and treatment protocol for oesophageal cancer will be followed.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Lower thoracic oesophageal cancer

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: The case is discussed by the oncology committee and a treatment decision is made

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: The patient has a very aggressive cancer. The invasion of the oesophageal wall without affecting adjacent structures points to a T3 tumour. The presence of metastases in two lymph nodes classifies the malignant tumour as N1. For T3, N - in staging, the histological grade is irrelevant. The CT scan shows no metastases. The stage of the malignant tumour is classified as III A.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by tumour resection and oesophagus reconstruction.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Five to six weeks after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, the response to treatment is assessed by contrastenhanced CT, PET/CT, oesophagoscopy, followed by surgery.

cases.title: Epigastric abdominal pain accompanied by muscle contracture
kp: NGT, fluids, antibiotics, PPI → suture + omental patch + lavage
cases.presentation: A 32-year-old patient, a programmer at an IT company, is brought by ambulance to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain. The current illness began suddenly the night before, with intense pain in the epigastrium. The patient was attending the Electric Castle festival, where he consumed alcohol and smoked tobacco. From the onset, the pain began to increase steadily in intensity, accompanied by nausea and anorexia for food and liquids. The following morning, the clinical picture changed dramatically, with the patient complaining of severe epigastric pain ("like a knife stuck in the stomach"), which then spread throughout the abdomen. He had two episodes of vomiting, both of which exacerbated the pain. The patient is an occasional beer drinker and smokes 10-15 cigarettes a day. He works about 10 hours a day, often late into the night, and eats according to a chaotic schedule. On physical examination, his general condition is altered, his skin is pale and sweaty, his breathing is shallow, he is immobile and in a fetal antalgic position. His blood pressure is 110/60 mmHg, AV 95 beats/minute. The abdomen does not follow respiratory movements and is immobile. No bowel sounds are heard on auscultation. Superficial palpation reveals skin hyperesthesia. There is generalized, intense, constant abdominal muscle contracture, giving the sensation of rigidity or a "wooden abdomen". On rectal examination, the Douglas pouch is sensitive. Leukocytosis of 12,000/mmc, with neutrophilia. Abdominal ultrasound reveals the presence of free fluid in Morrison's recess and in the Douglas pouch. Abdominal X-ray shows pneumoperitoneum.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation
Characteristics In both sexes Perforated gastro-duodenal ulcer

Pain is the most important symptom and is present from the onset. Initially epigastric, it later migrates to the right flank and then becomes generalised. The pain is aggravated by any movement. Vomiting may occur and signs of shock are visible. Physical examination reveals peritoneal signs, with a rigid, "wooden" abdomen being a characteristic sign. Breathing difficulties and the disappearance of liver dullness are the result of subphrenic gas accumulation and diaphragmatic irritation, but these are not constant signs.

Perforated appendicitis The pain starts around the navel, sometimes in the epigastrium, then moves to the right iliac fossa. After perforation, the pain is felt in the lower abdomen at first, then becomes generalised. Pneumoperitoneum is present, signs of peritonitis are present, but there is no muscle rigidity.
Acute gastroenteritis Nausea and vomiting precede abdominal pain, which is colicky in nature. Watery or even bloody diarrhoea, fever and myalgia occur. Laboratory tests indicate leukocytosis.

Acute cholecystitis The pain is usually localised in the right hypochondrium. Initially colicky, it then becomes persistent and progressively intensifies. Nausea and vomiting are common symptoms. Fever of 38-39°C occurs, there may be signs of toxemia, and leukocytosis is constantly present. The right hypochondrium is very sensitive to palpation, sometimes a painful tumor mass is felt in the gallbladder.

Acute pancreatitis The pain is intense and localised in the epigastrium and radiates dorsally, or to both hypochondria, "in a bar". Vomiting is early, profuse and does not relieve the patient. There is usually a history of biliary disease or alcohol consumption. Palpation of the abdomen indicates sensitivity or even defence, but without rigid contracture.
Ascending cholangitis The pain is located in the epigastrium and does not become generalised. Jaundice is always present, as are chills and high fever, followed by sepsis.

Intestinal infarction/isc haemia There may be predisposing factors, such as heart or valve disease, or liver disease. The onset occurs with colicky abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, and shock. After the infarction, the pain becomes generalised, with tenderness and muscle weakness on palpation. A hard, imprecisely defined tumour mass (infarcted loop) may be palpable. The abdomen is silent on auscultation – "silentium abdominale".
Basal pneumonia Respiratory signs, fever, nausea, vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain. No signs of peritonitis.

Myocardial infarction When the posterior and inferior cardiac walls are affected, abdominal signs may appear, with intense epigastric pain. Associated with this, the patient may experience vomiting. Signs of shock, tachycardia and dyspnoea are present, but there are no signs of peritonitis.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Perforated gastric or duodenal ulcer.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: The patient is informed about the diagnosis, the current stage of the disease and the necessary treatment. A nasogastric suction tube is inserted and two venous access routes are established. Hydro-electrolytic rebalancing is initiated. Proton pump inhibitors, analgesics and broad-spectrum antibiotics are administered intravenously. Immediate surgery is proposed.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: Peritonitis secondary to perforated peptic ulcer is a severe nosological condition in the absence of immediate and correctly performed surgery. Without treatment, the disease will progress to toxic-septic shock, followed by organ failure syndrome and, subsequently, death. Ulcer perforation is a life-threatening condition. Since the patient is young and has no associated pathologies, he has a good prognosis following prompt and correct treatment.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Surgical treatment consists of suturing the ulcerative perforation when the ulcer is "young" or sealing the perforation by filling it with omentum sutured to the edges of the ulcer when the ulcer is chronic and calloused. Abundant peritoneal lavage with warm saline solution is mandatory and is followed by drainage of the sloping areas. The surgical approach can be open or laparoscopic. In this case, laparoscopic surgery is preferred, as it allows for better visualisation of the surgical field and minimises the risk of complications. is preferred because the patient is young, active, and the onset of peritonitis occurred less than 6 hours ago.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Disappearance of abdominal peritonitis symptoms and signs, resumption of digestive tolerance and intestinal transit, absence of pathological products in the drainage tubes, improvement in general condition.

cases.title: Haematemesis with haemodynamic instability in a patient with ulcer
cases.dx: Bleeding peptic ulcer with haemodynamic instability
kp: IV PPI; surgery if endoscopic failure / re-bleeding
cases.presentation: The patient, IG, a 60-year-old turner, is brought in by ambulance to the emergency room with vomiting containing blood. The current illness began suddenly this morning with the onset of vomiting red blood, accompanied by dizziness, which is why he called an ambulance. The patient mentions epigastric pain for about 3 years, when a gastroscopy was performed, revealing a duodenal ulcer. He was recommended treatment with Controloc, which the patient followed sporadically. He smokes fifteen cigarettes a day and consumes strong alcohol daily. On physical examination, the patient is of normal weight, pale, anxious, and afebrile. The abdomen participates in respiratory movements, is slightly distended, with accelerated hydroaerial sounds. Axillary temperature 37.20C. Laboratory tests show an increase in white blood cell count (12,000/mm³), haemoglobin 8 g/dl, haematocrit 23%. BP = 80/60 mm Hg, pulse 110/min.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation
Characteristics In both sexes Haemorrhagic gastro-duodenal ulcer
Haemorrhagic vomiting, history of ulcer.
Ruptured oesophageal varices Abundant haemorrhagic vomiting, presence of liver cirrhosis, signs of porto-caval collateral circulation.
Haemorrhagic gastric neoplasm Less profuse haemorrhagic vomiting, presence of melena or occult bleeding, weight loss, neoplastic impregnation syndrome.
Mallory-Weiss syndrome Occurs mainly in alcohol consumers and manifests itself through haemorrhagic vomiting, which is usually self-limiting.
Haemobilia Haemorrhagic vomiting, associated with jaundice.
Haemorrhagic oesophageal neoplasm Less severe haemorrhagic vomiting, signs of oesophageal stenosis, neoplastic impregnation syndrome.
Haemoptysis Blood elimination is accompanied by coughing, and its appearance is aerated.
Swallowed nasopharyngeal haemorrhages Presence of nasal bleeding, ENT consultation confirms the diagnosis.
Vomiting of red-coloured food (beetroot, strawberries, raspberries, etc.)
The medical history highlights the ingestion of such foods, with no decrease in blood pressure, haemoglobin or haematocrit.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding from a duodenal ulcer. Haemorrhagic shock. Secondary anaemia.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: The patient is offered emergency upper endoscopy to confirm the diagnosis and endoscopic therapy. The clinical picture indicates a medical-surgical emergency requiring immediate resolution, as the patient's life is in danger. Oral intake is stopped and coagulation tests are performed. The patient is informed of the urgent nature of his condition and signs an informed consent form for both endoscopic therapy, for the administration of blood and blood products, and for the possibility of surgery if endoscopic therapy is unsuccessful. Hydroelectrolytic and haemodynamic rebalancing therapy is instituted with crystalloid and colloid solutions and, if necessary, the administration of blood and blood products.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: As the patient is elderly and there is obvious systemic involvement, the severity of the disease is high, but the prognosis may be favourable if treatment is initiated quickly and appropriately.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Emergency upper endoscopy is recommended to confirm the diagnosis, followed by endoscopic haemostasis if necessary. At the same time, hydroelectrolytic and haemodynamic rebalancing therapy is initiated with crystalloid and colloid solutions and, if necessary, blood and blood products. If endoscopic therapy fails, emergency surgery is recommended to achieve haemostasis, with or without physiopathological intervention to treat the ulcerative disease.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Haemodynamic stabilisation, increased haemoglobin and haematocrit, resumption of intestinal transit and food tolerance, rapid improvement in general condition.

cases.title: Melena, postprandial vomiting, loss of appetite and weight loss
kp: Melena, postprandial vomiting, anorexia, weight loss
Correct metabolic disorders; gastrectomy + D2 or palliative gastro-jejunostomy
cases.presentation: Patient DP, a 55-year-old professional driver, presents at the clinic's outpatient department complaining of black stools, nausea and postprandial vomiting. The current illness began insidiously about 4 weeks ago, with black stools and an intense foul odour. This symptom recurred every 1-2 days, which is why the patient went to see his family doctor. The laboratory tests indicated by the doctor showed low Hb and Ht levels (12 g/dL and 35%, respectively), which is why a digestive endoscopy was recommended. The patient had lost approximately 4 kg in weight over the previous 4-5 weeks and had been experiencing loss of appetite, nausea, early satiety and decreased appetite for meat products for approximately 3 months; postprandial vomiting had appeared in the last 2 weeks. He smokes twenty cigarettes a day and consumes alcohol occasionally. On physical examination, the patient is of normal weight and pale. The abdomen participates in respiratory movements, with hydroaerial sounds present, without spontaneous pain on superficial or deep palpation. The patient reports slight discomfort on deep palpation of the epigastrium. Laboratory tests show decreased Hb and Ht values (11 g/dL and 35%, respectively). Upper digestive endoscopy reveals an ulcerative, haemorrhagic, stenosing tumour located in the gastric antrum.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics Gastric ulcer Similar symptoms (haemorrhagic risk, stenotic character for old, neglected distal gastric ulcers). Pain syndrome present, with characteristic rhythm related to eating. The diagnosis is confirmed by upper digestive endoscopy with biopsy.
Benign gastric tumours The presence of ulcerated tumours (adenomas) may be accompanied by similar symptoms. The diagnosis is confirmed by upper digestive endoscopy with biopsy.
Other benign gastric Lymphoma, gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GIST). The diagnosis is confirmed by upper digestive endoscopy with biopsy. tumours Chronic anaemia syndrome

It may be caused by bleeding from an ulcerative lesion or tumour located anywhere in the digestive tract. A differential diagnosis will also be made with other causes of anaemia: iron deficiency anaemia, haemolytic anaemia, other haematological syndromes.
Gastric evacuation failure Other causes of antral stenosis (chronic gastric or duodenal ulcer, ca-los), gastric dyskinesia (vagus nerve damage).

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Gastric cancer.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: Staging investigations: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest and abdomen. Endoscopic biopsy with histopathological results from the tumour.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: A diagnosis of gastric cancer is an absolute emergency - a delayed emergency. The patient's life is in immediate danger due to the risk of haemorrhage and, in the long term, due to the progression of the neoplastic disease (local tumour extension and distant metastasis).

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Depending on the CT staging, surgical treatment (subtotal gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y gastrojejunal anastomosis) will be recommended, preceded or not by neoadjuvant chemotherapy; in the present case, taking into account the characteristics of the tumour, surgical treatment (subtotal gastrectomy with Roux-enY gastrojejunal anastomosis) will be recommended, preceded or not by neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

Melasma, postprandial vomiting, loss of appetite and weight loss the haemorrhagic role of the formation, surgery takes precedence over neoadjuvant treatment (if the haemorrhagic episode recurs). Postoperatively, the patient will undergo an oncological consultation with continuation of adjuvant oncological treatment.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Periodic oncological and surgical monitoring: medical history, clinical examination, tumour markers (CA 19-9 and CEA), abdominal imaging (ultrasound, CT) and chest imaging.

cases.title: Abdominal pain and distension, vomiting and cessation of bowel movements
kp: Erect X-ray air–fluid levels; CT for cause/ischaemia
Rebalance + NGT; surgery for strangulation or failure
cases.presentation: Male patient, economist, 58 years old, presents to the emergency room with cessation of bowel movements for faeces and gas, abdominal distension and vomiting. The current illness began approximately 5-6 months ago with constipation that progressively worsened, culminating in complete cessation of intestinal transit for faeces and gas eight days ago. Since then, the patient has experienced intermittent, colicky abdominal pain, accompanied by significant abdominal distension. Three days ago, vomiting began, initially bilious and recently cloudy and foul-smelling; one day ago, the abdominal distension worsened, becoming predominant in the right iliac fossa. Physical examination reveals an obese patient with pale, dry skin and mucous membranes, intense thirst, and a distended abdomen without postoperative scars; palpation of the abdomen is painful, especially in the right iliac fossa, with muscle guarding at this level; percussion reveals marked tympanism. Abdominal auscultation: rare bowel sounds. Rectal examination reveals an empty rectal ampulla. Laboratory tests reveal leukocytosis (16,500/mm³), anaemia (Hb = 10.4 mg/dl), renal failure (serum urea = 90 mg/dl, serum creatinine = 2.0 mg/dl). Plain abdominal X-ray: highly distended small bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels, dilated colon with air-fluid levels and a cecal diameter of 14 cm! Abdominal computed tomography additionally reveals an infiltrated and stenotic segment 6 cm long at the rectosigmoid junction, with a small amount of ascites.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics Acute appendicitis The pain begins around the navel, followed by nausea and vomiting, anorexia; after a few hours, the pain migrates to the right iliac fossa. Physical examination usually does not reveal abdominal distension; palpation of the right iliac fossa is painful, accompanied by muscle guarding and later by contracture; typically, Blumberg's, Rovsing's, Mandl's, and psoas signs are present. It occurs more frequently in young people, and the onset is most often sudden.
Cecal diverticulitis The clinical signs are similar to those of acute appendicitis; ultrasound and computed tomography differentiate between the two; abdominal distension does not occur.
Crohn's disease with ileocecal localisation, complicated by occlusion

The clinical syndrome may be similar to a certain extent; however, abdominal distension differs, as in this case it is limited to the small intestine, with the colon having a normal calibre; these patients often have a characteristic appearance, are thin (not obese as in our case), with a longer history of abdominal pain, are anaemic, and may have (in the past or present) abdominal abscesses and recurrent perianal fistulas; abdominal X-ray and CT scan will make the difference.

Sigmoid diverticulitis Painful formation in the left iliac fossa; in our case, however, the formation is completely painless and firm; in the absence of inflammatory tumour, the clinical picture is similar to that of acute "left-sided" appendicitis. Abdominal ultrasound/CT scan will rule out diverticulitis. Rapidly developing ascites in decompensated cirrhosis

The patient is usually known to have liver cirrhosis, often ca-sestic, with episodes of jaundice and liver decompensation in the past, signs of portal hypertension present; abdominal distension is painful and sets in quickly; it is caused by the rapid accumulation of ascites fluid (dullness on percussion, not tympanism!); ultrasound/CT confirms.
Neglected generalised peritonitis (days), due to perforated ulcer

Intense, sudden onset, lancinating pain, initially epigastric, later diffuse, continuous, most commonly in young patients with a history of ulcerative disease. Presents with generalised muscle guarding; contracture, on late presentation, of lesser intensity, but with significant distension and cessation of transit; does not present with colic pain
; patient in shock; X-ray, ultrasound, abdominal CT reveal pneumoperitoneum, free fluid and multiple intraperitoneal abscesses. Perforated Meckel's diverticulitis

To a certain extent, the symptoms are similar to those of acute appendicitis, with pain in the right iliac fossa; in cases of late presentation (as in the case presented), abdominal distension predominates in relation to defence and, especially, muscle contracture, which diminishes; however, abdominal X-ray/CT scans will show no cecal distension.

Severe acute pancreatitis Sudden onset, with continuous epigastric pain (not colicky), nausea with frequent vomiting, often triggered by alcohol consumption or cholecystokinetic foods (in the case of gallstones – often known), high amylasemia, lipasemia; Undiagnosed/untreated for 8 days, it will cause a much more severe alteration of the general condition. The antecedents and imaging will establish the correct diagnosis.

Enteromesent eric infarction It is the abdominal condition with the bleakest prognosis; the onset is usually sudden, with particularly intense, continuous (non-colicky) abdominal pain that does not respond to analgesics; the deterioration in general condition is rapid and severe, with the onset of septic shock; cold, marbled skin; it is frequently associated with arterial fibrillation; abdominal distension with signs of peritoneal irritation; auscultation reveals "deathly silence" – abdominal silentium; abdominal ultrasound/tomography reveals typical signs of extensive acute intestinal ischaemia (pneumoneteria), ascites.

Volvulus cecal Intense, continuous pain with sudden onset (not progressive); abdominal X-ray shows an enormously distended loop of large intestine, with the long axis oriented from the right iliac fossa to the epigastrium or left hypochondrium.

Sigmoid volvulus It represents the torsion of a long loop of the sigmoid colon around the mesenteric axis; this results in a "double closed loop" variant; The sigmoid "balloon" is enormous, distended, symmetrical, ovoid, oriented from the left iliac fossa to the right hypochondrium; radiologically, there is an enormously dilated intestinal loop, with a "coffee bean" appearance, with two hydroaerial levels; the descending colon has a tapered appearance at the level of the torsion axis; Abdominal CT also reveals a greatly distended sigmoid loop with twisted mesentery.

Right renalureteral colic Sudden onset of colicky, intermittent pain, localised in the right lumbar region, with typical radiation through the right flank towards the right iliac fossa and genitals; frequently associated with macroscopic or microscopic haematuria

; sometimes significant abdominal distension is present (reflex intestinal paralysis); typically, the patient is agitated, "can't find their place"; general condition is not affected; imaging reveals hydronephrosis/hydronephrosis of varying degrees.
Neoplasm Multiple episodes of constipation in the past, which become progressive sigmoid and more severe, with subocclusive syndrome (König), appearing stenotic with
5-6 months ago, culminating in the current episode of intestinal occlusion complete acute intestinal neglected

, generated by a neglected sigmoid stenotic tumour and impending left abdomen; over time (during the 8 days), distension perforation dias-abdominal evolves until reaching the "critical cecal diameter"
; initially manifested by colicky pain in the left lower quadrant

– 14 cm – Lowman– – 14 cm – Lowman–Davis index (indicating imminent perforation/ Davis index (indicating imminent perforation/rupture) cecal explosion) – radiological warning sign (X-ray, ultrasound, CT); clinically , this moment is reflected by very painful distension at the right iliac fossa, with incipient signs of peritoneal irritation and a change in the nature of the pain, from colicky-intermittent to continuous and very intense. The neglected, old nature of intestinal obstruction, This is also confirmed by the deterioration in general condition, faecal vomiting and severe dehydration.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Neglected acute intestinal obstruction due to a stenosing sigmoid neoplasm and imminent diastatic perforation of the caecum.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: The patient will be informed of the need for emergency hospitalisation, followed by paraclinical investigations, carried out in parallel with preoperative preparation (aggressive rehydration through infusions, antibiotics, insertion of a central venous catheter, nasogastric tube). This will be followed by emergency surgery under general anaesthesia; The tactic will be a "two-stage" intervention: the first stage will consist of a Hartmann-type rectosigmoid resection, followed 4-6 weeks later by the removal of the colostomy and reintegration of the colon into the transit tract through colo-rectal anastomosis.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: The current illness is severe, as it represents an acute, life-threatening complication that has been neglected (onset 8 days ago!), with imminent diastatic perforation of the caecum, occurring in an obese, smoker, hypertensive, long-term carrier of undetected rectosigmoid cancer, the patient being severely dehydrated and debilitated.

As far as the emergency examinations (chest and abdominal X-ray, abdominal ultrasound, computed tomography) can determine, the approximate stage of the sigmoid tumour is: T3, N1, M0; However, it should be noted that, under the given circumstances, complete staging is practically impossible due to the manner of presentation/admission/intervention (emergency, respectively immediate emergency).

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: In this particular case, a "two-stage" surgical approach is recommended. It begins with an initial vigorous rebalancing of fluids and electrolytes, performed using peripheral venous catheters and a central catheter (which is also useful for monitoring central venous pressure), the insertion of a urethral-vesical catheter, a nasogastric suction tube (to effectively decompress the digestive tract – emptying the stomach will also ensure safe orotracheal intubation by preventing aspiration bronchopneumonia) and proton pump inhibitors. The operation must be performed early (the imminence of diastatic perforation of the cecum requires it!); it will consist of Hartmann's rectosigmoid resection (with closure of the distal rectal stump and temporary terminal colostomy upstream); complete emptying of the toxic entero-colic fluid and gas content is required – retrograde "milking" of the small intestine until its contents are completely removed and evacuated by the nasogastric suction tube and aspiration of the faecal-gas content from the colon when it is opened. This normalises the intraintestinal pressure (interrupting the vicious circle generated by distension!) and, consequently, the abdominal pressure, which will enable safe laparorrhaphy and prevent the onset of postoperative intra-abdominal hypertension syndrome. Under these conditions, the safety of postanaesthetic extubation and the avoidance of pulmonary complications will also be ensured. The enormous fluid-gas distension of the colon does not allow for the performance of a "per primam" colorectal anastomosis, which necessitates the performance of a temporary terminal colostomy upstream. After 4-6 weeks, the patient will be readmitted and the final stage of the intervention (removal of the colostomy and colorectal anastomosis) will be performed. Adjuvant oncological treatment will be indicated (or not) by the oncologist (multimodal treatment) 4 weeks postoperatively, depending on the result of the definitive staging after examination of the resection specimen (anatomopathology).

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Effective volume replacement will be reflected by the resumption of renal function (30-60 ml/hour, provided that the urine collection bag was empty upon admission – anuric patient), stabilisation of blood pressure and PVC to normal values. Postoperatively, normal intestinal transit will resume early through colostomy, allowing resumption of feeding. and oral hydration and rapid recovery; body temperature will normalise; early mobilisation will be possible; administration of low molecular weight heparin and effective hydration will prevent the development of deep vein thrombosis of the pelvic limbs.

cases.title: Diffuse abdominal pain after electrical conversion of a heart rhythm disorder
kp: Pain out of proportion after cardioversion / AF
cases.presentation: The patient, a 71-year-old electrician, now retired, presents to the surgical department with diffuse abdominal pain. The patient, known to have had a mechanical prosthesis in the mitral position for 9 years, with chronic anticoagulant treatment, presented to the cardiology department 4 days ago with a picture of atrial tachycardia with block. Electrical conversion to sinus rhythm was performed, and on the third day of hospitalisation, it was decided to implant a permanent pacemaker, a procedure that required discontinuation of anticoagulant therapy for 14 hours. During the course of treatment, the patient complained of intense abdominal pain, which progressively worsened and did not respond to minor painkillers. On physical examination, the patient is of normal weight, psychomotor agitated, tachypneic, haemodynamically stable, BP = 180/100 mmHg. The abdomen is distended, with diffuse pain on superficial and deep palpation, more pronounced on abdominal wall decompression, without hydro-aerial sounds. Laboratory tests reveal metabolic acidosis; creatinine = 0.95 mg/dL, APTT = 36 seconds, leukocytes = 15.8*10⁹/μL with 88% neutrophils, cardiac enzymes unreactive. Emergency echocardiography excludes the presence of intracavitary thrombi or mobile masses at the level of the mechanical mitral prosthesis, which is normofunctional. An emergency abdominal-pelvic CT angiography is performed. A complete occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery distal to its origin is identified, extending over 3.5 cm, as well as distension of the ileal loops with fluid content and air-fluid levels.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics Mesenteric ischaemia Acute Severe abdominal pain, with sudden onset, located around the navel or diffuse, decreasing in intensity as it progresses towards infarction; nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, melena or rectal bleeding; progressive abdominal distension; pallor, sweating, shock, altered general condition; discrepancy between the increased intensity of pain and the other accompanying signs; paralytic ileus predominates in the infarction phase, and muscle contracture is associated with perforation.

Chronic Marked postprandial abdominal pain, occurring in recurrent episodes, periombilical, colicky in nature, usually with onset and remission within the first 1-3 hours after eating; marked weight loss; aversion to food due to anticipation of pain; vascular murmurs; patient with peripheral vascular disease.
Venous Abdominal pain with insidious onset, moderate intensity, lasting up to 5-14 days, nausea, vomiting; meteorism; hypercoagulability.

Non-occlusive Moderate abdominal pain, progressively worsening, bloating, nausea, vomiting; hypotension, heart failure, hypovolaemia, cardiac arrhythmias; patient possibly intubated and sedated, with masking of clinical picture.

Ischemic colitis Sudden onset of moderate abdominal pain, localised in the affected colon segment, more frequently in the flank and left iliac fossa, diarrhoea, melena or rectal bleeding in the first 24 hours after the onset of pain, nausea, vomiting, anorexia.
Intestinal obstruction Small intestine Colic abdominal pain, nausea, bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, cessation of faecal and gas transit, marked hydro-aerial rumbling; previous surgery.
Large intestine Progressively worsening abdominal pain, prolonged interval between painful episodes that gradually shortens, faecal vomiting (late), cessation of faecal and gas transit.
Paralytic ileus Diffuse abdominal discomfort, absence of colicky pain, hydro-aerial noises; incomplete cessation of faecal and gas transit; recent surgery.
Acute colonic pseudoobstruction (Ogilvie syndrome)

Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, cessation of faecal transit, marked abdominal distension; hydro-aerial noises present; more common in the right colon; hospitalised patient with severe associated pathology or postoperative status, metabolic disorders.

Volvulus Sudden onset of severe, continuous abdominal pain, accompanied by pallor, sweating, tachycardia, shock, early vomiting, cessation of faecal and gas transit; peritoneal irritation in the area of the volvulated loops or high ointment picture.

Intestinal intussusceptio n Classic association: colicky, severe, intermittent abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, gelatinous stools with mucus and blood (haematochezia); palpable tumour in the right hypochondrium, free right iliac fossa (Dance's sign).

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Acute mesenteric ischaemia.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: The indication for revascularisation is assessed and emergency surgery is proposed, consisting of exploratory laparotomy and, depending on the stage of the lesions identified intraoperatively, segmental enterectomy ± colon resection with exteriorisation of the intestinal stumps in the form of a stoma, or laparorrhaphy. Anticoagulation with continuous heparin infusion, water and acid-base rebalancing therapy, and broadspectrum antibiotic prophylaxis are initiated.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: Considering the patient's age and associated pathology, as well as the degree of intestinal lesions, with the stage of reversible mesenteric ischaemia having been exceeded, with extensive infarction of the ileum and right colon, a grim, possibly lethal prognosis can be deduced. Mortality reaches up to 90% when more than half of the small intestine is resected.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: An exploratory laparotomy is indicated, with assessment of the extent of the lesions, resection of non-viable intestinal segments and preservation of the intestine with changes. reversible ischaemia. In this case, intraoperative exploration confirms the extension of the intestinal infarction to the ileum and right colon, with viable small intestine approximately 200 cm from the angle of Treitz. The case does not indicate revascularisation. Extended right hemicolectomy and enterectomy are performed, with terminal ileostomy externalised in the left iliac fossa and transverse colon mucosal fistula.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: The patient requires monitoring in the intensive care unit. The delimitation of new intestinal ischaemic areas is clinically assessed by inspection of the ileostomy and mucosal fistula. If there is suspicion, a second-look laparotomy is performed 24-48 hours postoperatively, with reassessment of viability and determination of the appropriateness of intestinal resection. The resumption of transit at the ileostomy is monitored, followed by the initiation of oral feeding – a high-calorie diet, intravenous fluid replacement, and broad-spectrum antibiotic prophylaxis. The patient is monitored cardiologically. Anticoagulation with continuous heparin is maintained, followed by conversion to Sintrom with a target INR of 2.5-3.5. In the context of favourable evolution, the patient will benefit from reintegration into transit 3 months postoperatively.

cases.title: Diffuse abdominal pain, bloody and mucous diarrhoea, and weight loss
kp: Medical first; surgery for complications/refractory disease
cases.presentation: Patient A.B., a 45-year-old engineer from an urban environment, with no significant medical history, smoker, presents at the gastroenterology clinic with diffuse abdominal pain, bloody and mucous diarrhoea, low-grade fever and weight loss of approximately 10 kg in 2 months. The current illness began insidiously 2 months ago with intermittent diffuse abdominal pain, weight loss of 10 kg in the last 2 months, daily diarrhoea with mucus for 2 weeks, then with blood in the last week, and low-grade fever for 3 days. He has smoked ten cigarettes a day for 20 years and consumes alcohol occasionally. Clinical examination on admission reveals a patient with pale skin and mucous membranes, normal weight (BMI-23), clinically normal lungs, BP-120/70 mmHg, HR-61 b/min, with rhythmic heart sounds, soft abdomen, mobile with breathing, spontaneously painful and on palpation in the right hemiabdomen. Axillary temperature 37.40C. Laboratory tests reveal anaemia Hb 11.2, increased white blood cell count (14,000/mm³), with a left shift in the white blood cell formula.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics Ulcerative colitis The disease affects the rectum and colon, the damage is continuous, the thickening of the intestinal wall is discreet, there are no intestinal granulomas, with superficial ulcerations.

Shigellosis The clinical picture is that of food poisoning, differing from Crohn's disease in terms of dehydration and significant deterioration in general health, associated with hypotension and tachycardia. Repeated stool cultures are mandatory and decisive in the differential diagnosis.

Salmonellosis They are more severe in clinical expression. Endotoxins with enterotoxic, neurotoxic and leukopenic effects, together with the effects of exotoxins, amplify the picture of acute gastroenterocolitis, associating important systemic manifestations: chills, fever, headache, severe dehydration, hypotension. The presence of arthritis or osteomyelitis-like manifestations in salmonellosis complicates the differential diagnosis, especially for cases of Crohn's disease with extra-digestive manifestations. Repeated stool cultures, blood cultures or urine cultures confirm the diagnosis.

Amoebiasis The differential diagnosis is made colonoscopically and morphologically (predominantly cecal and ascending colon involvement), revealing multiple small ulcers with normal mucosa between them. Rectosigmoidoscopy is used to collect pathological products from the ulcers to identify trophozoites. Stool cultures are the second most important procedure for differential diagnosis. Most patients have a history of travel to tropical countries.

Intestinal tuberculosis Bacillary impregnation syndrome, characterised by night sweats, low-grade fever, and weight loss, is difficult to differentiate from the clinical picture of Crohn's disease. Radiologically, tuberculosis is dominated by circumferential ulcerations and shortdistance stenoses, whereas Crohn's disease is characterised by predominantly linear ulcerations and long-distance stenoses. Calcifications of the mesenteric lymph nodes and active pulmonary lesions support the diagnosis of tuberculosis. Endoscopically, tuberculosis does not show the "cobblestone" sign, which is common in Crohn's disease. Morphologically, caseous granuloma
Diffuse abdominal pain, bloody and mucus-containing diarrhoea, and weight loss

Evidence found in the intestinal wall, usually intraoperatively, or in the abdominal lymph nodes, confirms the differential diagnosis, similar to direct bacteriological examination or culture on Lowenstein medium.

Venereal lymphogranulom atosis This is a sexually transmitted disease. The differential diagnosis is required with Crohn's disease due to the presence of diarrhoea syndrome, associated or not with rectal bleeding, perianal abscesses or rectovaginal fistulas. Rectoscopy reveals an ulcerated, granular or simply oedematous mucosa. Specific serological tests for Chlamydia trachomatis confirm the diagnosis.

Intestinal tumours intestinal Pseudotumoral forms of Crohn's disease can create diagnostic pitfalls both in the clinical and intraoperative stages, with only morphopathological arguments being able to clarify the diagnosis. Intestinal tumours, including rare forms of lymphoma that usually affect the caecal region, may have radiological correlates such as stenosis or fistulas. In approximately 7% of pseudotumoral forms of Crohn's disease, the preoperative diagnosis falsely suggested an intestinal tumour.

Behcet's disease Approximately 50% of cases present digestive lesions usually located in the ileocecal segment. Colonoscopy reveals ulcers of the cecal mucosa, usually deep, with biopsy revealing small vasculitic lesions, sometimes with thrombosis, changes that are absent in Crohn's disease. The ulcers are very similar to those in Crohn's disease, but the edges are more regular, with the surrounding mucosa appearing normal.

Collagenous colitis collagenous Unlike Crohn's disease, the colonic mucosa has a normal pattern, but biopsies, especially from the right colon, will reveal an increased number of lymphocytes in the lamina propria and superficial epithelium, and in particular, a thickened band (60-70 μm) of collagen, subepithelial, at which an increased number of fibroblasts can be seen. It should be noted that electron microscopy studies have confirmed that the basement membrane of the epithelium is normal, the lesion being expressed only by the band of collagen deposited under the epithelium.

Lymphocytic colitis colitis Affects the entire colon, and here the colonic mucosa has a normal macroscopic pattern. Lymphocytic colitis is defined by the presence of lymphocytes and plasma cells at the intraepithelial level. There are also increased numbers of eosinophils and neutrophils in varying proportions.

Pseudomembrano us colitis It is not only a clinical-pathological condition correlated with broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, but also a colitis described in patients with Hirschsprung's disease, leukaemia, or even after laborious colonoscopies. Pseudomembranes are present on rectoscopic examination, in most cases representing a characteristic element of differential diagnosis with Crohn's disease. In the absence of membranes, the presence of focal epithelial necrosis in the interglandular spaces or eosinophilic exudate with fibrin and polynuclear cells in the lamina propria, which frequently erupts into the intestinal lumen, is indicative of pseudomembranous colitis.

Ischemic colitis colitis Affects the left colon in 70% of cases. It is characteristic of patients over 50 years of age and is usually self-limiting after 1-2 weeks. After this interval, segmental ischaemic colitis develops or complications arise: strictures, gangrene, fistulas, perforations. Colonoscopy should be performed as early as possible (within the first 48 hours) to highlight the haemorrhagic nodules in the submucosa, which disappear after 3-5 days, a feature not seen in Crohn's disease. Only a biopsy reveals elements that differentiate in favour of ischaemic aetiology (macrophages with iron deposits and submucosal fibrosis).

Colitis secondary to drugs or chemical agents The use of contraceptives has been the cause of colitis with a clinical and morphological appearance similar to Crohn's disease, but discontinuation of use has resulted in remission of symptoms. Treatment with methotrexate or gold salts has caused rare cases of colitis with clinical and endoscopic features similar to Crohn's disease. The defining features for the differential diagnosis were mild, non-ulcerative morphological aspects, with evidence of eosinophils in the lamina propria. Lesions induced by the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can mimic Crohn's disease, and discontinuation of their administration will induce healing.

Radic enterocolitis A differential diagnosis is required due to the clinical picture being similar to that of Crohn's disease. Symptoms may appear clinically even months/years after the completion of radiotherapy. Rectosigmoidoscopy reveals mucosal oedema and an altered vascular pattern. Complications such as fistulas, perforations or stenoses can closely mimic Crohn's disease.
Diffuse abdominal pain, bloody and mucus-containing diarrhoea, and weight loss

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Inflammatory bowel disease.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: The patient is admitted to the gastroenterology department for further investigation. The clinical picture is typical of inflammatory bowel disease, but this needs to be confirmed by colonoscopy with terminal ileoscopy and histopathological examination.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: Since the patient is relatively young, there are no comorbidities, and the disease is fairly recent, with no other complications, the severity of the disease is moderate and the prognosis is favourable with appropriate treatment.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Despite the progress made, medical treatment remains empirical because the aetiology of the disease is not yet known. There are three types of medical treatment: curative, symptomatic and nutritional. Smoking cessation is mandatory. Curative treatment includes sulfasalazine, corticosteroids and immunosuppressants.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Improvement of symptoms and healing of intestinal wall lesions monitored by colonoscopy and terminal ileoscopy.
