cases.title: Abdominal pain located in the right iliac fossa
kp: Migrating pain to RIF, nausea, low fever
cases.presentation: Patient VH, a 28-year-old electrical engineer, presents at the surgical clinic outpatient department with pain in the right iliac fossa. The current illness began suddenly the previous morning, with diffuse, persistent abdominal pain located around the navel, followed a few hours later by nausea and vomiting. During the night, the pain moved to the right iliac fossa, persistent, moderate in intensity, accentuated by coughing and movement. He has had no appetite since the onset of the illness and is "in a bad mood". He smokes twenty cigarettes a day and drinks alcohol occasionally. On physical examination, the patient is of normal weight, pale, anxious, and feverish. The abdomen participates in respiratory movements, is slightly distended, and has no hydroaerial sounds. In the right iliac fossa, there is skin hypoesthesia, pain on superficial and deep palpation, and muscle guarding. The pain in the right iliac fossa is accentuated by flexing the thigh on the abdomen and by deep palpation in the left iliac fossa. Axillary temperature 38.20C. Laboratory tests show an increase in the number of leukocytes (12,000/mm³), with a left shift in the leukocyte formula. Simple urine test: rare leukocytes, no bacteriuria.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics In both sexes Acute appendicitis Diffuse and persistent peri-umbilical pain, followed by nausea and vomiting. The pain then migrates to the right iliac fossa. Loss of appetite, fever, altered general condition. Pain on palpation in the right iliac fossa (McBurney or Lange points) and signs of peritoneal irritation. Blumberg, Rovsing, psoas and obturator signs.
Cecal diverticulitis Identical to those of acute appendicitis.

Meckel's diverticulitis Identical to those of acute appendicitis. Meckel's diverticulum is present in 2% of the general population, twice as common in men, located on the terminal ileum 50-60 cm from the ileocecal valve. Inflammatory complications (diverticulitis), intestinal obstruction (volvulus or intussusception) and gastrointestinal haemorrhage (rectal bleeding, especially in children) are usually due to the presence of ectopic tissue: pancreatic or gastric mucosa.
Inflammatory bowel diseases – Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis

Crohn's disease – colicky abdominal pain, diarrhoea, gastrointestinal bleeding, anaemia, weight loss, abscesses, enterocutaneous fistulas, perianorectal abscesses and fistulas, toxic megacolon. In ileocecal Crohn's disease, pain and signs of peritoneal irritation are located in the right iliac fossa.

Lithiasis and urinary tract infections Severe abdominal pain in the flank and lower back, radiating downwards towards the genitals and the medial aspect of the thigh, nausea, vomiting, haematuria, dysuria, pollakiuria. Lumbar muscle spasm. Muscle spasm in the flank diminishes with deep inspiration.
Acute gastroenteritis Nausea and vomiting precede diffuse abdominal pain, which is colicky in nature. Watery or bloody diarrhoea, myalgia, fever and leukocytosis are present.

Acute pancreatitis Epigastric abdominal pain with dorsal and "bar-like" radiation, of high intensity, nausea, vomiting, anorexia and marked alteration of general condition. History of gallstones or alcoholism. In situations where ascites migrates along the parietocolic groove to the right iliac fossa, the pain is sometimes most intense at this level. Acute cholecystitis
Pain in the right hypochondrium radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, positive Murphy's sign. An inflamed, distended and ptotic gallbladder may manifest as pain in the right iliac fossa.

Perforated duodenal ulcer Sudden, intense epigastric pain, muscle contracture. History of chronic gastroduodenal ulcer, treatment with non-specific anti-inflammatory drugs or H. pylori infection. Gastric juice migration along the right parietocolic groove causes pain and signs of peritoneal irritation in the right iliac fossa.

Sigmoid diverticulitis Pain and signs of peritoneal irritation in the left iliac fossa in elderly people, nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, fever, leukocytosis. When the sigmoid loop is long and located in the right iliac fossa, abdominal pain is most severe at this level.

In women Mittelschmerz Unilateral pain in the lower abdomen, in the middle of the menstrual cycle, caused by the rupture of the ovarian follicle. The pain is moderate in intensity, lasts for hours or days, without fever or leukocytosis and without changing the general condition. There are no signs of peritoneal irritation and the gynaecological examination shows normal results.

Pelvic inflammatory disease Purulent vaginal discharge, exocervicitis, sensitivity to cervical mobilisation, sensitive and altered adnexa. Fever and leukocytosis, dysuria, pollakiuria, with little change in general condition. History of genital infections with Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia.
Ovarian cyst Torsion Severe pelvic pain with sudden onset and altered general condition, adnexal mass, history of ovarian cysts.

Ruptured ectopic pregnancy Sudden onset in a woman with clinical signs of pregnancy or amenorrhea, typically 6-8 weeks after the last normal menstrual period, with lower abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, anaemia, or haemorrhagic shock. Positive pregnancy test.

In children Mesenteric lymphadenitis Child with recent or ongoing acute respiratory infection, with fever and leukocytosis. Abdominal pain is diffuse and more pronounced in the right iliac fossa, due to inflammatory changes in the mesenteric lymph nodes. Acute gastroenteritis
Nausea, vomiting, colicky abdominal pain, watery or bloody diarrhoea, fever, myalgia.
Yersinia enterocolitica infection Pain in the right iliac fossa, fever, vomiting and haemorrhagic diarrhoea. History of community infection (nursery, kindergarten).
Pneumococcal pneumonia Respiratory symptoms, fever, nausea, vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain.
Intussusception In young children (one year old) nausea, vomiting and colicky abdominal pain with "jelly-like" stools and a "sausage-like" abdominal mass
Sigmoid diverticulitis "Acute appendicitis on the left." Diverticulitis is common in the elderly.
Cecal cancer Tumour mass in the right iliac fossa, anaemia, intestinal transit disorders, variable inflammatory signs.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Acute appendicitis.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: The patient is offered emergency surgery/appendectomy. The clinical picture is typical, so imaging confirmation is not necessary. Laparoscopic surgery allows abdominal exploration and resolution of other conditions requiring surgical treatment. Oral intake is stopped and coagulation tests are performed. If the doctor or patient still considers imaging confirmation necessary, a contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan or abdominal ultrasound is performed.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: Since the patient is young, has no comorbidities, and has recent-onset, localized appendicular inflammation, the severity of the disease is low and the prognosis is favorable with appropriate treatment.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Open or laparoscopic appendectomy, depending on the surgeon's experience and the patient's preference. If surgical treatment is not available or if the patient refuses surgery, broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment covering the intestinal flora is administered.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Disappearance of fever and abdominal symptoms, resumption of bowel movements and food tolerance, rapid improvement in general condition.

cases.title: Abdominal pain located in the left iliac fossa
kp: LIF pain + fever + bowel habit change
Antibiotics; drainage of abscess; Hartmann for III–IV
cases.presentation: A 68-year-old female patient, retired (former accountant) from an urban area, is brought to the emergency room by her family due to intense abdominal pain, more pronounced in the left iliac fossa, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. History of the current illness: for approximately 4 years, the patient has experienced episodes of abdominal pain characterised by cramps or dull pain located in the left iliac fossa, accompanied by constipation. She is a smoker (10 cigarettes per day) and consumes alcohol occasionally. The current episode of abdominal pain began 24 hours ago, with the same cramping in the left iliac fossa, but the pain has not subsided. In the last 4 hours, the pain has increased in intensity, becoming excruciating, and subsides for short periods if she sits in a crouched position. For 2 hours, she has been experiencing nausea and vomiting. She has not had a bowel movement for 36 hours. Personal medical history: appendectomy at age 18, cholecystectomy for acute calculous cholecystitis via median incision at age 51. Physical examination: 1.72 m tall, 90 kg weight. He has not lost weight recently. On palpation, abdomen with muscle contracture and signs of peritoneal irritation. Axillary temperature is 38.30C. BP = 120/65 mmHg, pulse 100 beats per minute, shallow breathing, suffering facies. Laboratory tests: leukocytosis (16,500/mm³) with 84% neutrophils. Urinalysis shows normal results.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics In both sexes Acute perforated Severe abdominal pain, more pronounced in the left iliac fossa, accompanied by sigmoid diverticulitis nausea and vomiting. Signs of peritoneal irritation present. Fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, suffering facies. Stopping of gas and faecal transit. History of painful episodes with cramps or dull pain located in the left iliac fossa, accompanied by constipation.

Perforated gastric/duodenal ulcer Sudden onset of extremely intense epigastric pain with abdominal muscle contraction. There is usually a history of gastric or duodenal ulcer or treatment with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Clinical signs of acute abdomen, pneumoperitoneum.

Inflammatory bowel Colic abdominal pain associated with diarrhoea. Lower gastrointestinal bleeding, diseases – leading to anaemia. Weight loss. Entero-cutaneous and perianorectal abscesses and haemorrhagic fistulas, toxic megacolon. rectocolitis, Crohn's disease Ureteral lithiasis and Severe abdominal pain in the flank and lower back, radiating downwards towards the upper/lower urinary genitals and the medial aspect of the thigh, nausea, vomiting, haematuria, dysuria, tract infections pollakiuria. Sometimes, when ureteral lithiasis is located in the iliac region, the pain is strictly in the left iliac fossa, without lumbar pain or pain in the left flank. Lumbar muscle contracture. Muscle contracture in the flank diminishes with deep inspiration. In lower urinary tract infections, pain is predominantly in the hypogastrium, with the symptoms of upper urinary tract infections overlapping with upper ureteral lithiasis. Pyuria is present and responds favourably to antibiotic treatment.

Acute pancreatitis Very intense abdominal pain in the epigastric region, radiating to the back. Associated with anorexia and marked deterioration in general condition, with nausea and vomiting. Cold sweats, tachycardia, ta-hypnosis. A history of gallstones or increased alcohol consumption can usually be detected. In some situations, the ascites migrates along the left parietocolic groove towards the left iliac fossa, and the pain is most intense at this level.

Acute appendicitis Pain with periombilical onset, diffuse and persistent. After a few hours, the pain migrates to the right iliac fossa. Other symptoms may occur, such as general malaise with loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting, fever, tachycardia, tachypnea. Palpation of the right iliac fossa is painful (McBurney or Lange point) and signs of peritoneal irritation are noted - Blumberg, psoas, Rowsing, obturator, Mandel, etc.

Meckel's diverticulitis Symptoms and signs are almost identical to those of acute appendicitis. Meckel's diverticulum is located in the terminal ileum, approximately 50-80 cm from the ileocecal valve, and is present in approximately 2-3% of the general population, more commonly in males. Meckel's diverticulum can cause inflammatory complications (Meckel's diverticulitis or Meckelitis), haemorrhagic complications, and intestinal obstruction through volvulus or intussusception. These manifestations are due to the presence of ectopic pancreatic tissue or gastric mucosa.
Herpes zoster Burning pain in the left iliac fossa, associated with (and) herpetic rash. The pain is usually superficial. Difficult to diagnose in the pre-eruptive phase.

Acute appendicitis Rarely, acute appendicitis can cause characteristic pain, but located in the left iliac fossa (e.g. mesoceliac appendix, against a background of mobile cecum). The diagnosis is usually made by imaging or laparotomy/laparoscopy.

Strangulated left inguinal/femoral hernia Pain in the left groin area, visible and palpable formation, irreducible, firm consistency, sometimes with inflammatory phenomena. Attempts to reduce it are extremely painful. There is usually a known history of inguinal hernia.

Ischemic colitis Ischemic Diffuse abdominal pain syndrome, more pronounced after meals. Loss of appetite and weight, diarrhoea, constipation, nausea and vomiting. Abdominal cramps or a feeling of fullness after eating may occur.

Colorectal cancer Diarrhoea, constipation or alternating diarrhoea and constipation. Anaemia (more common in the ascending colon), occlusive syndrome (more common in the left colon and rectum). Signs of malignant infiltration – fatigue, weight loss, loss of appetite, pale appearance of the skin and mucous membranes. Changes in stool appearance (blood or mucus on the surface, "pencil-thin")

Psoas abscess "Cold" abscess Spontaneous pain and tenderness in the left iliac fossa, groin area, and front of the thigh. Tendency to maintain slight flexion of the thigh on the abdomen. Associated: prolonged and irregular fever, weight loss, altered general condition. Possible personal pathological/hereditary history of tuberculosis.

Infectious colitis infectious It causes dull and/or colicky pain, located in the left iliac fossa, hypogastrium or right iliac fossa. Associated symptoms: fever, chills, myalgia, arthralgia, headache. The patient presents with diarrhoea, with more than 10 watery or bloody stools, sometimes accompanied by rectal tenesmus. The patient experiences pain on palpation of the lower abdomen, but without frequent signs of peritoneal irritation.

Irritable bowel syndrome Chronic abdominal pain syndrome, relieved by intestinal prokinetics. Gaseous dyspepsia and tenesmus. Diarrhoea alternates with constipation. Sometimes presence of mucus, absence of blood in stool. Often anxiety or depression.

In females Ruptured ectopic pregnancy Brutal onset, usually 6-8 weeks after the last menstrual cycle. Women with amenorrhea or clinically detected pregnancy. Progressive pain in the lower abdomen accompanied by vaginal bleeding that can lead to anaemia or even haemorrhagic shock. Elevated betaHCG, positive pregnancy test.
Ovarian cyst Torsion Known history of ovarian cysts. Intense pain in the pelvis, sudden onset and altered general condition. An adnexal mass can sometimes be palpated.

Pelvic inflammatory disease Painful syndrome of varying intensity in the hypogastrium, accentuated by mobilisation of the cervix. Pain in the area of the adnexa. Purulent vaginal discharge. Signs of exocervicitis. Accompanied by urinary signs (pollakiuria, bladder tenesmus, dysuria), sometimes fever and leukocytosis. Discomfort in the genital area, but general condition relatively preserved. History of gonococcal or Chlamydia infections.

Mittelschmerz Pain occurring in the middle of the menstrual cycle, following the rupture of the ovarian follicle, which occurs unilaterally in the lower abdomen (iliac fossa, inguinal region, hypogastrium). It lasts from a few hours to a few days and is of moderate intensity. It is not associated with leukocytosis, fever or alteration of the general condition. No signs of peritoneal irritation. Normal findings on gynaecological examination.

In children Mesenteric lymphadenitis Diffuse abdominal pain, more pronounced in the right iliac fossa. Fever, leukocytosis, altered general condition. A recent history or examination reveals an acute respiratory infection.
Pneumococcal pneumonia Respiratory symptoms predominate. Diffuse abdominal pain. Associated with fever, nausea and vomiting with general malaise.
Yersinia enterocolitica infection Diffuse abdominal pain, with fever and vomiting. Haemorrhagic diarrhoea often occurs. Characteristic when the child enters communities (school).
Intestinal intussusceptio n Colic-like abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, which can lead to dehydration. Signs of intestinal obstruction, sometimes the invaginated intestinal mass can be palpated.
Acute gastroenteritis Colic-like abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting, fever, watery or bloody diarrhoea, general malaise, dehydration, myalgia.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Acute perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with generalised peritonitis.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: The clinical picture is suggestive of generalized peritonitis. Symptomatology, medical history, anamnesis, and physical examination lead to the diagnosis of acute perforated diverticulitis as the source of peritonitis. Oral intake of food and liquids is discontinued. A nasogastric tube is inserted. Peripheral and central venous catheterisation is performed. Contrast-enhanced CT scanning of the abdomen and pelvis is extremely useful in determining the cause of peritonitis, if the patient's general condition allows it and the examination is available. The patient is offered surgery, which has two objectives: to treat the generalized peritonitis and to repair the perforation of the hollow organ that led to it. The situation and proposed treatment, risks, complications and possible consequences are presented. The patient's informed consent for surgery is obtained. Bladder catheterisation. Emergency laboratory tests – complete blood count, biochemistry, ionogram, coagulation profile, Astrup test. Compensation of vital functions, hydroelectrolytic and acid-base rebalancing.
Intravenous antibiotic treatment. Preparation and transfer of the patient to the operating theatre. Close monitoring throughout the above stages. The family or relatives are informed.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: The patient's condition is serious, and the risk is life-threatening in the absence of immediate emergency surgery. Because peritonitis due to acute perforated diverticulitis is hyperseptic, purulent or stercoral, the natural progression of the disease in the absence of surgical treatment will lead to septic shock, multiple organ failure and death within a few hours.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Emergency surgical treatment – Hartmann's operation: segmental resection of the sigmoid colon, closure of the distal stump and temporary left iliac terminal colostomy. Cleaning, lavage and drainage of the peritoneal cavity. Pre-, intra- and post-operative rebalancing of electrolytes and acid-base balance, intravenous antibiotic treatment. The second stage of the intervention, restoration of the continuity of the digestive tract through colo-rectal anastomosis, follows 3-6 months after the initial operation.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Disappearance of abdominal and general clinical manifestations – pain, nausea, vomiting, fever. Resumption of intestinal transit for gas and faeces. Normalisation of vital parameters and laboratory tests.

cases.title: Newly developed constipation and difficulty in defecation with pencil-thin stools
cases.presentation: "pencil-thin" stools A 60-year-old Caucasian male from an urban environment presents to the hospital's surgical outpatient clinic with recent onset of intermittent constipation and pencil-thin stools. The medical history reveals that for about 6 months he has had intermittent episodes of constipation (bowel movements every 2-4 days). Previously, bowel movements were daily. The current appearance of the stool is pencil-like, and defecation is difficult. After defecation, the patient sometimes complains of a feeling of incomplete emptying. He reports that he sometimes observes streaks of fresh blood or mucus on the surface of his stool. The patient has lost approximately 7 kg in weight over the last 3 months, despite not changing his eating habits. From his medical history, we note that: he has been a cigarette smoker (about one pack a day) since the age of 20; he has type II diabetes mellitus and is treated with oral antidiabetic medication, maintaining his blood sugar within limits of up to 140 mg%; he has chronic ischaemic heart disease and essential hypertension for which he is receiving medication, he has mixed dyslipidaemia and hepatic steatosis for which he is not receiving the prescribed medication. He has no history or family history of neoplasms. He has never had a lower digestive endoscopy. He is a former accountant, currently retired due to illness. Physical examination reveals: ICM of 32; BP: 140/90 mm Hg, pulse 78/min. The abdomen is globular due to subcutaneous cellular tissue, without postoperative scars, participating in respiratory movements, without sensitivity to superficial and deep palpation, without distinguishing intra-abdominal tumour masses.

Diagnosis based on symptoms – chronic abdominal pain relieved by intestinal prokinetics, gassy dyspepsia, tenesmus Frequently associated with anxiety or depression

Newly developed constipation and difficulty passing stools that are "pencil-thin"

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Given the reported symptoms and age, the most likely diagnosis is colon or rectal cancer. The digestive symptoms for which he sought consultation are those of a slow-growing obstructive lesion, as indicated by the disturbance of intestinal transit and the change in stool appearance (pencil-thin). These changes are suggestive of malignant lesions of the left colon (especially the sigmoid colon or rectosigmoid junction) or rectum.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: A rectal examination will be performed, which can sometimes detect the tumour. The patient will be prepared for a colonoscopy. If a tumour is found, biopsies will be taken and sent for histopathological examination. If the endoscopic examination reveals a tumour on the colon, computed tomography (CT) scans of the chest, abdomen and pelvis will be performed with contrast medium to allow for accurate staging. If the tumour is located in the rectum, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and transrectal echoendoscopy will be performed for the same purpose. Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) will be collected and specific laboratory tests will be performed to explore and assess the preoperative metabolic status.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: Given the relatively rapid weight loss and the subocclusive phenomena described in the medical history, an advanced local stage of the disease can be assumed, which implies an urgent need for endoscopy and other staging investigations, as well as the initiation of treatment.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: If no acute occlusive episode occurs during the preparation period for endoscopy, the type of therapeutic sequence will be assessed based on the results of the endoscopic examination, histopathological examination and staging imaging tests, and will be proposed to the patient. The patient is the only one who can decide whether and what kind of treatment to accept. To this end, they will read and sign the "patient's informed consent" form.

If an occlusive episode occurs during preparation, the case becomes a surgical emergency. Occlusive syndrome is a life-threatening medical emergency (see also Chapter: Acute surgical abdomen, Subchapter: Intestinal obstruction). This requires surgery to restore optimal digestive transit and prepare for possible radical oncological surgery in approximately 4-6 weeks. Usually, in such situations, a diverting colostomy ("on a stick") is performed, either on the sigmoid colon or on the transverse colon, upstream of the occlusive tumour.

cases.title: Rectal bleeding, anaemia and tumour on rectal examination
kp: Rectal bleeding, anaemia, tumour on DRE
cases.presentation: A 50-year-old patient, a locksmith by profession, consults his family doctor for repeated episodes of rectal bleeding, asthenia and precordial pain. The current illness began two months ago with repeated rectal bleeding during bowel movements, in small amounts. Bowel movements are normal, one per day, with no noticeable changes in the last two months. Physical examination reveals an overweight patient with slightly pale skin. The abdomen participates in respiratory movements, shows no sensitivity to superficial or deep palpation; percussion reveals tympanism, and hydroaerial sounds are present. A rectal examination is performed and a slightly haemorrhagic rectal tumour is identified with the lower pole 7 cm from the anal orifice. Laboratory tests reveal moderate microcytic hypochromic anaemia (Hb = 10.9, Hct = 29%). Colonoscopy revealed a vegetative, haemorrhagic tumour starting 9 cm from the anal orifice and extending cranially for approximately 5 cm. Histopathological examination of the biopsies confirmed the diagnosis of moderately differentiated G2 adenocarcinoma. MRI revealed a semi-circumferential tumour 8 cm from the anal orifice, located on the right posterolateral rectal wall, measuring 5 cm and invading the perirectal fat; Three macroscopically round, suspicious adenopathies measuring between 5 and 10 mm are identified in the mesorectum (Figure 1 A-C). Thoracoabdominal CT with contrast does not reveal any secondary pulmonary or hepatic lesions. Two suspicious round lymph nodes are identified along the inferior mesenteric artery.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics Internal haemorrhoids Internal Important: The appearance of rectal bleeding or haemorrhoids in a patient over the age of 40 should raise suspicion of rectal cancer and requires a colonoscopy for diagnosis.

Haemorrhagic haemorrhagic Specific to rectocolitis are the diarrhoeic stools that accompany rectal bleeding. The phenotype of the patient with haemorrhagic rectocolitis is: young, underweight patient with multiple diarrhoeic stools associated with rectal bleeding, possibly with a family history of autoimmune diseases.
Rectal polyp (adenoma/benign tumour)

The presence of friable rectal polyps leads to rectal bleeding, with fresh red blood, especially when passing more consistent stools. Colonoscopy with multiple biopsies is required to determine whether the polyp is benign (tubular or villous adenoma) or malignant (rectal adenocarcinoma).

Rectal cancer Clinically, rectal cancer manifests itself through intestinal transit disorders. Middle or distal rectal tumours, through invasion/thrombosis of haemorrhoidal veins, will trigger the appearance of symptomatic haemorrhoids. The presence of a friable tumour will lead to rectal bleeding, usually with fresh red blood, especially when passing more consistent stools. Stenotic tumours will result in thin, pencil-like stools, with a predominance of constipation or alternating constipation and diarrhoea. As it progresses, stenosis creates the conditions for the onset of subocclusive or even frank occlusive syndrome. Villous tumours will produce a rectal syndrome with the production of excessive amounts of mucus that is evacuated transanally between stools. Sometimes, significant losses of mucous fluid from large villous tumours can lead to dehydration and electrolyte imbalances.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Middle rectal cancer.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: To confirm the diagnosis of rectal cancer, a rectoscopy/colonoscopy is required to visualise the lumen of the rectum and the overlying colon and, if tumours are identified, will take multiple biopsies for histopathological examination. To determine the stage of the tumour, a series of additional investigations are required. Rectal MRI is the gold standard for staging rectal cancer. It highlights the tumour and its extension into the mesorectum, visualises the perirectal fascia and can differentiate between tumours that have invaded the rectal fascia, known as CRM+ (colorectal margin positive), and those that have not invaded it and are at least 1 mm away from it, known as CRM- (colorectal margin negative). MRI also identifies the presence of lymph nodes in the mesorectum suspected of being invaded. Endorectal ultrasound. Its role is to determine tumour invasion into the rectal wall. It can also identify suspicious lymph nodes in the mesorectum near the rectal wall, but has difficulty visualising the rest of the lymph nodes in the mesorectum. Observation. MRI accurately visualises the location of the tumour, its relationship with neighbouring anatomical structures and the presence of suspicious lymph nodes in the mesorectum. Endorectal ultrasound more accurately identifies early-stage tumours that have penetrated only as far as the muscularis propria. Contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominal computed tomography: identifies suspicious lymph nodes in the superior rectal and inferior mesenteric arteries, periaortic adenopathies, the presence of liver, lung or other systemic metastases, and the presence of peritoneal deposits in the Douglas pouch or other abdominal quadrants.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: With appropriate treatment, the prognosis for patients with colorectal cancer is generally good, as rectal cancer responds to adjuvant or neoadjuvant radio-chemotherapy. The 5-year survival rate for stage IIIB rectal cancer is 72%. Even in stage IV, with systemic metastases, a 5-year survival rate of 40% can be achieved if the entire tumour volume, meaning the primary tumour and systemic metastases, is successfully removed. Given the patient's relatively young age, absence of comorbidities and stage IIIB tumour, with appropriate treatment, the patient's prognosis is favourable with a 5-year survival rate of approximately 72%.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: For this patient with mid-rectal cancer stage CT3N2M0 (IIIB), the optimal treatment is multidisciplinary and begins with long-course neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy 52Gy followed 10-12 weeks after completion of RCT by anterior resection of the low rectum with total mesorectal excision and low colo-rectal anastomosis protected by a temporary lateral ileostomy on a rod.

For large T3 rectal cancer located in the middle and lower portion of the rectum, neoadjuvant radiotherapy with a total dose of 52 Gy combined with sensitising chemotherapy as the first therapeutic step aims to reduce tumour sizeand sterilise the tissues close to the resection plane in order to facilitate surgical resection and reduce the risk of incomplete resection (R1 or R2) and, implicitly, the risk of local recurrence. Given that the tumour is 8 cm from the OA, the recommended distal resection margin is 2 cm. Ileostomy is recommended because the anastomosis is located less than 8 cm from the OA and preoperative radiotherapy is a significant risk factor for the development of an anastomotic fistula. The ileostomy will be reintegrated into the transit after 3-4 weeks or after completion of adjuvant chemotherapy.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: During the first 5 years after surgery, oncological monitoring is required to identify local and systemic recurrence at an early stage. After surgery, patients are referred to the oncology committee, which determines the need for adjuvant chemotherapy and includes the patient in a postoperative follow-up programme consisting of:
– clinical examination and serum tumour marker sampling every 3 months for the first 3 years after surgery, every 6 months in years 4-5 after surgery, and then annually;

– colonoscopy 6 months postoperatively and annually thereafter; – MRI 6 months postoperatively and then annually; – CT scan 6 months after surgery and then annually (Note: MRI and CT scans can be alternated at 6month intervals);
– Surgical consultation at the end of oncological treatment and then annually.

cases.title: Abdominal pain accompanied by bloody diarrhoea and general malaise
kp: Exclude C. difficile/CMV; X-ray colon diameter
IV steroids, fluids, antibiotics; colectomy if no response
cases.presentation: A 28-year-old Norwegian patient of Jewish descent, who emigrated to Australia, a civil engineer by profession, visiting Romania for 10 days, presents to the emergency department with bloody diarrhoea, accompanied by moderate abdominal pain and subfebrile temperature up to 37.8°C, which began a week ago. He has lost 4 kg in weight this week, and his general condition is affected. From his personal history, we note erythema nodosum three years ago. He recalls that his father, now 59 years old, a farmer and heavy smoker, had similar symptoms in his youth and was diagnosed with sclerosing cholangitis five years ago. Our patient had five bowel movements per day during the last week. Physical examination of the young man reveals slight pallor of the skin and bilateral conjunctival redness. His heart rate is 90/min. A rectal examination reveals grade I haemorrhoids, a slightly hypertonic anal sphincter, the presence of blood on the examiner's glove, and no palpable tumours. Laboratory tests reveal: ESR = 30 mm/h, haemoglobin (10.5 g/dl), platelets (500,000/mm3 ), hypoalbuminaemia, CRP (30 mg/l). Sigmoidoscopy up to 22 cm from the anal opening reveals pale mucosa with blurred vascular pattern, microhaemorrhages, friable on contact with the endoscope and with several pseudopolyps; several biopsies are taken. The biopsies reveal crypt distortions, acute inflammation (cryptitis), accompanied in places by crypt abscesses with numerous PMNs, plasma-lymphocytic infiltrate in the lamina propria.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics Ulcerative colitis ulcerative Prevalence is high in Europe, especially in Norway; the overall incidence is 7.3/100,000 inhabitants, with a prevalence of 116/100,000 inhabitants; there is a north-south gradient, with maximum incidence in Iceland, but recently high incidences have been found in Australia and New Zealand; prevalence is also high among Ashkenazi Jews (prevalence is 3-5 times higher); in addition, the young man has a first-degree relative who is very likely to have UC (up to 15% of patients with UC have a first-degree relative with this condition). The patient is a non-smoker, as smoking halves the risk of developing UC. There is continuous inflammation of the mucosa, limited to the colon (lower digestive endoscopy), without granulomas (histopathological). Intestinal manifestations include diarrhoea, intestinal haemorrhage and abdominal pain. Diarrhoea occurs during the day and at night; it appears as an initial symptom in 52% of cases and in the first year in 85-100% of cases. Five to twenty small stools per day are described. In proctitis and proctosigmoiditis, proctalgia, rectal tenesmus, and an urgent need to defecate occur, and diarrhoea may be absent (due to rectal spasm). Lower gastrointestinal bleeding occurs as an initial symptom in 80% of cases and in the first year in 100% of cases. Depending on the location and severity of the condition, there may be rectal bleeding with red blood covering the stool or pseudohaemorrhoidal rectal bleeding at the end of defecation (in proctitis and proctosigmoiditis), diarrhoea mixed with partially digested blood in extensive colitis, diarrhoea mixed with partially digested blood and pus in severe forms. Abdominal pain is non-specific; pain may occur in the projection area of the left colon. Proctalgia and rectal tenesmus also occur in distal involvement.

Crohn's disease It is a transmural inflammation that can extend from the oral cavity to the anus, with some areas remaining unaffected. Diarrhoea occurs in approximately 75% of cases, but varies depending on the location of the lesions. In the case of ileal lesions, there are 5-6 semi-formed stools per day, without blood; in cases of severe and extensive involvement of the terminal ileum or its exclusion from the digestive tract, malabsorption of acids and bile salts, manifested by explosive watery stools - collogenic diarrhoea; secondary to bile acid malabsorption, lipid malabsorption occurs, manifested by steatorrhoeic diarrhoea; in colonic involvement, rarely with rectal involvement, rectal tenesmus and numerous small stools may occur. Bloody diarrhoea is much rarer than in RCUH (20% versus 100%). Abdominal pain occurs in approximately 75% of patients and correlates with the anatomical location of the condition. In ileal involvement, pain occurs in the right iliac fossa and hypogastrium, ranging from discomfort to constant pain; when it becomes colicky, it suggests an infectious complication or stenosis. Anal involvement may be isolated (in 70% of cases) or accompany other locations (30% of cases); it manifests as anal fissures, deep ulcerations, perianal fistulas, perianal and anal abscesses, and anal canal stenosis. Anal involvement is absent in RCUH.

Infectious colitis infectious There is no chronic diarrhoea; stool culture can identify the presence of Clostridium difficile toxin A or B infection; infection with Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter jejuni, E. coli; also amoebiasis or other parasites; infection with cytomegalovirus, herpes virus; fungal infections. They often have clinical manifestations similar to inflammatory bowel diseases, especially UC (bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain). The endoscopic appearance of some infectious colitis is very similar to that of UC. It should be noted that an acute infection may trigger a first flare-up of a pre-existing/latent inflammatory bowel disease. The following conditions are more common:

– Bacterial colitis caused by Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Escherichia coli – Parasitic colitis caused by Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia, Balantidium coli – Colitis caused by sexually transmitted germs, the most common being proctitis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Herpes simplex (HSV), Treponema pallidum – similar in manifestation to ulcerative haemorrhagic proctitis
– Colitis caused by opportunistic germs (Cytomegalovirus, Histoplasma, Mycobacterium avium) in immunocompromised patients

– Intestinal tuberculosis – frequently affects the terminal ileum and sometimes the ascending colon; intestinal tuberculosis is a stenosing, fistulising and malabsorptive disease, with manifestations similar to Crohn's disease. The definitive diagnosis is histopathological.

The tests used to diagnose these conditions are bacterial or viral stool cultures, stool parasite tests, serological tests (Chlamydia, HSV, CMV), and histological examination of mucosal biopsies (HSV, CMV). For Entamoeba, a microscopic examination of the exudate covering the amoebic ulcers is performed on a slide, with direct visualization of the germ.

Non-infectious colitis Non-infectious Microscopic colitis (collagenous and lymphocytic) is characterised by the deposition of a layer of collagen and/or a lymphocytic infiltrate under the colonic epithelial basement membrane. It occurs in middle-aged women and manifests as watery diarrhoea. The diagnosis is exclusively histopathological, as there are no endoscopic changes in the colonic mucosa.

Colitis Ischemic Ischemic colitis occurs in elderly people with heart disease and manifests itself through bloody diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Sometimes Crohn's disease is difficult to diagnose, even based on endoscopic and histological criteria. The differentiation is made based on the evolution over time, which is spontaneous towards healing within weeks in ischemic colitis. There are vasculitides with intestinal involvement, which can have bloody diarrhoea as a symptom.
Colorectal cancer The differential diagnosis is made based on the location of the lesions, endoscopic and radiological appearance, and histopathological examination.

Iatrogenic diarrhoea Positive history of antibiotic use (pseudomembranous colitis), NSAIDs (NSAID-induced enteritis), contraceptives (contraceptive-induced colitis). In the case of pseudomembranous colitis, a positive test for Clostridium difficile confirms the diagnosis.

Anal Anal Ulcerative haemorrhagic proctitis may manifest only as small amounts of rectal bleeding at the end of defecation, which can be confused with rectal bleeding caused by haemorrhoids or anal fissures.

Irritable bowel syndrome Irritable bowel It manifests itself with explosive diarrhoea (but without blood or pus, sometimes with mucus), abdominal pain, but without weight loss. It should be noted, however, that the diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome is always a diagnosis of exclusion.
Diverticulitis It can manifest with abdominal pain, fever, and bloody stools.
Radicular colitis It can occur several years after radiotherapy in the pelvic area and can cause repeated rectal bleeding.

Gluten enteropathy It presents with chronic diarrhoea and weight loss due to gluten intolerance. The diagnosis is serological - anti-endomysium antibodies, anti-transglutaminase antibodies and histological examination of duodenal biopsies.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Haemorrhagic rectocolitis.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: A stool culture allows us to detect Clostridium difficile in the faeces. Coproparasitological examination, detection of a sexually transmitted disease. A colonoscopy with evaluation of the terminal ileum (ileocolonoscopy) is the gold standard, helping us to detect early lesions, diagnose UC, assess the extent of recto-colonic involvement and disease activity, allows us to make a differential diagnosis with other conditions (Crohn's disease), assess therapeutic response, and monitor for dysplasia and malignancy. In severe cases, sigmoidoscopy is sufficient to assess severity and a simple abdominal X-ray is sufficient to highlight colonic distension. A simple abdominal X-ray is useful in cases of complications: toxic megacolon, perforation, intestinal obstruction. A double contrast radiological examination allows the degree of colon distensibility to be assessed. Initially, there is an irregular, finely granular appearance of the mucosa, with decreased colonic distensibility and dehaustration. Subsequently, ulcerations appear, which in the profile image give the appearance of marginal spicules and addition images, and in the P-A image, opaque suspended spots were found. In advanced stages, "buttonhole" ulcerations appear. Radiological examination with contrast medium is contraindicated in severe/fulminant UC, as there is a high risk of precipitating toxic megacolon. Scintigraphy with Technetium-labelled leukocytes highlights the accumulation of neutrophils in the inflamed tissue and allows the location, extent and activity of the inflammatory process to be assessed. Colon MRI for therapy monitoring; may be useful for assessing UC activity and complications. Abdominal-pelvic CT allows assessment of disease activity and complications, aids in the differential diagnosis with Crohn's disease, and is useful for assessing the perineum. Ultrasound can detect moderate thickening of the colon wall, measuring 7-8 mm, with submucosal hyperechogenicity and preservation of layer differentiation for a long period.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: The patient has left-sided haemorrhagic rectocolitis (lesions extend up to 22 cm from the anal opening), according to the Montreal classification: E2, in moderate flare-up (Truelove and Witts severity criteria).

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: First-line treatment is 5-ASA or oral salazopyrine, in loading doses for 3-4 weeks. If the response is favourable, maintenance therapy is continued with the same drugs, but in lower doses. If there is no response after 4 weeks, systemic steroids are introduced for oral administration (Prednisone 30-40 mg/day). After clinical remission is achieved, the doses of corticosteroids are gradually reduced to 0 and maintenance treatment with 5-ASA derivatives or oral Salazopyrine is introduced.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Patient follow-up requires assessment of disease activity, secondary effects of the therapy used, and detection of complications. The role of treatment is to achieve clinical remission (number of stools/day, presence of blood in the stool, abdominal pain and monitoring of the patient's weight), then biological remission (haemoglobin, albumin, C-reactive protein), and then endoscopic remission of the disease. We are interested in the healing of the mucosa at the level of the lesions, which will lead to a decrease in the number of flare-ups, the number of hospitalisations, surgical therapy and the possible risk of colorectal cancer. 5-ASA - the initial dose is 3-4 g/day (1 g x 3-4/day) when administered orally or 1.5 g/day (0.5 g x 3/day) when administered topically (suppositories, enemas). The loading dose is maintained until faecal remission, then reduced to 1.5-2 g/day - the maintenance dose for preventing recurrence. Medications administered orally are effective in the colon and terminal ileum. The only effective drug for purely intestinal locations is Pentasa 4 g/day. Suppositories are effective in proctitis; enemas are effective in colitis affecting up to the splenic flexure. As a side effect, renal failure due to interstitial nephropathy should be monitored. Systemic corticosteroids (prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone) are effective in treating moderateto-severe or fulminant flare-ups of ulcerative colitis. They can be administered orally, starting with a dose of 0.5-1 mg/kg/day of prednisone, with a gradual reduction in doses as symptoms resolve, initially decreasing by 10 mg/week to 30 mg/day, then by 5 mg/week until treatment is discontinued. In fulminant forms, parenteral corticosteroid therapy is indicated (prednisolone 40-60 mg/day IV).

The numerous and significant adverse effects of corticosteroids limit their use to acute episodes and for a short period of time. Their use is not recommended for maintaining remission or preventing postoperative relapses. For this purpose, 5-ASA (mesalazine) preparations are very effective. There are cases in which the patient becomes corticosteroid-dependent, so that when corticosteroid doses are discontinued or reduced, the symptoms return. The recommendation is to gradually reduce the dose of corticosteroids until they are stopped, while simultaneously initiating immunosuppressive therapy (azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine), which will be maintained for at least 3-4 years. Corticosteroid treatment is discontinued gradually to allow time for the adrenal cortex, whose cortisol secretion has been inhibited, to regain its synthesis capacity. In RCUH, azathioprine is indicated for inducing remission in resistant forms, associated with corticosteroids, in maintaining remission in chronic-active forms, in corticosteroid-dependent patients. Azathioprine and 6Mercaptopurine (at a dose of 2-3mg/kgc/day) are indicated in haemorrhagic colitis in patients who cannot tolerate corticosteroids or who do not respond well to corticosteroids (corticosteroid resistance). They are used in combination with corticosteroids for several months, given the slow onset of action of the immunosuppressant. Another indication is in corticosteroid-dependent patients. The use of immunosuppressants instead of corticosteroids to maintain remission aims to eliminate the significant side effects that occur with prolonged corticosteroid treatment. The recommended dose of azathioprine is 1-1.5 mg/kg/day for a minimum period of 2-4 years. Side effects: neutropenia, lymphopenia. Cyclosporine can be used in severe RCUH that is resistant to other therapies. The response is rapid (2 weeks), so it can be used in the preamble to long-term therapy with azathioprine. When using immunosuppressants, early detection of possible skin cancer and cervical dysplasia is necessary. Probiotics are used in maintenance treatment for patients with UC who cannot tolerate 5-ASA derivatives. Studies have shown that probiotics reduce the need for corticosteroids in most patients.

cases.title: Anal pain
cases.dx: Anal pain: fissure / abscess / thrombosed haemorrhoid
kp: Character and timing of pain, swelling, fever
cases.presentation: Patient DD, aged 33, programmer analyst, presents to the Emergency Department with severe perianal pain. The current illness began insidiously three days ago, with the patient experiencing 2-3 episodes of diarrhoea that resolved spontaneously, followed by the onset of discomfort and continuous pain in the left perianal region. The pain, which was initially only present on palpation, became spontaneous and rapidly increased in intensity. For approximately 12 hours, the patient has been unable to sit down due to pain, has chills and a fever of 380C. He self-administered 400 mg of ibuprofen per os, which provided short-term relief of symptoms. The patient has no other significant personal or family history of disease. He drinks alcohol occasionally and does not smoke. On physical examination, the patient is overweight (186 cm/93 kg), anxious, in an antalgic position – lying on his right side. In the left perianal region: oedema covering an area of 3/4 cm, hyperaemic, warm skin that is extremely painful on palpation. Rectal examination can only be performed superficially due to exacerbated pain, competent sphincter hypertonic. On palpation, the lesion is fluctuant. Laboratory examination reveals leukocytosis (12,500/mm3 ) with a left shift in the leukocyte formula.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics Perianal abscess Perianal abscess is an infectious process affecting the lax perianal or perianorectal tissue and evolving into a purulent collection in this location. Clinically, it manifests as spontaneous progressive perianal pain and, on palpation, may evolve with chills and fever. Clinical: perianal oedema, hyperaemic skin, fluctuation on palpation. Perianal abscess may spontaneously fistulate with almost complete remission of pain and partial evacuation of the purulent collection. Local examination is painful and a complete examination is performed intraoperatively under anaesthesia.

Perianal fistula Perianal fistula is a chronic complication of a perianal abscess. It consists of the persistence of an abnormal connection between the anal canal and the perianal skin after the drainage of a perianal abscess. The tract is lined with granulation tissue. A perianal fistula is not painful. Perianal pain in this case may be caused by recurrent exacerbations of the chronic local infection with the appearance of recurrent abscesses along the fistula tract.

Haemorrhoidal disease Hemorrhoidal Hemorrhoidal disease consists of pathological dilations of the hemorrhoidal plexuses. Depending on their location, haemorrhoids are divided into external haemorrhoids, located distally from the dentate line and covered by skin, and internal haemorrhoids, located proximally from the dentate line and covered by the mucosa of the anal canal. Their diagnosis and staging is done through clinical examination and anoscopy. Uncomplicated haemorrhoids are virtually asymptomatic. Pain in haemorrhoidal disease is caused by haemorrhoidal thrombosis, the concomitant presence of an anal fissure, the presence of an ulceration that may occur in the haemorrhoidal bundles, and incarcerated haemorrhoidal prolapse.

Anal fissure An anal fissure is a linear, radial ulceration of the skin at the end of the anal canal, distal to the dentate line. In most cases, it affects the posterior commissure of the anal opening. It can be acute or chronic. The pain can be intense, occurs during defecation, may be accompanied by bleeding, and is followed by a burning sensation after the passage of faeces. The diagnosis is made by clinical examination. A complete examination is painful and may require local anaesthesia or sedation.

Benign/malignant anal or anorectal tumours These are evident on clinical examination. They can be painful in the event of inflammatory complications – septic, strangulation, torsion, etc. A histopathological biopsy, endoscopic examinations and additional imaging are necessary to clarify the diagnosis.

Anitis and anorectitis These are inflammatory conditions affecting the perianal skin, anal canal and sometimes the rectum. They can have infectious causes: bacterial, viral, fungal or traumatic, radicular, allergic, chemical, etc. They can evolve with local pain. The diagnosis is clinical, anoscopic and requires dermatological consultation.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Perianal abscess.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: The patient is offered surgery: incision of the abscess, evacuation and debridement of the remaining cavity. The clinical picture is typical, so imaging confirmation is not necessary. Oral intake is stopped and coagulation tests are performed. If the doctor or patient still considers imaging confirmation necessary, a transperineal ultrasound examination may be requested. In exceptional cases where the clinical examination is inconclusive, when we suspect a possible supraleval extension or the presence of an abscess as a complication of an intra-abdominal septic process, etc., we may request an MRI or CT scan, depending on the situation.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: Since the patient is young, there are no comorbidities, the onset is recent and the location is perianal, the severity of the disease is low and the prognosis is favourable with appropriate treatment. There is a risk of perianal fistula in 30-60% of cases.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Emergency surgical treatment: incision, evacuation, debridement and drainage of the remaining abscess cavity under spinal anaesthesia or locoregional anaesthesia – perianal block. Collection of pus for bacteriological examination and antibiogram. Combination with antibiotic treatment depending on the surgeon's decision.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Remission of pain and fever, disappearance of purulent secretions in the remaining cavity of the abscess, improvement of the local inflammatory reaction, healing per secundam of the abscess cavity and surgical wound.

cases.title: Bleeding during bowel movements
kp: Bright red bleeding at defecation, prolapse
Anoscopy; colonoscopy if >45–50 or alarm signs
cases.presentation: Patient VA, aged 48, an IT programmer, presents at the Surgery Clinic Outpatient Department with bleeding during defecation, anal discomfort and itching, as well as the appearance of perianal swelling. The current illness began insidiously about two years ago with minor bleeding after bowel movements. The patient describes the bleeding as red blood, initially visible only on toilet paper, then also in the toilet, occurring mainly after hard stools. The bleeding occurs periodically, lasts for several days and stops spontaneously or after self-administration of Detralex and Hemorzon ointments (as recommended by the pharmacist). During periods of bleeding, she also experiences discomfort, anal itching and pruritus. In the last two months, the symptoms have worsened, with the addition of perianal "growths", which initially appeared after bowel movements but disappeared after a few minutes. However, in the last week, they have not disappeared, are sensitive and stain her underwear with slightly bloody mucous discharge. The patient is overweight, has had two pregnancies with caesarean section deliveries, is sedentary due to the nature of her profession, does not exercise, and has an unbalanced diet with little fluid intake, which leads to periodic episodes of constipation (hard stools every 2-3 days). Physical examination of the perineal region reveals two prolapsed internal haemorrhoidal nodules, external haemorrhoids and haemorrhoidal skin tags. Rectal examination reveals normal sphincter tone, with no palpable formations in the lower rectum. Manual reduction of the haemorrhoidal prolapse is followed by spontaneous re-prolapse of the two haemorrhoids. Rigid anoscopy reveals normal-appearing lower rectal mucosa, voluminous internal haemorrhoids, two of which have a tendency to prolapse.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics Haemorrhoids The main complaints of patients with haemorrhoidal disease are rectal bleeding and prolapse. Prolapse occurs after a bowel movement and is used to classify the degrees of internal haemorrhoids. In addition to rectal bleeding and prolapse, patients with haemorrhoidal disease also complain of other symptoms: itching, burning, pain.

Anal fissure Pain is the most important symptom and has the following characteristics: it occurs after a bowel movement, can last from a few minutes to several hours, and is secondary to intense anal spasm. Less commonly, anal fissures may also cause bleeding, usually in the early days.

Anorectal cancer An irregular, parenchymal tumour, usually ulcerative-vegetative, palpable by rectal examination. In addition to rectal bleeding and tenesmus, the patient experiences pain and frequent, reduced bowel movements (with mucus and blood). It may be associated with regional (adenopathy) and general (weight loss, anaemia, etc.) neoplastic signs.

Inflammatory bowel Perianorectal abscesses and fistulas, colicky abdominal pain, diarrhoea, lower diseases – Crohn's gastrointestinal bleeding (haematochezia, rectal bleeding), anaemia, weight loss, disease enterocutaneous fistulas. and haemorrhagic rectocolitis Perianal abscesses

Perianal pain, varying in intensity, most often severe. Examination of the perineal region reveals a swollen, indurated area with oedema corresponding to the purulent collection. Sometimes, in the case of deep abscesses, the swelling is not obvious. Rectal examination is painful, and digital palpation of the collection area reveals a swollen and sensitive intraanal area. Most often, the patient has fever, sweating, chills, and pallor (septic state).

External haemorrhoidal thrombosis White-purple, hard, painful swelling, located superficially subcutaneously in the anocutaneous area. It can vary in size from a few millimetres to 3-4 cm. Bleeding may occur only if spontaneous rupture occurs with partial evacuation of the thrombus.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Haemorrhoidal disease.
Bleeding during bowel movements

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: The patient is scheduled for surgical treatment. Prior to the operation, she will undergo a colonoscopy for the differential diagnosis of rectal bleeding, taking into account AHC.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: The disease is not serious, but it is at an advanced stage (stage IV).

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: The recommended treatment is surgery (haemorrhoidectomy). Concurrently and subsequently, hygienicdietary and medication treatment will follow to regulate intestinal transit, venotrophic and local antiinflammatory.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: After surgery and healing of the surgical wounds, the patient should no longer experience bleeding or haemorrhoidal prolapse.

cases.title: Haematochezia
cases.presentation: A 68-year-old retired man presents to the emergency department reporting the appearance of large amounts of fresh blood in his stool, covering the faeces. He reports that bleeding is the only symptom and acknowledges two more such episodes at intervals of several months. The patient is known to have haemorrhoidal disease, for which he underwent minimally invasive treatment approximately five years ago and was recommended treatment with Detralex. He also has grade II obesity, high blood pressure and chronic ischaemic heart disease, for which he is being treated with Enalapril and Nitrites. On physical examination, the patient is pale, BP 90/55 mmHg, HR 122/min, local abdominal examination without pathological findings. Rectal examination: fresh blood on the glove finger, no palpable masses in the rectal ampulla, normal sphincter tone. Laboratory tests indicate: Hb = 8.7g/dl, Ht = 27%, Urea = 32 mg/dl, creatinine = 1.4 mg/dl.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: In 80% of cases, the aetiology of an HDI is colorectal or anal. Clinical situation

Characteristics Haemorrhoidal disease haemorrhoidal Painless bleeding, fresh blood on the surface of the stool and/or toilet bowl; the most common cause of HDI in young people. Haemorrhoidal pathology can mask more serious lesions!!! Be careful with the diagnosis!
Anal fissure Bleeding may occur after a prolonged history of pain during defecation; it is not a characteristic symptom. Rarely significant bleeding.
Diverticular haemorrhage Arterial bleeding, often massive, painless. The source is located in the right colon.
Angiodysplasia These are most commonly located in the ascending colon and caecum and are arteriovenous malformations that cause self-limiting bleeding in the elderly; massive bleeding is rare.
Inflammatory colitis Infectious HDI occurs in the context of a septic syndrome. Etiology: Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, E. coli.
Ischemic colitis Elderly patients with cardiovascular disease. Location: splenic flexure or rectosigmoid junction. HDI occurs in association with diarrhoea; usually self-limiting.
Colorectal cancer HDI associated with signs of malignant infiltration; prolonged bleeding, rarely massive. Common cause in elderly patients. More common in the right colon.
Inflammatory bowel More common in patients with ulcerative colitis during periods of disease activity; only disease 4% of cases are severe. Other intestinal disorders
Ulcerations caused by high NSAID consumption, Meckel's diverticulum, benign or malignant tumours, Rendu-Osler disease

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: In this case, considering the patient's age, personal medical history and presentation, we can consider diverticular bleeding, with further tests to confirm the diagnosis. Haematochezia associated with haemodynamic instability may indicate HDS; in this case, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy should be performed. To highlight a possible HDS

It is recommended to insert a nasogastric tube (aspiration + lavage). Positive aspiration indicates a voluminous HDS externalised through haematochezia. Negative aspiration makes the diagnosis of HDS unlikely, but not impossible (VPN = 64%). It is important to avoid attributing the disease to haemorrhoids without investigating other causes of HDI. What paraclinical investigations do you recommend? In terms of recommended paraclinical investigations, we can mention: Level 1 investigations, aimed at establishing the biological context in which blood loss occurs: Complete blood count, Coagulation profile, Electrolytes, Blood group and Rh factor, Urea, Creatinine Level 2 investigations, with a dual purpose, diagnostic and therapeutic: Colonoscopy, CT angiography/angiography, scintigraphy with Tc99m-labelled red blood cells.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: Vital signs are monitored. The patient's condition is serious, given the haemodynamic instability on presentation with tachycardia, hypotension, fresh blood on rectal examination, recurrence of bleeding, presence of comorbidities, age > 60 years, serum creatinine above normal values and haematocrit on presentation < 35%.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: ▪ Haemodynamic and respiratory monitoring ▪ Two wide venous access routes ▪ Volume replacement with crystalloids, colloids and MER at Hb values below 7g/dl ▪ Maintaining INR between 1.5 and 2.5 and platelets at 50,000/mm3 ▪ Insertion of a nasogastric tube and urinary catheter ▪ Oxygen therapy ▪ Preparation for colonoscopy ▪ Diagnostic and/or therapeutic colonoscopy.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: The patient must be hospitalised and re-evaluated:
– Haemodynamic and respiratory monitoring, diuresis – Hb, Ht – Cessation/recurrence of rectal bleeding.

cases.title: Liver tumour
cases.presentation: Patient OA, a 63-year-old pensioner, known to have chronic viral hepatitis C, comes to the clinic for his annual liver ultrasound screening. The patient was diagnosed 20 years ago with viral hepatitis C (for which he was treated with interferon, ribavirin and hepatoprotective agents). For about 3 months, he has been experiencing dyspeptic symptoms, loss of appetite and asthenia. The patient is active, walks briskly for two hours every day; he smokes five cigarettes a day; he does not consume alcohol or toxic substances. The physical examination reveals a patient of normal weight, afebrile, with hepatomegaly of increased consistency, sensitive to palpation. The spleen is palpable at the edge of the left costal margin. Laboratory tests showed hepatocytolysis syndrome (ASAT = 94 u/l, ALAT = 92 u/l), mild inflammatory syndrome (VSH = 21-43 mm, fibrinogen = 520 mg/dl), with the rest of the usual laboratory tests being within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a heterogeneous, micronodular liver with a formation approximately 2 cm in diameter, located in segment III, heterogeneous, with anarchic vascularisation. The portal vein measures 12 mm, and the spleen is slightly enlarged. No free fluid is evident in the peritoneal cavity. On contrast-enhanced abdominal-pelvic MRI, the liver lesion appears hypervascularised in the arterial phase, becoming hypodense in the late phase, located in contact with the portal venous branch afferent to segment III of the liver. The serum alpha-fetoprotein value is 21.9 ng/ml. Chest CT scan revealed no pathological changes.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation
Characteristics Primary malignant liver tumours Hepatocellular carcinoma

Occurs in patients with a history of chronic liver disease/cirrhosis of viral (B, C) or alcoholic aetiology, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, exposure to aflatoxin B1 (diet), primary biliary cirrhosis, haemochromatosis. May manifest as pain in the right hypochondrium, bloating, jaundice, weight loss. Sometimes appears as a palpable tumour mass in the right hypochondrium or epigastrium. It may be associated with signs of portal hypertension. There is a risk of rupture (spontaneous or post-traumatic) with consequent intraperitoneal haemorrhage, as well as thrombosis of adjacent portal venous branches (through compression or invasion). It causes increases in serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels.

Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinom a It occurs in patients with a history of primary sclerosing cholangitis, ulcerative colitis, parasitic infections (Clonorchis sinensis), Caroli's disease, and intrahepatic gallstones. It is most often asymptomatic, but sometimes appears as a palpable tumour mass in the right hypochondrium.

Invasive gallbladder cancer in the liver It occurs more frequently in elderly women with a history of gallbladder stones, porcelain gallbladder, and choledochal cysts. It can cause pain in the right upper quadrant, obstructive jaundice, anorexia, weight loss, and abdominal enlargement (ascites). It sometimes appears as a palpable tumour mass in the right upper quadrant.
Secondary malignant liver tumours (liver metastases) Liver metastases from colorectal cancer

They can be diagnosed concomitantly with colonic/rectal cancer or subsequently in a patient with a history of treated colonic/rectal cancer (surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy). They can cause pain in the right hypochondrium, obstructive jaundice, and tumour-type hepatomegaly. They cause a dynamic increase in serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels, only if CEA levels were elevated at the time of diagnosis of the primary colonic/rectal tumour.

Hepatic metastases of neuroendocrine tumours They are diagnosed concomitantly with a malignant gastrointestinal/neuroendocrine carcinoid tumour or subsequently in a patient with a history of such treated neoplasia. They cause a specific clinical picture as a result of hypersecretion and increased serum levels of a certain hormone or peptide (chromogranin A, neuron-specific enolase, serotonin, histamine, insulin, gastrin, VIP, glucagon, somatostatin). They can cause pain in the right hypochondrium, obstructive jaundice, and tumour-like hepatomegaly.
Liver metastases with another point of origin (stomach, pancreas, breast, melanoma, GIST, ovary, etc.)

They are diagnosed concomitantly with a cancer originating from a non-colorectal and non-neuroendocrine site (stomach, pancreas, breast, melanoma, GIST, ovary, etc.) or appear later in a patient with a history of such treated neoplasia. They can cause pain in the right hypochondrium, obstructive jaundice, and tumour-type hepatomegaly. Depending on their location, they can cause increases in the serum levels of certain tumour markers (pancreas, stomach – carbohydrate antigen CA 19-9, ovary – antigen CA 125).

Benign liver tumours Simple hepatic cyst It is asymptomatic in most cases (it is discovered incidentally by liver ultrasound). When large, it can cause abdominal pain, a feeling of epigastric fullness or early satiety (by compressing the stomach) and may become palpable.

Hydatid cyst of the liver It causes dyspeptic symptoms, allergic reactions (skin rashes), pain, fever, jaundice (bile duct rupture) or appears as a palpable tumour mass in the right hypochondrium. It is more common in people who have contact with animals (herbivores).
Hepatic haemangioma In most cases, it is asymptomatic. When it reaches large sizes, it can cause abdominal pain and nausea. Spontaneous rupture with consecutive intraperitoneal haemorrhage is rare.

Hepatic adenoma Adenoma It occurs in patients with a history of oral contraceptive use (females) or anabolic steroids (males). It causes pain in the right hypochondrium. At a diameter of more than 5 cm, it presents a significant risk of malignant transformation, respectively rupture (spontaneous or post-traumatic) with consecutive intraperitoneal haemorrhage.
Focal nodular hyperplasia It occurs more frequently in females; in most cases, the lesion is asymptomatic. It does not pose a risk of rupture or malignant transformation.

Pyogenic liver abscess Occurs in patients with a history of intra-abdominal infection (ulcerative perforation, appendicitis, colonic diverticulitis, perforated digestive cancers), inflammatory bowel disease, benign or malignant obstructive jaundice, invasive procedures on the biliary tree (stent placement) or post-liver transplant (following hepatic artery thrombosis). It manifests itself through fever, chills, pain in the right hypochondrium, and general malaise.
Polycystic liver disease Occurs in patients with a family history of polycystic kidney or liver disease. It manifests as hepatomegaly with a bumpy surface.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Hepatocellular carcinoma of the hepatic segment III. Viral cirrhosis of the liver C.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: Given the patient's medical history and the results of laboratory and imaging tests (ultrasound, MRI), a diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma is highly likely. An image-guided (ultrasound, CT) liver biopsy of the lesion is not necessary. The patient should be evaluated by a multidisciplinary team (gastroenterologist, radiologist, surgeon, oncologist). Based on the existing clinical data, the patient is eligible for anatomical liver resection (hepatic segmentectomy III).

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: The patient has viral hepatitis C in the portal stage (liver cirrhosis). He has no other comorbidities, and his performance index is optimal. The absence of ascites and jaundice indicates the absence of vascular or parenchymal decompensation of liver cirrhosis. The liver tumour in segment III is small (2 cm), and imaging examinations (abdominal-pelvic MRI, chest CT) have not revealed any secondary loco-regional or distant metastases. The pre-treatment TNM stage is IA (T1aN0M0). As a result, surgical excision of the liver tumour is being considered. Pre-treatment assessment of liver function reserve is mandatory in view of liver resection. This involves the use of the Child-Pugh classification of liver cirrhosis severity, the indocyanine green (ICG) liver perfusion test, and the percentage assessment of the remaining liver volume after liver resection (CT volumetry).

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Segmental liver resection (anatomical – hepatic segmentectomy III) using the classic approach. Laparoscopic approach in cirrhotic patients is possible, but more difficult due to fibrosis and potential blood loss; it requires experience in minimally invasive liver surgery. The segmental extension of the liver resection is dictated by the contact of the tumour with the portal pedicle of the hepatic segment III. Intraoperative ultrasound is mandatory and allows the detection of any concomitant hepatic lesions not identified by preoperative imaging, as well as visualization of the portal pedicle of the hepatic segment III. The surgical intervention must be preceded by complex treatment aimed at supporting liver function and correcting coagulation disorders and hypoproteinemia. A reserve of iso-Rh blood and fresh frozen plasma will be provided for the day of surgery.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: The early postoperative period will involve monitoring consciousness, haemodynamics (pulse, BP, CVP, SaO2 ), respiration (respiratory rate and amplitude), temperature curve, abdominal condition, and the volume and appearance of peritoneal drains. Early identification of specific post-hepatic resection complications will be sought: haemorrhage, biliary leakage, liver failure. In the medium and long term, oncological monitoring of patients after liver resection for hepatocellular carcinoma is necessary for the early detection of neoplastic recurrence. Oncological check-ups will include medical history and clinical examination, routine laboratory tests, serum alpha-fetoprotein measurement (every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6-12 months) and advanced imaging (CT or MRI of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis, every 3-6 months for the first 2 years, then every 6-12 months).
