cases.title: Pain in the right hypochondrium, bloating and scleral subicterus in a patient with hepatic cystic formation
kp: RUQ pain, sub-icterus, eosinophilia, rural/sheep exposure
cases.presentation: A 20-year-old female patient from a rural area with no significant medical history presents with bloating, bitter taste, erythematous rash accompanied by pruritus, and jaundice. The symptoms of the condition date back about a year, with an insidious onset of biliary dyspeptic symptoms. Over time, generalised erythematous skin rashes appeared, accompanied by pruritus (several episodes remitted spontaneously). For approximately 3 months, the patient has complained of a painful sensation in the right hypochondrium. About a week before presentation, the patient experienced worsening colicky pain in the right hypochondrium, accompanied by sclerotegumentary jaundice, nausea, bilious vomiting, headache and subfebrile temperature (38.2°C). The pain subsided after administration of antispasmodics and analgesics. On presentation: scleral subicterus; otherwise normal physical examination. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a large cystic liver mass (approximately 17 cm in diameter) occupying almost the entire right hepatic lobe; the mass was delimited by a 2 mm thick hyperechoic wall and contained dozens of small cystic formations inside. Laboratory tests showed cholestasis (total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dl, with direct fraction 3.5 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase 160 IU/l, positive bile pigments in urine), eosinophilia (22%), inflammatory syndrome (ESR 22-46). Ag HBs – negative, Anti-HCV – negative.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics Hepatic hydatid cyst Occurs following infestation with Taenia echinococcus eggs. The patient's rural origin (and presumed more frequent contact with dogs) is an argument in favour of this diagnosis. The clinical picture of a hydatid cyst includes non-specific symptoms and clinical signs, with the diagnosis being established on the basis of imaging and serological tests. In this case, the appearance of a thick-walled cyst with vesicles inside strongly suggests the hydatid nature of the cyst. Eosinophilia occurs in parasitic diseases. The determination of anti-echinococcus IgG antibodies and the completion of imaging investigations (computed tomography and magnetic resonance cholangiography) provide additional arguments for the diagnosis. Fistulisation of the cyst into the bile ducts is suggested by biliary symptoms and obstructive jaundice. and obstructive jaundice. Magnetic resonance cholangiography would reveal cysticbiliary communications.

Simple biliary cyst is the main situation to be considered in the differential diagnosis of hepatic hydatid cyst. A simple biliary cyst can reach large sizes, but has a thin wall and transonic content. An uncomplicated hydatid cyst may have a similar appearance, in which case the diagnosis is clarified by determining anti-echinococcus antibodies. However, in most cases, hydatid cysts have a different appearance on imaging and can be differentiated from simple cysts by several specific signs: double wall, membrane detachment, daughter cysts inside (sometimes honeycomb-like) and inhomogeneous content.

Obstructive jaundice The obstructive nature of jaundice is demonstrated by the increase in total bilirubin due to the direct fraction, as well as alkaline phosphatase (cholestasis enzyme). The obstructive presence of bile pigments in the urine also supports the obstructive nature of jaundice; discolouration of the stools would have been an argument, but this characteristic is not mentioned in the case presentation. Formally, the question of differential diagnosis with pre-hepatic and hepatocellular jaundice arises, but there are no features of these types of jaundice. Laboratory tests (absence of anaemia, negative hepatitis tests) make these diagnoses even more unlikely.

The low bilirubin levels, combined with pain and low-grade fever, suggest a benign aetiology of the jaundice; malignant jaundice would have been progressive, painless, apyretic, intensely pruritic and with very high bilirubin levels. However, the imaging (ultrasound) strongly suggests a benign aetiology (ruptured hydatid cyst in the bile ducts) of the jaundice.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Ruptured hepatic hydatid cyst in the bile ducts. Obstructive jaundice Diagnostic reasoning:
– clinical picture with biliary and allergic symptoms in a patient with possible contact with dogs during childhood;

– ultrasound appearance; – eosinophilia; – rupture in the bile ducts is supported by the appearance of obstructive jaundice; – jaundice is proven by increased bilirubin, the obstructive nature by increased direct bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase, as well as by the presence of bile pigments in the urine; the aetiology of jaundice is – in the clinical context – hydatid.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: – anti-echinococcus antibodies – ± magnetic resonance cholangiography and/or abdominal computed tomography

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: The hydatid cyst is in the complication phase (ruptured in the bile ducts). Other possible complications:
– angiocolitis – rupture into the peritoneal cavity

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Surgical treatment preceded and followed by antiparasitic treatment.

– Absolute surgical indication – The objectives of surgical treatment are: – inactivation (sterilisation) of the parasite – evacuation of the cyst contents – Prevention of intraperitoneal dissemination of hydatid content
– treatment of the posthydatid hepatic cavity – treatment of complications (cystic biliary fistulas)
– post-operative antiparasitic treatment (albendazole)

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Postoperative progress will be monitored using imaging (abdominal ultrasound). Anti-echinococcus antibodies do not decrease following treatment, nor do they increase to even higher levels in the event of reinfection.

cases.title: Abdominal pain located in the right hypochondrium
kp: US: thick wall, stones, pericholecystic fluid
cases.presentation: Patient PA, a 46-year-old programmer, presents to the Emergency Department with pain in the right hypochondrium, nausea, vomiting, and fever. The current illness began suddenly 24 hours ago, after a lunch rich in cholecystokinetic foods, with pain localised in the right hypochondrium radiating to the back, accompanied by nausea, bloating, and vomiting of food and bile. The general physical examination reveals an overweight, anxious patient with a moderate fever of 38.50C. The local physical examination reveals tenderness on palpation in the right hypochondrium and a positive Murphy's sign. Laboratory tests reveal leukocytosis (16,000/mm³) with a left shift in the leukocyte formula. Abdominal ultrasound reveals a distended gallbladder with multiple stones and thickened walls measuring 6 mm, with a double contour.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation
Characteristics Acute calculous cholecystitis Persistent pain in the right hypochondrium radiating to the back, fever, nausea, vomiting, positive Murphy's sign.
Biliary colic Pain in the right hypochondrium radiating to the right shoulder, right interscapular region or back, nausea, vomiting.
Acute angiocolitis Pain in the right hypochondrium, fever, sclerotic jaundice (Charcot-Villard triad)
Acute pancreatitis Intense epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, fever, general malaise. History of gallstones or alcoholism.

Perforated gastro-duodenal ulcer Sudden, intense epigastric pain, muscle contracture. History of chronic gastro-duodenal ulcer, treatment with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or Helicobacter pylori infection.
Acute hepatitis Asthenia, fatigue, loss of appetite, pain in the right hypochondrium, nausea, vomiting.

Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome Fitz-Hugh-Curtis Pain in the right hypochondrium radiating to the right shoulder, recent history of pelvic inflammatory disease (Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae), fever, hepatodiaphragmatic adhesions.
Inferior myocardial infarction Precordial pain radiating to the epigastrium, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, hypercholesterolemia.

Lithiasis and urinary tract infections Severe abdominal pain in the flank and lumbar region, radiating downwards towards the genitals and the medial aspect of the thigh, nausea, vomiting, haematuria, dysuria, pollakiuria. Lumbar muscle spasm. Muscle spasm in the flank diminishes with deep inspiration.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Acute calculous cholecystitis.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: The patient is offered hospitalisation, intravenous antibiotic treatment and surgery: laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: Since the patient presented with acute calculous cholecystitis with re-onset recent onset, in the absence of complications and comorbidities, the severity of the disease is low and the prognosis is favourable with appropriate treatment.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy within the first three days of symptom onset. Preoperative preparation consists of hydroelectrolytic rebalancing treatment, broad-spectrum antibiotics (third-generation cephalosporins or aminoglycosides and metronidazole) and analgesics (NSAIDs or opioids).

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Disappearance of fever and abdominal symptoms, resumption of bowel movements and food tolerance, rapid improvement in general condition.

cases.title: Abdominal pain located in the right hypochondrium, chills, fever and jaundice
kp: Charcot triad: pain, fever with chills, jaundice
US dilated CBD; MRCP; cholestasis labs
Antibiotics + urgent ERCP decompression, then cholecystectomy
cases.presentation: Patient MA, a 66-year-old pensioner, presents at the surgery clinic complaining of intense pain in the epigastric region and right hypochondrium, associated with nausea, vomiting and general malaise. The current illness began suddenly a day ago, following a meal rich in fats and carbonated drinks, with the sudden onset of epigastric pain and pain in the right hypochondrium, associated with nausea, initially vomiting food and later bile. During the evening, she had a fever (38.20C) with chills. Physical examination: obese patient (BMI over 33 kg/m²), no abdominal scars, marked tenderness on deep palpation of the epigastrium and right hypochondrium, no signs of peritoneal irritation. Examination of the skin reveals jaundiced colouration and yellow sclera. The urine is cloudy, and the stool examined after rectal coughing is acholic. Axillary temperature is 37.90 C. Blood pressure is 170/85 mmHg, with a ventricular rate of 90 beats/minute. Laboratory tests reveal the following: leukocytosis (16,200/mm³), with marked granulocytosis, hepatocytolysis syndrome (TGP 198 U/l, TGO 180 U/l), cholestasis syndrome (alkaline phosphatase 793 U/l, gamma glutamyl transpeptidase 1241 U/l), hyperbilirubinaemia (total bilirubin 7.2 mg/dl, with direct bilirubin 5.4 mg/dl). The ultrasound examination shows the main bile duct with a diameter of 9.4 mm, with inhomogeneous content; gallbladder with thickened walls, with multiple hyperechoic formations inside.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation
Characteristics Obstructive jaundice: Choledocholithiasis with acute cholangitis

Sudden onset, following a meal rich in fats and carbonated drinks, with epigastric pain and pain in the right hypochondrium, associated with nausea and vomiting, initially alimentary and later bilious, headache, persistent bitter taste, altered general condition; chills, fever and jaundice.
Obstructive jaundice: Malignant stenosis of the main bile duct
The absence of pain in the context of jaundice syndrome suggests rather a tumour obstruction – cholangiocarcinoma or extrinsic compression – gallbladder or pancreatic tumour.
Obstructive jaundice: Benign strictures Iatrogenic – post-cholecystectomy, choledochotomy, following an episode of acute pancreatitis or angiocolitis, parasitic infestations.
Obstructive jaundice: Autoimmune diseases Primary sclerosing cholangitis, primary biliary cirrhosis.
Obstructive jaundice: Portal vein thrombosis Manifests as pain, fever and jaundice, but imaging tests do not show dilation of the bile ducts.

Biliary colic: Acute cholecystitis Sudden onset, following a high-fat meal, with epigastric pain and pain in the right hypochondrium radiating to the back, associated with nausea and vomiting, initially food-related and later bilious, headache, persistent bitter taste, general malaise, fever.
Biliary colic: Dysfunction of the sphincter of Oddi.
It usually evolves with cholestasis, and imaging reveals dilation of the bile ducts. The diagnosis of this lesion is established accurately by performing manometry of the sphincter of Oddi.
Acute pain located in the upper abdomen Acute pancreatitis, duodenitis, gastric ulcer, inferior myocardial infarction, diffuse oesophageal spasm.

Cholestasis due to benign or Vaterian ampulloma, primary biliary cirrhosis, primary sclerosing malignant obstruction of the cholangitis, granulomatous hepatitis, amyloidosis, alcoholic hepatitis, nonbile ducts alcoholic steatohepatitis.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Gallbladder and common bile duct stones with acute cholangitis.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: Confirm the diagnosis: The diagnosis of choledocholithiasis with acute cholangitis is based on the clinical picture: pain, fever, jaundice (Charcot's triad), on biological examinations (presence of cholestasis, jaundice syndrome and hepatocytolysis syndrome) and on imaging examinations (transabdominal ultrasound examination - which revealed gallbladder stones with signs of acute cholecystitis, dilation of the main bile duct and the presence of stones in the bile duct). According to the Tokyo guidelines, the diagnosis of choledocholithiasis with acute cholangitis is probable if at least two elements of Charcot's triad are present and is considered certain if, in addition to this triad, the characteristic biological and imaging changes are also present. Confirmation of the lithiasic origin of acute cholangitis: Abdominal ultrasound examination reveals the presence of gallstones, with signs of acute lithiasic cholecystitis, dilated main bile duct with inhomogeneous content, highly suggestive of choledocholithiasis, thus supporting the diagnosis of choledocholithiasis with cholangitis.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: The Tokyo classification distinguishes three stages of severity of angiocolitis, depending on the severity of the clinical picture, the degree of response to antibiotic therapy, and the presence or absence of organ failure. According to this classification, the stages of angiocolitis are as follows:
– grade I (mild): moderate septic picture, rapid response to antibiotic therapy; – grade II (moderate): frank septic picture, no systemic sound and delayed response to antibiotic therapy;

– grade III (severe): septic state with organ failure. Considering the patient's clinical condition, corroborated by the data obtained from the clinical and paraclinical examination, but also the fact that she has a number of associated cardiovascular comorbidities, the severity of the disease is high, and the prognosis may become reserved in the absence of appropriate therapeutic measures.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Given the patient's clinical condition, diagnosis and associated comorbidities, the appropriate treatment for this patient involves several approaches: – supportive treatment to restore electrolyte and acid-base balance, in order to correct any imbalances and rehydrate the patient

– analgesic, antispastic and anti-inflammatory treatment – treatment of liver damage by administering hepatoprotective medication – appropriate treatment of associated chronic conditions – empirical antibiotic therapy targeting Gram-negative bacteria and intestinal flora bacteria. Subsequently, antibiotic therapy will be adapted to the results obtained from bacteriological tests (bile cultures, blood cultures)
– performance of endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with endoscopic sphincterotomy, in order to decompress the bile duct and extract stones from the bile duct

– Dynamic monitoring of the patient, with surgery (laparoscopic cholecystectomy) proposed when the dynamic transaminase values return to normal. We may encounter a situation in which, following the initiation of antibiotic, analgesic, and antispasmodic treatment, the patient's clinical evolution follows a course of marked improvement, with the disappearance of clinical symptoms and remission of jaundice syndrome, cholestasis syndrome, and hepatocytolysis. In these situations, remission of cholangitis and passage of the bile duct is possible, which can be objectively confirmed by performing an abdominal ultrasound examination. Under these conditions, laparoscopic cholecystectomy may be attempted without the need for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, subject to the undiagnosed persistence of choledochal lithiasis on imaging, which may require further endoscopic examination depending on clinical evolution. There are situations in which choledocholithiasis causing acute cholangitis cannot be addressed endoscopically, thus preventing decompression of the main bile duct. In such situations, where decompression is absolutely necessary, surgical drainage of the main bile duct (Kehr drainage) is performed, either by conventional means or laparoscopically (depending on the hospital's equipment and the surgeon's experience).

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: The disappearance of clinical symptoms, normalisation of biochemical tests, resumption of intestinal transit, food tolerance and rapid improvement in general condition are clear indicators of the patient's favourable progress.

cases.title: Haematemesis in a patient with chronic liver disease
kp: Vasoactives, antibiotics, banding; TIPSS if refractory
cases.presentation: 65-year-old patient BC presents to the emergency department of the surgical clinic with an episode of hematemesis. The current symptoms began suddenly an hour ago with vomiting containing large amounts of dark red blood, followed by a rapid deterioration in consciousness. The patient has a history of chronic viral hepatitis C, diagnosed 10 years ago. On presentation, the physical examination reveals a disoriented, drowsy patient with scleral subicterus, slightly distended abdomen, painless on palpation, splenomegaly, BP = 75/40 mmHg, pulse = 115 beats/minute. Laboratory tests upon presentation showed Hb = 8 mg/dl, Ht = 24%, INR = 2, total bilirubin = 1.5 mg/dl, with the rest of the usual laboratory tests within normal limits. An abdominal ultrasound performed 3 months ago showed hepatomegaly with a polycyclic contour, granular hepatic parenchyma and repermeabilisation of the round ligament, portal vein with a diameter of 14 mm, with hepatopetal flow, transonic gallbladder, homogeneous spleen with a long axis of 15 cm, and normal ultrasound findings for the rest of the abdominal organs.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics Ruptured oesophageal varices The most likely cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) in patients with liver disease. Oesophageal varices are a direct consequence of portal hypertension. Approximately 50% of patients with liver cirrhosis have oesophageal varices. HDS due to ruptured oesophageal varices manifests as recurrent episodes of hematemesis without vomiting, accompanied or not by melena; fatigue and anorexia may also be present. Physical examination may reveal sclero-tegumentary jaundice, stellate angiomas, palmar erythema, collateral circulation in the abdominal wall ("jellyfish head"), abdominal distension, splenomegaly, and ascites.

Haemorrhagic gastro-duodenal ulcer The most common cause of severe HDS. It should be considered even if the patient has a history of liver disease. HDS from gastro-duodenal ulcer is frequently associated with the use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or alcohol. HDS from gastroduodenal ulcer may be associated with painful episodes in the epigastrium or right hypochondrium.

Oesophagitis Identical to those of ruptured oesophageal varices. The condition is more common in alcoholics. Bleeding is generally less severe and self-limiting. Symptoms include odynophagia, dysphagia, and gastro-oesophageal reflux.
Erosive gastritis/duodenitis Identical to those of ruptured oesophageal varices. The condition is more common in alcoholics. Bleeding is generally less severe and self-limiting.

Mallory-Weiss HDS caused by longitudinal tears in the mucosa of the oesophagogastric junction syndrome following an effort to vomit. The condition is more common in alcoholics. Bleeding is caused by longitudinal generally less severe and self-limiting. tears in the mucosa of the oesophagogastric junction following an effort to vomit. Angiodysplasia Identical to those of ruptured oesophageal varices. Oesophageal, gastric, periampullary neoplasms

Benign tumours: leiomyomas, lipomas, polyps (hyperplastic, adenomatous, hamartomatous). Malignant tumours: adenocarcinomas, mesenchymal neoplasms (including GIST), lymphomas, Kaposi's sarcoma, carcinoid, melanoma, metastases.
Haematemesis in patients with chronic liver disease Symptoms may include dysphagia, early satiety, involuntary weight loss/cachexia. Dieulafoy's ulcer

The bleeding originates from a dilated, tortuous arteriola (considered a congenital vascular malformation) located in the gastric submucosa, which bleeds after eroding the mucosa. The condition is more common in male patients. Clinical picture: haemorrhagic shock, anaemia, recurrent episodes of haematemesis in the past, accompanied or not by melena.
Drug-induced HDS Aspirin, steroidal or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, alendronate, tetracycline, quinidine, potassium chloride, anticoagulants.
Infectious causes Helicobacter pylori, cytomegalovirus, Candida albicans, herpes simplex virus.
Less common causes Haemobilia, pancreatic haemorrhage, aorto-enteric fistula, Cameron's erosions (in of HDS hiatal hernia).

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to ruptured oesophageal varices in a patient with chronic liver disease in the portal stage.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: ▪ Discontinuation of oral intake ▪ Securing the airway (oro-tracheal intubation if the patient is unconscious), oxygen therapy ▪ Insert 2 peripheral venous catheters of at least 16G ▪ Blood tests: complete blood count, electrolytes, liver tests (transaminases, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, γ-GT), coagulation profile, kidney tests (urea, creatinine), blood type

▪ Monitor diuresis by inserting a urethral-vesical catheter ▪ Insertion of a central venous catheter for CVP monitoring ▪ Administration of octreotide 50 μg i.v. in bolus, followed by 50 μg/h i.v. ▪ Electrolyte rebalancing by administering crystalloid solutions (saline, 500 ml in 30 min) up to a maximum volume of 2 litres

▪ Administration of fresh frozen plasma ▪ Isogroup transfusions, isoRh if haemoglobin falls below 7 g/dl (ideal Hb = 8-10 g/dl) ▪ Emergency upper digestive endoscopy + attempt at endoscopic ligation of oesophageal varices or sclerotherapy

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: According to the Orphanides classification, the patient has suffered a major HDS (loss of between 1500-2000 ml of blood). With a Rockall score of 9, the patient is at high risk of death.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) is indicated if haemorrhage cannot be stopped by pharmacological and endoscopic means. If TIPS is not possible, a surgical portosystemic shunt (e.g. mesenteric-caval shunt through graft interposition) is recommended.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: It is necessary to detect any continuation of the HDS episode or rebleeding. For this purpose, a nasogastric tube is inserted, and the pulse, blood pressure, haemoglobin and haematocrit values are monitored. Signs of rebleeding include: hematemesis with fresh blood or melena in a stabilised patient, marked drop in blood pressure, increased pulse rate, decrease in haemoglobin by 3g (or haematocrit by 9%) within 24 hours in the absence of transfusion.

cases.title: Severe epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting and elevated pancreatic enzymes
kp: Severe epigastric pain to the back; enzymes >3×
US (gallstones); CT after 72 h; severity scores
Fluids, analgesia, enteral feeding; ERCP if cholangitis; step-up for infected necrosis
cases.presentation: The patient, a 56-year-old retired man with a history of cardiovascular disease, presents to the emergency department with excruciating abdominal pain in the epigastric region, nausea and anorexia. The current illness began suddenly, about four days ago, with abdominal and epigastric pain, which later became "radiating" to the back, associated with nausea and two episodes of vomiting with gastric contents. The patient is a smoker but does not consume alcohol. On general clinical examination, the patient is overweight (BMI = 27 kg/m²), with generalised pallor, sweating, and fever (38.20C). The patient is dyspnoeic, tachypnoeic (18 breaths/minute), tachycardic (AV = 110 bpm), and slightly hypotensive (BP = 90/70 mmHg). On physical examination: distended abdomen with skin hyperesthesia and diminished hydroaerial sounds. Laboratory tests show leukocytosis 16,200/mm³with left shift of the leukocyte formula, CRP = 20 mg/dl, Hb = 10 g/dl, with a haematocrit of 49%, amylasemia 500 U/L, lipasemia 2000 U/L, amylasuria 800 U/L, AST = 80 U/L, ALT = 87 U/L, serum FA = 100 IU/L, BT = 1.2 mg/dl, BD = 0.9 mg/dl, serum urea/BUN = 40 mg/dl, serum creatinine = 1.3 mg/dl, serum Na = 110 mEq/L, serum glucose = 150 mg/dl, serum Ca = 7 mg/dl, with Astrup parameters revealing compensated metabolic acidosis. An empty abdominal X-ray shows a dilated mesoceliac enteral loop without pneumoperitoneum. Abdominal ultrasonography reveals a diffusely hypoechoic pancreas, surgically absent gallbladder with CBP and CBIH – not dilated, significant aerocolia and aeroenteria.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics Acute pancreatitis nausea, vomiting, anorexia, diarrhoea, subfebrile fever; symptoms present in a patient with a history of gallstones or alcohol or nicotine consumption, familial hypertriglyceridaemia, autoimmune diseases, chronic medication (antipsychotic antipsychotic/antidepressant/antidiabetic/chemotherapy). Clinical – fever, pallor, sweating, dehydration, dyspnoea with tachypnoea, crackles in the left bases, tachycardia, hypotension; abdominal – sensitivity to superficial/deep epigastric palpation, with muscle guarding/positive epigastric Blumberg sign, shifting dullness in the flanks, diminished hydroaerial sounds; Cullen's sign or Gray Turner's sign may appear on the skin.

Pancreatic pseudocyst Anamnestic, the symptoms of acute pancreatitis mentioned above may be found, blurred or not, with onset approximately 4-6 weeks before presentation to the doctor. The current clinical picture is less pronounced, with possible palpable epigastric pseudotumour/HD/HS formation.

Peripancreatic abscess Anamnestically, the symptoms of acute pancreatitis mentioned above may be present, whether blurred or not, with onset approximately 4-6 weeks prior to presentation to the physician. The current clinical picture is more pronounced, with possible palpable epigastric pseudotumour formation/HD/HS. Feverish syndrome, psychomotor agitation – much more pronounced than in uncomplicated acute pancreatitis.
Perforated gastric/duodenal ulcer with generalised peritonitis or penetration into the pancreas

Sudden onset of epigastric pain, "lancinating" in nature, of high intensity associated with nausea, coercive vomiting, marked anorexia; clinically – pallor, profuse sweating, tachycardia, abdominal with positive Blumberg sign, muscle guarding, muscle contracture, up to "Wooden abdomen". Personal history of dyspeptic ulcer syndrome/chronic gastroduodenal ulcer, treatment with non-selective non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or Helicobacter pylori infection. The migration of gastric/duodenal juice towards the omental bursa, subhepatic, then along the right parietal-colic fissure, causes pain and signs of peritoneal irritation in the epigastric and HD areas. In the case of ulcerative pancreatic penetration pancreatic ulcerative penetration, it is difficult to differentiate from an episode of severe acute pancreatitis (the pain symptoms, the nature of the pain, "bar-like", etc., being superimposable). Acute perforated appendicitis with generalised peritonitis

Anorexia, with initial diffuse and persistent epigastric/periombilical pain, followed by nausea and vomiting. Subsequently, the pain migrates to the right iliac fossa, associated with fever and general malaise. Sensitivity to superficial and deep palpation in the right iliac fossa (McBurney or Lange points) and signs of peritoneal irritation. Blumberg, Rovsing, psoas and obturator signs – positive. In the case of appendicular perforation into the peritoneal cavity, the colic and appendicular contents migrate through the right parietal-colic fissure, at the subhepatic level, omentum bursa, mimicking either a perforation of a hollow organ with generalized peritonitis (perforated gastric/duodenal ulcer) or the signs of peritoneal irritation of severe acute pancreatitis.
Perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with generalized peritonitis (purulent/faecal oid = Hinchey 3/4)

Pain, tenderness and signs of peritoneal irritation in the left iliac fossa in usually elderly people, associated with nausea, possible episodes of diarrhoea or constipation, fever. When the sigmoid loop is long and may be located in the right iliac fossa, abdominal pain may be most severe at this level. In the case of diverticular perforation (blocked peridiverticular abscess – perforated = purulent peritonitis or diverticulum perforated directly into the large peritoneal cavity = faecal peritonitis), the contents of the abscess/colon migrate through the right or left parietal-colonic recess, at the subhepatic level, omentum bursa, mimicking either a perforation of a cavitary organ with generalised peritonitis (perforated gastric/duodenal ulcer, perforated acute appendicitis) or the signs of peritoneal irritation of severe acute pancreatitis.

Acute cholecystitis Pain in the right hypochondrium radiating to the back/right shoulder, nausea, vomiting, fever, positive Murphy's sign. An inflamed, distended and ptotic gallbladder may manifest as pain in the right iliac fossa/right hypochondrium, which may mimic the symptoms of acute pancreatitis. At the same time, in the case of acute microlithiasis cholecystitis with choledochal "passage", when the duodenal papilla is "violated" by calculi, the appearance of acute cholecysto-pancreatitis may be outlined, with painful symptoms, followed by the biochemical picture of acute pancreatitis.
Angiocolitis with or without associated choledocholithiasi s

Charcot-Villard triad: high fever, jaundice, pain in the right hypochondrium; late association with nausea, vomiting, acholic stools, hyperchromic/choluric urine, skin pruritus. Sensitivity to superficial and deep palpation in the Cha-uffard pancreaticduodenal triangle, with signs of peritoneal irritation at this level. The haemodynamic response is similar to any acute surgical abdomen.

Acute mesenteric ischaemia/enterom esenteric infarction Diffuse abdominal pain, often starting after eating, moderate/severe, constant, sometimes like colic, not responding to opioid painkillers, starting with nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, progressive diarrhoea with later stopping of bowel movements, possible bloody stools/rectal bleeding. Personal history of cardiovascular disease (mechanical valves, atrial fibrillation, sinus node disease, acute myocardial infarction, etc., with or without associated anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy) in a patient over 60 years of age. Clinical – dyspnoea with tachypnoea, tachycardia, arterial hypotension, fever, altered cognitive status, with global distension, abdominal bloating, with possible signs of peritoneal irritation at the time of perforation of ischaemic cavitary organs. Due to the nature of vomiting, anorexia, pain and abdominal distension, the clinical picture can be confused with that of acute pancreatitis.

Chronic pancreatitis Chronic, intermittent abdominal pain lasting several hours, localised in the epigastric region or in the upper abdomen, with a tendency to radiate posteriorly "in a bar", often starting after meals (pain exacerbated by eating, especially hyperlipidic/hyperproteic foods), often associated with steatorrhoeic diarrhoea and long-term weight loss. Personal history of chronic alcohol consumption, diabetes mellitus or previous episodes of acute pancreatitis. Local abdominal examination – may be similar to that in acute pancreatitis, but with much reduced intensity.

Ascending colon/transverse colon neoplasm Dull, "muffled" abdominal pain, predominantly in the right iliac fossa/right flank/right hypochondrium, associated with fatigue, pallor, night sweats, diarrhoea, changes in bowel habits, rare haematochezia or rectal bleeding, weight loss. They become obstructive in the advanced stages of the disease, the tumour processes may be palpable, when they can also perforate, outlining the clinical picture of an acute surgical abdomen/pain complaints with reduced twisting compared to acute pancreatitis.
Low intestinal obstruction due to colonic obstruction Same as "Neoplasm of the ascending colon/transverse colon".
Transverse colon diverticulitis with or without diverticular perforation
Same as "Sigmoid diverticulitis".

Gastric neoplasm Dyspepsia, selective dysphagia ("fear of meat"), nausea, food-related vomiting (undigested food), postprandial fullness, anorexia, weight loss; in very advanced cases of haemorrhagic gastric tumours (upper gastrointestinal bleeding manifested by haematemesis and/or melena); gastric tumours – may invade the celiac plexus, causing severe pain similar to that of acute pancreatitis; large tumours – favour the onset of gastric emptying failure syndrome – coercitive vomiting with undigested food, severe dehydration, cachexia; in distant disease extension, metastases or palpable pathological adenopathies (Sister-Mary-Joseph – umbilical, Vircow-Troissier – left supraclavicular, Irish – left anterior axillary) may be identified, with or without bilateral basal pleurisy, jaundice, hepatomegaly. Rarely, gastric tumours can perforate into the large peritoneal cavity, presenting as a perforated gastric/duodenal ulcer with generalised peritonitis, culminating in significant pain.
Gastritis/Gastroent eritis/Bacterial/vira l gastroenterocolitis

Nausea and vomiting precede diffuse abdominal pain, which is colicky in nature. Watery/osmotic or haemorrhagic diarrhoea, myalgia, arthralgia, fever and anorexia are present. Clinically, pain sensitivity is diffuse, with rare signs of peritoneal irritation.

Ulcerative disease/peptic ulcer Epigastric/retrosternal pain, with a "burning" character, onset postprandial (gastric ulcer – immediately postprandial, duodenal ulcer – 2-3 hours postprandial), which can "wake the patient from sleep", with complete or partial spontaneous remission with self-medication with antacids or consumption of alkaline liquids. Epigastric pain may be associated with dyspepsia (bloating), heartburn, dysphagia with odynophagia, early postprandial satiety, weight loss, nausea, rare vomiting. In cases of haemorrhagic gastric/duodenal ulcers, upper gastrointestinal bleeding may occur, manifested by haematochezia or melena, but in small quantities. Personal history of dyspeptic ulcer syndrome/chronic gastro-duodenal ulcer, treatment with non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs or Helicobacter pylori infection. The perforative complications mentioned in "Perforated gastric/duodenal ulcer with generalised peritonitis or penetration into the pancreas" may lead to confusion with the clinical picture of acute pancreatitis.

Pancreatic neoplasm The clinical symptoms are pretty vague, showing up in the later stages of the cancer, and include: loss of appetite, weight loss weight loss, fatigue, "dull" epigastric pain, predominantly nocturnal, which may radiate posteriorly "in a band" (especially in advanced cases of the disease when invasion of the celiac plexus occurs); obstructive jaundice "Painless", associated with acholic stools, hyperchromic/choluric urine, and pruritus, is characteristic of cephalo-pancreatic tumours. Clinically, in advanced cases: palpable epigastric tumour, palpable gallbladder (Curvoissier-Terrier sign), umbilical SisterMary-Joseph node, left supraclavicular adenopathy (Virchow-Troissier), hepatomegaly, shifting dullness in the flanks (ascites), migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau's sign). The differential diagnosis with acute pancreatitis is made by referring to the pain syndrome, especially since there are cases of pancreatic neoplasms (especially mucinous/intraductal ones) that initially manifest as severe acute pancreatitis due to obstruction of the exocrine pancreatic duct system.

Acute viral hepatitis Clinical symptoms are dominated by anorexia, fatigue, nausea, rare vomiting with mixed contents, low-grade fever, diffuse abdominal pain, predominantly in the right hypochondrium. Clinically – hepatomegaly, tenderness in the right hypochondrium, negative Murphy's sign, no signs of peritoneal irritation. The differential diagnosis with acute pancreatitis is based on pain complaints.

Ascites syndrome Subjective complaints include: asthenia, fatigue, peripheral oedema, anorexia, postprandial fullness. Personal history of acute or chronic viral hepatitis, liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoproteinemia with hypoalbuminemia, congestive heart failure, advanced intra-abdominal neoplasms with peritoneal carcinomatosis. Clinical – painless abdominal distension, no tenderness, with shifting dullness in the flanks. The differential diagnosis with acute pancreatitis is made in terms of shifting dullness in the flanks and abdominal distension.
Chronic viral hepatitis decompensated, with portal hypertension, ascites syndrome and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

Clinical symptoms are dominated by anorexia, fatigue, nausea, rare vomiting with mixed content, subfebrile fever, diffuse abdominal pain, predominantly in the right hypochondrium, constipation, peripheral tremor of the upper limbs, confusion, altered consciousness. Clinically – porto-caval collateral circulation, abdominal distension, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, tenderness in the right hypochondrium, negative Murphy's sign, no signs of peritoneal irritation; in cases of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, against a background of ascites syndrome – signs of peritoneal irritation may be observed, associated with subfebrile/fever. The differential diagnosis with acute pancreatitis is based on pain complaints and ascites syndrome, with the latter being more significant in cases of hepatic decompensation.

Irritable bowel syndrome Symptoms include: changes in bowel movements (constipation with small stools, painful defecation requiring laxatives; alternating with diarrhoea – low volume, associated with rectal tenesmus), abdominal pain (diffuse, but may predominate in the lower abdomen, colicky in nature, without irradiation, which may be accentuated by eating and diminished by stool emission), meteorism, flatulence with precursor pain in the left hypochondrium; minor associated symptoms: mucus present in stool, dyspepsia, heartburn, nausea, with rare vomiting, dyspareunia, low libido, prostatism, worsening of symptoms during the premenstrual period, anorexia, weight loss. Symptoms usually begin at a young age, diarrhoea is very rarely associated with steatorrhoea, and clinically, no epigastric tenderness or signs of peritoneal irritation are identified. Diarrhoea syndrome and pain complaints make the differential diagnosis with acute pancreatitis.

Macroamylasemia The clinical symptoms may suggest mild acute pancreatitis, especially in the absence of alcohol abuse or lithiasis. The final differential diagnosis is made following biochemical and radiological examinations.
Macrolipase-mia Same as "Macroamylasemia".

Malabsorptive syndromes Malabsorptive Colic-like, intermittent abdominal pain, onset following the ingestion of foods rich in gluten/lactose/lipids, followed by nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Diarrhoea may be steatorrhoeic in appearance, hence the differential diagnosis with diarrhoea syndrome in acute pancreatitis.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm Asymptomatic until expansion/risk of rupture. In case of expansion, the clinical picture consists of dull, continuous abdominal pain, located in the hypogastric/mesoceliac region, with posterior and flank irradiation; the pain may be associated with hypotension, tachycardia, syncope, peripheral cyanosis, and altered cognitive status. Clinically, a pulsatile abdominal mass can be palpated from the umbilical level to the hypogastrium. The differential diagnosis with acute pancreatitis is made based on the pain syndrome and haemodynamic instability, which are more severe in the case of abdominal aortic aneurysm. Acute myocardial infarction Acute myocardial infarction

The symptoms of myocardial infarction are characterised by fatigue, pallor, sweating, with the cardinal symptom being precordial pain radiating to the base of the neck, left shoulder, and mandible; sometimes the pain is "burning" in nature/postprandial fullness/epigastric pain; it may also be associated with coughing, wheezing, inspiratory dyspnoea, tachycardia, tachypnoea and, initially, high blood pressure. The differential diagnosis with acute pancreatitis is made in the presence of epigastric pain, which is much more pronounced in acute pancreatitis. Laboratory tests and an ECG confirm the diagnosis.

Left basal pneumonia Irritating cough, later productive, with muco-purulent sputum, subfebrile/fever, tachycardia, dyspnoea with tachypnoea, central cyanosis, altered cognitive status, pleuritic pain alternating between respiratory phases, with posterior dorsal irradiation. Clinically, tracheal deviation, lateral cervical adenopathy, pulmonary rales (crepitant, wheezing, snoring) can be identified, with reduced vesicular murmur in the pneumonic focus, underlying the area of submatity/pulmonary dullness. The differential diagnosis with acute pancreatitis is made in terms of pain symptoms – located more cranially in the case of pneumonia.

Pleuritic syndromes Pleuritic Dyspnoea with orthopnoea, irritative/productive cough (depending on aetiology), pleural pain with a "stabbing" character, radiating to the shoulder; the patient may also present with peripheral oedema, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, night sweats, fever, haemoptysis, weight loss in weight. The physical examination is similar to that for pneumonitis, with the addition of pleural friction during auscultation. The differential diagnosis with acute pancreatitis is made by referring to the pain syndrome as well as to the pleural effusion (evacuation puncture with biochemical, cytological and bacteriological examination determines the diagnosis).

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Severe acute necrotising pancreatitis.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: Given the severity of the disease and its aetiology, the patient is admitted to the intensive care unit. Oral intake is stopped, coagulation tests are performed, a nasogastric/nasojejunal tube is inserted, acid-base and hydro-electrolytic rebalancing treatment is instituted, analgesic and prophylactic antithrombotic treatment is started, a urinary catheter is inserted to monitor diuresis and intravesical pressure, cardiac, blood pressure and oxygen saturation monitoring; empirical antibiotic therapy is not recommended until the risk of severity has been stratified and the aetiology of the disease has been elucidated; in the case of invasive procedures, dual combination antibiotic therapy (aerobic + anaerobic) will be administered.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: The patient is middle-aged, a smoker, with neuropsychiatric comorbidities (under treatment) and a history of surgery, with symptoms appearing over 72 hours ago, associated with haemodynamic instability and inflammatory syndrome; biologically, the patient already presents hypocalcaemia with severe pancreatic involvement, documented by radiological imaging. To date, clinically, biologically and radiologically, the patient can be classified as having severe acute necrotising pancreatitis of post-medicinal aetiology with peripancreatic collections (most likely septic). The patient's prognosis is serious, with a Ranson score (on admission 3 points) and an APACHE-II score of 18 points.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Oral intake is stopped, coagulation tests are performed, a nasogastric/nasojejunal tube is inserted, initiate acid-base and hydro-electrolytic rebalancing treatment, start analgesic and prophylactic antithrombotic treatment, insert a urinary catheter to monitor urine output and intravesical pressure, monitor heart rate, blood pressure and oxygen saturation; empirical antibiotic therapy is not recommended. Next, an abdominalpelvic CT scan with FNA aspiration of peripancreatic collections is recommended. If necrosis and collections peripancreatic collections are of septic aetiology, antibiotic treatment is instituted, followed by drainage of the peripancreatic collections (ideally minimally invasive, without opening the peritoneum: transgastric endoscopic drainage, CT-guided retroperitoneal drainage, laparoscopic pancreatic drainage and necrosectomy, open pancreatic drainage and necrosectomy). Early enteral nutrition can be administered either through an endoscopically placed naso-jejunal catheter or through a feeding jejunostomy (endoscopic/percutaneous/surgical). In order to further stabilise the patient and reduce the risk of MSOF, central venous access for haemodiafiltration is also considered in the Intensive Care Unit.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Reduction in Ranson severity scores (at 48 and 72 hours), APACHE II, as well as the absence of peripancreatic necrosis/collections (on abdominal-pelvic CT with contrast medium at 48 and 72 hours), reduction of biological impact and SIRS, and non-development of MSOF, are promising signs.

cases.title: Diffuse abdominal pain with "wooden abdomen"
cases.presentation: Patient AM, an unskilled worker, aged 45, presents to the emergency department complaining of severe diffuse abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. The current illness began suddenly, approximately 6 hours before the emergency presentation, with sudden, intense pain in the epigastrium (feeling of being "stabbed with a knife") that later radiated to the flank and right iliac fossa and, after about 1 hour, spread throughout the abdomen, accompanied by nausea and vomiting (initially food-related, later bilious). The patient has no significant family or personal history, is a smoker (approx. 20 cigarettes/day) and consumes alcohol almost daily (100-200 ml of spirits). The general clinical examination reveals an underweight, anxious patient with moist skin and a suffering facies. Locally, there is a normally shaped abdomen, which does not participate in respiratory movements, with marked sensitivity to palpation and generalised muscle contracture ("wooden abdomen"). Axillary temperature is 37.60 C; laboratory tests show leukocytosis (17,000/mm3 ), increased CRP (17.8 mg/l); ultrasound shows moderate free fluid subhepatically, perisplenically and in Douglas. An abdominal X-ray shows bilateral pneumoperitoneum.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation
Characteristics Acute peritonitis-type abdomen. Perforated gastric/duodenal ulcer.

Sudden onset of severe pain, classically described as a "stabbing knife" in the epigastrium (at the moment of perforation), followed by generalised pain throughout the abdomen, typically associated with nausea and reflex vomiting, subfebrile temperature, and delayed ileus-type transit disorders (dynamic). The abdomen is usually immobile, palpation is very painful, and intense muscle contracture frequently occurs, giving the classic sign of a "wooden abdomen." In elderly or frail patients, contracture may be replaced by muscle guarding, but other signs of acute peritonitis are frequently associated: Blumberg's sign, skin hyperesthesia, Mandel's sign. Auscultation reveals abdominal silence. Contributing factors (smoking, NSAID use, history of ulcerative disease) are frequently identified in the patient's medical history.

Acute peritonitis-type abdomen. Perforated diverticulitis The initial pain is located in the left iliac fossa, later becoming generalised. It is frequently associated with a fever above 380Celsius. Clinically, the pain is most intense in the left iliac fossa, and muscle contracture is generally replaced by defence. There are signs of acute peritonitic abdomen. The personal history may include episodes of complicated/uncomplicated diverticulitis.

Acute peritonitis-type abdomen. Posttraumatic peritonitis Occurs in the context of closed or open abdominal trauma through perforation of a hollow organ. The clinical picture is that of acute peritonitis, with the intensity of symptoms depending on the affected organ and the degree of contamination of the peritoneal cavity.

Acute peritonitis-type abdomen. Postoperative peritonitis The onset of pain, fever, and ileus in a recently operated patient, most commonly in the context of surgical intervention with digestive anastomosis. The pain may sometimes be less evident in the context of antibiotic and analgesic treatment or in frail patients, in which case the changes in the context of dynamic ileus are more prominent.

Acute peritonitis-type abdomen. Pelviperitonitis It occurs exclusively in women, sometimes with a history of genital infections. The clinical picture is less dramatic, with symptoms and signs mainly located in the lower abdomen.
Acute peritonitis-type abdomen. Peritonitis in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis

It occurs in the context of outpatient peritoneal dialysis treatment in patients with chronic renal failure. Contamination occurs through the dialysis catheter, the infection is not massive, and the clinical picture is generally more blurred. Abdominal pain and fever frequently occur, and clinically there are signs of peritoneal irritation.

Acute occlusive abdomen Transit disorders predominate, with intestinal transit stopping for gas and faeces, nausea and vomiting (initially food-related, later bilious and faecal). The pain is less intense and is often colicky. Clinically, the abdomen is significantly distended, with marked tympanism, sensitive to palpation, but without signs of peritoneal irritation.

Acute vascular abdomen. Enteromesenteric infarction The condition occurs in a specific context (atherosclerosis, emboligenic risk), the pain is intense, frequently associated with signs of shock (hypotension, tachycardia). Clinically, there are signs of peritoneal irritation, without frank contracture.

Acute haemorrhagic abdomen. Haemoperitoneum Occurs in a traumatic context, abdominal pain is less intense, there is peritoneal irritation due to blood. Associated with signs of hypovolaemic shock (sometimes difficult to differentiate from septic shock).
Organ torsion syndrome Severe pain, often located in the area of the affected organ.

Acute pancreatitis Bar-like pain in the epigastric region, radiating to the back. Clinically, there is tenderness on palpation in the epigastric region, with signs of irritation at this level, the rest of the abdomen being generally free on clinical examination.

Gastric/duodenal ulcer in a penetration crisis The pain is different in nature, less intense and radiates posteriorly. As there is no free perforation in the peritoneal cavity, there are no signs of peritoneal irritation.
Acute medical abdomen. Biliary colic Intense pain in the right hypochondrium, nausea and vomiting, without signs of peritoneal irritation.

Acute medical abdomen. Renal-ureteral colic The pain is characteristic, starting in the back and radiating anteriorly to the iliac fossa and inferiorly to the inner thigh and genitals. There is tenderness on palpation of the abdomen, but no signs of irritation.

Extra-abdominal conditions. Acute myocardial infarction Inferior myocardial infarction may present with digestive symptoms, such as abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting through a vagal reflex mechanism, but there are no signs of peritoneal irritation and the abdominal examination is often without pathological findings.

Extra-abdominal conditions. Basal pneumonia Pain in basal pneumonia may radiate to the abdomen but is typically stabbing in nature, exacerbated by inspiration. Clinical examination of the abdomen reveals no major changes.
Extra-abdominal conditions. Shingles.
The characteristic metameric rash appears, the pain is very intense but is localised at the parietal level, with no signs of irritation.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Perforated gastric/duodenal ulcer. Generalised peritonitis.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: The patient requires emergency surgery; surgical intervention is recommended – ulcer suturing, lavage, drainage. To confirm the diagnosis and determine the aetiology of the digestive perforation, an abdominal and pelvic CT scan with contrast medium may be indicated.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: The patient is young, with no significant comorbidities, the disease is approximately 6 hours from onset (chemical peritonitis phase), and the prognosis is good with appropriate surgical treatment initiated early.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Prompt surgical intervention, suturing of the perforated ulcer, lavage and drainage of the peritoneal cavity. Access can be via laparotomy or laparoscopy. Laparoscopic surgery alleviates postoperative pain, reduces wound complications (infection, evisceration, eventration), allows early mobilisation and shortens the duration of hospitalisation and postoperative recovery. For gastric ulcer location, excision of the ulcer margins for biopsy (to rule out a malignant process) is considered. It can be combined with omentoplasty, the fixation of an omental flap at the level of the ulcer suture. Postoperatively, antisecretory therapy (proton pump inhibitors) and antibiotic therapy for Helicobacter pylori (which is positive in over 90% of cases of complicated ulcers) are initiated.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: The patient should be afebrile, with inflammation markers (leukocytes, CRP) tending towards normalisation, resumed intestinal transit, and minimal pain. The presence of fever (above 38.5-390C), inflammation (leukocytosis, elevated CRP) and pain should raise suspicion of an intraperitoneal abscess, which has developed in the context of suboptimal treatment of peritonitis.

cases.title: Abdominal pain in a patient with thoracoabdominal trauma
cases.presentation: A 40-year-old male driver wearing a seatbelt is involved in a road accident. The car he was driving (Dacia Logan) skidded on a bend at 80 km/h, crashed into a tree, deployed the airbag and suffered significant deformation of the driver's door, which protruded into the passenger compartment. Upon arrival at the emergency department (40 minutes after the accident), the patient is conscious, haemodynamically stable and complains of pain (spontaneous and on palpation) in the lower left hemithorax and left hypochondrium, without muscle guarding, Blumberg's sign negative. Bone crepitus is felt on palpation of the lower left hemithorax. The chest X-ray shows only a fracture of the ninth and tenth ribs on the posterior axillary line, without displacement. FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) ultrasound reveals a small amount of fluid in the peritoneal cavity. Toxicology tests are negative. BP = 110/60 mmHg, pulse = 85/min, Hb = 10g%. Urine appears normal.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation
Characteristics Chest contusion with rib fractures. Abdominal contusion with ruptured spleen.

Given the considerable impact energy, which deformed the driver's door, we expect possible internal organ injuries. Chest pain and bone crepitus suggest rib fractures, which are confirmed by chest X-ray. Decreased haemoglobin and a positive FAST ultrasound suggest haemoperitoneum. Abdominal pain, associated with left rib fractures and the presence of free fluid in the peritoneum on abdominal ultrasound, suggests a possible ruptured spleen. Splenic rupture is the most common type of injury in closed abdominal trauma.
Thoracic contusion with rib fractures. Abdominal contusion with rupture of other parenchymal organs.

Unlike abdominal wounds, abdominal contusions may be followed by multiple injuries in several regions of the abdomen, without necessarily having any visible traumatic marks on the outside. Haemoperitoneum can also result from liver lacerations, mesenteric or other visceral injuries caused by a counterblow or tearing mechanism. A significant increase in transaminases may suggest liver damage. If pancreatic trauma is suspected, measuring lipase and amylase levels in the blood and peritoneal fluid can guide the diagnosis. However, to confirm the diagnosis, a contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan is necessary.
Thoracic contusion with rib fractures. Abdominal contusion with rupture of the hollow viscera.

The peritoneal fluid detected by ultrasound may also originate from trauma to a hollow organ (stomach, duodenum, small intestine, colon, bladder, etc.). In this case, there should be signs of acute peritonitis: increasing pain, muscle guarding, positive Blumberg's sign, fever. However, these signs may be obscured by the concomitant presence of blood in the peritoneum. To confirm the diagnosis, a CT scan with contrast medium is necessary. In the absence of haematuria, a bladder rupture is unlikely.
Chest contusion with rib fractures.
Diaphragmatic rupture is more common in crush injuries and falls from height. A possible herniation in
Abdominal pain in patients with thoracoabdominal trauma Abdominal contusion with diaphragmatic rupture.

The herniation of abdominal viscera could have been observed on the chest X-ray, but the absence of this herniation does not rule out a possible diaphragmatic rupture. To confirm the diagnosis, a contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominal CT scan is necessary.
Thoracic contusion with rib fractures. Abdominal contusion with retroperitoneal organ injuries and retroperitoneal haematoma.

In the absence of haematuria, renal trauma is unlikely. However, given the force and direction of action of the injuring agent (suggested by the deformation of the car body), it is possible that there is a retroperitoneal haematoma. Sometimes, through breaches in the posterior parietal peritoneum, blood from the retroperitoneal haematoma can enter the peritoneal cavity, thus producing a positive FAST ultrasound. To confirm the diagnosis, a CT scan with contrast medium is necessary.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Closed chest trauma with fracture of ribs IX and X on the posterior axillary line, without displacement. Abdominal contusion. Post-traumatic haemoperitoneum, possibly due to a ruptured spleen.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: After the initial assessment and initiation of volume resuscitation, blood compatibility tests and laboratory analyses are performed. The medical history and physical examination are completed. Given that the patient is haemodynamically stable, a secondary assessment requires an urgent chest, abdominal and pelvic CT scan with contrast medium to determine the extent of the injury. CT is non-invasive, quantifies haemoperitoneum and parenchymal organ injuries, and visualises the retroperitoneum or small haemothorax that escapes chest X-ray.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: CT confirms the fractures of the left IX and X ribs detected on chest X-ray and certifies the absence of any associated pelvic trauma or retroperitoneal haematoma. At the abdominal level, there is a laceration of the splenic parenchyma in the middle third of the spleen, involving a segmental vessel at which there is extravasation of contrast medium during the arterial phase. Haemoperitoneum is clearly visible perisplenically, subhepatically, interileally and in the Douglas pouch. No other lesions of the intra-abdominal and retroperitoneal organs are found. After the patient returned from the CT scan, despite sustained volume therapy, there was an increase in skin pallor and pulse rate to 96 beats/min, as well as a decrease in haemoglobin and blood pressure values: Hb = 8g%, BP = 100/40 mmHg. Because the CT scan revealed a grade IV spleen injury, and the radiologically visible contrast extravasation indicated active bleeding with a relatively high flow rate, corroborated by the tendency towards haemodynamic instability, emergency laparotomy was indicated to ensure haemostasis.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Splenectomy is recommended for grade IV splenic lesions. The approach is median laparotomy because it allows for good exploration of the abdominal cavity. This is necessary because there may be lesions that escape imaging investigations (e.g. peritonitis or small postcontusive haematomas in the intestinal wall that can lead to late intestinal perforations). After splenectomy and evacuation of blood from the peritoneum, the peritoneal cavity is washed with saline and drained.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Immediately after surgery, the response to volume resuscitation therapy is monitored, i.e. blood pressure stability, increase in haemoglobin levels, recolouring of the skin, decrease in pulse rate, etc. The appearance of the surgical wound and the secretions from the drainage tubes are also checked daily. Following splenectomy, there is an increase in platelet count, which requires the administration of antiplatelet agents (aspirin) as antithrombotic prophylaxis. The patient must also be immunised against infections with Pneumococcus, Meningococcus and Haemophilus Influenzae.

cases.title: Abdominal pain, pallor, dyspnoea and tachycardia after thoracoabdominal trauma
cases.presentation: A minor patient, aged 17, a competitive athlete, recently involved in a sports accident, presents at the emergency department with abdominal pain in the left hypochondrium and periumbilical area, pallor, dyspnoea, and tachycardia. The patient, a competitive athlete, was involved in a sports accident an hour ago during a hockey match. He had a strong impact with the metal blade of his opponent's skate, with the initial area of maximum contact in the left hypochondrium, minor head trauma, no loss of consciousness, no trauma to the limbs. Initially, the pain is located in the left hypochondrium, accentuated by inspiration, then after about half an hour, pain appears in the periombilical and epigastric areas, radiating to the left shoulder, followed by a feeling of physical fatigue and thirst, and slight tension in the abdominal muscles. The coach notices that he is pale. He is rushed to hospital. On physical examination: the patient is pale, his skin is cold and sweaty, with no signs of trauma, his abdomen has limited participation in respiratory movements, moderate abdominal pain on percussion and palpation, more pronounced in the left hypochondrium, diffuse muscle guarding, abdominal dullness displaced to the flanks, hydro-aerial noises, diminished. Cardio-respiratory and haemodynamic stable, with mild tachycardia and tachypnoea. FAST ultrasound shows free fluid in the splenic, subhepatic, interileal and Douglas spaces, in moderate amounts. Oliguria, normal-appearing urine. Hb value = 10.5g/dl.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation

Characteristics Haemothorax/hae mopneumothorax Chest complaints, especially dyspnoea/tachypnoea, are predominant, with dullness on percussion and decreased breath sounds in the affected area. The most common source of bleeding is local, from the site of the parietal or pleuro-pulmonary fracture. A blood loss of up to 750 ml in a 70 kg person does not cause significant haemodynamic changes, while between 750-1000 ml signs of hypovolaemic shock appear. Approximately 80% of cases are successfully treated by tube thoracostomy; indication for thoracostomy: rapid loss of more than 1000 ml of blood or more than 200 ml/hour for 4 hours after thoracostomy; transfusion necessary to maintain haemodynamic stability.

Diaphragmatic rupture Difficult to detect clinically. Chest pain accentuated by breathing and coughing, accompanied by signs of cardio-respiratory failure in thoraco-abdominal trauma, draws our attention to a possible diaphragmatic injury. The most common are ruptures of the diaphragmatic dome (radial, central or anterolateral), followed by phrenic-costal detachments (more commonly tears of the costal-diaphragmatic insertions between the anterior and posterior axillary lines). Usually, in dome injuries, hernias develop slowly, while in phrenic-costal detachments, visceral herniation is massive and occurs simultaneously with the trauma.

Traumatic splenic injuries The spleen is the organ most commonly affected in abdominal trauma. Clinical manifestations correlate with the severity of bleeding, associated intra/extraabdominal lesions and the patient's condition, with young patients being able to compensate clinically very well for massive bleeding. Patients complain of pain of varying intensity in the left hypochondrium, base of the hemithorax or left flank, radiating to the left shoulder (Kehr's sign) or base of the neck (Saegesser's sign), tenderness on palpation or decompression in the left hypochondrium, rarely a tumour mass with imprecise boundaries, dull on percussion, as an expression of a perisplenic haematoma, is palpated in the left hypochondrium. Symptoms and signs of hypovolaemic shock may occur: pallor, blurred vision, lipothymia, cold and clammy extremities, dyspnoea, thirst, tachycardia, tachypnoea, thready pulse, oliguria, decreased blood pressure. Moderate abdominal distension, shifting dullness (Ballantine's sign), paralytic ileus, diffuse abdominal contracture, sometimes signs
Diffuse peritoneal irritation, bulging of the Douglas pouch, is associated with the presence of haemoperitoneum. Traumatic liver injuries

Similar to those of splenic trauma, pain is mainly localised in the right hypochondrium, the base of the hemithorax and the right flank. Rapid decelerations can cause massive haemorrhages through detachment of the hepatic veins from the inferior vena cava and injuries to the hepatic pedicle. In the case of contusion trauma, the parenchymal fracture trajectories converge radially towards the point of impact, are irregular, with the appearance of both haemorrhage and biliary leakage in the case of vascular-biliary involvement. The right lobe is affected 5 times more frequently than the left.

Lesions of large abdominal vessels They are particularly serious, with death occurring before access to emergency services in almost 50% of cases. The clinical picture is dominated by marked haemodynamic instability, signs of hypovolaemic shock and rapid loss of consciousness. Almost total abdominal dullness in massive peritoneal effusion, abdominal distension, paralytic ileus, abdominal muscle contracture; surgical intervention for haemostasis must be performed as a matter of extreme urgency.

Traumatic gastric injuries Gastric wall ruptures are more common when the stomach is full; gastric contents rapidly cause chemical peritonitis with signs of hypovolaemic shock, intense abdominal pain, abdominal muscle contracture, ileus, and shifting dullness in the flanks. Much of the parietal haemorrhage can be found enterally or as an intragastric haematoma.

Traumatic duodenal injuries These are difficult to diagnose clinically. In almost a quarter of all abdominal trauma, the duodenum may suffer injuries, especially by crushing on the spine, but traumatic duodenal perforation is much rarer (0.2-3.7%). The mechanism of injury (sudden acceleration-deceleration), pain in the upper abdomen accompanied by tachycardia, fever and vomiting are the main symptoms that could guide the diagnosis.

Traumatic injuries of They manifest as abdominal pain, mainly in the lower abdomen, associated with the small intestine abdominal contracture, ileus, and tachycardia. Signs of hypovolaemic shock may occur, especially if the mesenteric vessels are damaged. Moderate abdominal fluid collection is clinically detected by movable dullness in the flanks. The presence of signs of peritonitis indicates surgical intervention, as untreated peritonitis has a serious prognosis. Traumatic injuries of They are rarer than traumatic injuries of the small intestine, with the transverse colon the colon being the most affected. Due to the high septicity of the colonic contents, the clinical picture develops more rapidly than in simulated injuries of the small intestine, and the general condition deteriorates rapidly. Traumatic rupture of the bladder

Intraperitoneal rupture of the bladder in abdominal trauma without pelvic fracture is due to bladder fullness and rapid compression-decompression. It is characterised by the absence of urination and the sensation of urination. Uroperitoneum manifests itself as abdominal pain (not very intense), abdominal distension, and movable abdominal dullness.

Traumatic renal injuries The kidney can be traumatised, especially in the case of lateral injuries, through compression on the spine. In approximately 70% of hepatic dilations, the integrity of the renal capsule is preserved. Bulging of the lumbar region, pain and tenderness on palpation may indicate a perirenal haematoma, and macroscopic haematuria frequently occurs. In severe trauma accompanied by intraperitoneal haemorrhage, abdominal pain is accompanied by muscle guarding, ileus, displaced abdominal dullness, and signs of hypovolaemic shock.

Traumatic pancreatic injuries Pancreatic injuries in closed abdominal trauma occur more frequently at the site where the pancreas intersects the spine (L2), are less common in trauma, but severe, with mortality reaching up to 25%. They are difficult to detect clinically, especially in a polytraumatic context. Their severity is due to the coexistence of adjacent organ injuries with which the pancreas forms a common anatomical-functional block and the onset of acute post-traumatic pancreatitis. Clinically, continuous, persistent periombilical pain, radiating posteriorly and to the left flank, raises a red flag, but the dominant symptoms are caused by the injury to the neighbouring viscera.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Traumatic splenic rupture with haemoperitoneum.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: Urgent laboratory tests are requested: complete blood count, liver and kidney function tests, cytolysis enzymes, pancreatic enzymes, coagulation profile, blood type, Rh factor. Volumetric rebalancing treatment with micro- and macromolecular solutions is instituted. An emergency chest X-ray is requested to detect haemoperitoneum/pneumoperitoneum and determine the need for possible pleural drainage, rapid radiological assessment of the mediastinum and possible rib/vertebral fractures, and radiological status of the diaphragm. Once the patient is haemodynamically stable, an emergency abdominal CT scan is requested to determine the extent of the injury and the therapeutic approach. The treatment options are explained to the patient and parents, and consent is requested for possible surgery.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: The chest X-ray reveals a left basal pulmonary contusion with minimal adjacent pleural effusion. CT scan reveals a splenic lesion with parenchymal involvement, approximately 5 cm in size, affecting the lower pole, with a trajectory towards the splenic hilum, with active bleeding from a segmental hilar branch, with a 4 cm diameter mesosplenic hypodense area, free fluid with perisplenic, perihepatically, interileally and at the Douglas pouch, in moderate quantity. According to the severity scale formulated by the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma, it falls within grade IV severity.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: The optimal treatment would be emergency segmental branch/splenic artery angioembolisation, with or without the need for surgery, depending on the evolution. If this option is not available, emergency surgery is recommended, with haemostasis, splenorrhaphy or subtotal splenectomy. Especially in young people, it is very important to preserve part of the parenchyma in order to preserve splenic functions, especially immune function, as OPSI (overwhelming postsplenectomy infections) are more common in this population.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: Patients with splenic trauma are monitored in the intensive care unit for at least 24-48 hours, depending on the extent of the injury and the therapeutic approach. The appropriate response to treatment is monitored by maintaining haemodynamic stability with adequate Hb and Ht values, favourable evolution of the general condition, minimal need for transfusions (less than 4U), remission of peritoneal haematomas/minimal secretions. on drainage tubes. Hb and Ht are measured every 6-12 hours, abdominal ultrasound is performed frequently, and CT scans may be performed frequently, every 24-72 hours.
