cases.title: Severe obesity
cases.presentation: ME, a 45-year-old obese patient who works as a cook, comes to the surgical clinic outpatient department requesting bariatric surgery. She complains of low energy levels, anxiety and increasingly low self-esteem. The patient's husband is alarmed by the loud snoring and breathing interruptions he has noticed in his wife during sleep. Both of the patient's parents are obese. She was of normal weight during adolescence, but began to gain weight steadily after the age of 25. She admits to having had snacking habits, which were encouraged by her professional environment. Over the past 4 years, she has tried to lose weight through the Dukan, Paleo, Atkins and Montignac diets, but without lasting results. Six months ago, she was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity and is being treated with metformin. The patient is currently obese, weighing 104 kg and measuring 168 cm in height. Her waist circumference is 99 cm, and her waist-to-hip ratio is 0.92.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: Clinical situation
Characteristics Obesity – classification etiopathogenetic – primary – secondary: endocrine: hypothyroidism, Cushing's disease, polycystic ovary

Obesity – WHO 2004 severity – grade I – BMI 30–34.9 kg/m2 – grade II – BMI 35-39.9 kg/m2 (severe obesity) – grade III – BMI ≥ 40 kg/m2 (morbid, extreme obesity) (BMI ≥ 50 kg/m2 syndrome, STH deficiency, hypothalamic obesity, hypogonadism, insulinoma, pseudohypoparathyroidism; genetic-monogenic: leptin or leptin receptor deficiency, proopiomelanocortin POMC deficiency, melanocortin MCR4 receptor deficiency; genetic syndromes: Prader-Wili, Carpenter, etc.; iatrogenic: antidepressants: lithium, tricyclics (amitriptyline, doxepin), SSRIs (paroxetine, sertraline); antipsychotics (olanzapine, quetiapine); anticonvulsants; antidiabetics (insulin, thiazolidinediones, sulfonylureas); corticosteroids; oestrogenprogestogens; antihistamines; beta-blockers superobesity)
(…) classification in surgical literature Obesity – clinical classification

– abdominal (android, central) with 2 components: visceral and subcutaneous Waist circumference > (80)88 cm in women, and > (94)102 cm in men Waist-tohip ratio > 0.85 in women, and > 0.90 in men Histologically, this type of obesity is usually hypertrophic Increased risk of diabetes mellitus

– Gluteofemoral (gynoid) Waist circumference < (80)88 cm in women, and < (94)102 cm in men Waist-tohip ratio < 0.85 in women, and < 0.90 in men Histologically, this type of obesity is usually hyperplastic

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Primary obesity grade II – BMI 37 (104/1.682) with android distribution. The causes of secondary obesity have been ruled out:
– medicinal causes were excluded from the medical history; – physical examination excluded phenotypes specific to Cushing's disease and genetic syndromes;
– laboratory tests: FT4, TSH, Anti-TPO, serum cortisol, FSH, LH, estradiol, progesterone, DHEA-S, testosterone hormone levels ruled out endocrine causes

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: Identify associated comorbidities Diabetes Fasting blood glucose: 128 mg/dL, glycaemic profile (values between 125-178 mg/dL), glycated haemoglobin HbA1c: 6.9% shows good control of diabetes with diet + metformin 2x1000 mg/day Sleep apnoea Cardiorespiratory polygraphy confirmed sleep apnoea syndrome – severe obstructive form. Apnoeahypopnoea index = 34 (at > 20) Metabolic syndrome This is confirmed as the patient meets 3 of the 5 criteria for metabolic syndrome: central obesity, triglycerides 224 mg/dL (> 150), HDL cholesterol 35 mg/dL (< 50). Nocturnal polysomnography is indicated but refused by the patient. Other preoperative clinical and paraclinical assessments
▪ Abdominal ultrasound screening – Hepatic steatosis. Gallbladder lithiasis – at least 3 stones measuring approx. 1 cm

▪ Thyroid ultrasound – no pathological changes ▪ Upper digestive endoscopy – no pathological changes. Helicobacter pylori negative (urease test) ▪ Pre-anaesthetic consultation – no drug allergies; no "short, thick neck"; no history of thromboembolic disease, Caprini score = 6 (high risk of thromboembolic event)

▪ Clinical cardiological evaluation, ECG, echocardiography – normal ▪ Psychiatric assessment, Anxiety disorder – social phobia ▪ Psychological assessment, self-esteem assessment – Rosenberg test: 14 points = low self-esteem; Alcohol

Use Disorder Test-core (AUDIT-C) = 2; Drug Abuse Screening Test (DAST) = 0; Millon Behavioral Medicine Diagnostic (MBMD); Questionnaire on Weight and Eating Patterns (QWEP); Becks Depression Inventory II = 10. The psychologist provides us with a written report on motivation, compliance, commitment, absence of psychopathies, addictions, psychotropic medication, etc.

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: The patient meets the criteria: BMI > 35 plus at least one obesity-related comorbidity (3 comorbidities: diabetes mellitus, sleep apnoea and metabolic syndrome).

He also has gallstones, which are not included in the chapter on obesity-related comorbidities, but which should preferably be treated concurrently with the bariatric procedure, as the subsequent weight loss process accentuates biliary lithogenic mechanisms, and subsequent minimally invasive surgery will be much more difficult on a scarred abdomen.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Of the few current bariatric procedures, such a case of obesity with recently developed type 2 diabetes benefits most from gastric bypass surgery, which, in addition to gastric restriction, also acts by altering the incretin-anti-incretin balance, improving glucose tolerance. The gastric sleeve procedure is technically easier and has a lower risk of post-operative complications, but the metabolic effect is somewhat reduced. Biliopancreatic diversion with or without duodenal switch is excessive for a BMI of 37. Gastric banding is the easiest procedure, but the metabolic effect is the lowest. The experience of the surgical team is also taken into account when choosing the procedure. Given that the excess weight is not very high (~40 kg), that the diabetes is recent and easily controlled with diet and ADO, and that there is no gastroesophageal reflux or contraindication for laparoscopy, it is decided to perform a laparoscopic longitudinal gastrectomy ("gastric sleeve") and cholecystectomy.

steps.q: How do you monitor the response to treatment?
a: The surgery went smoothly. The avulsion of a vein in the splenic hilum required topical haemostasis with Surgicel. On the fifth postoperative day, after radiological exclusion of gastric fistula, the left subphrenic drainage tubes were removed and oral feeding was resumed, with liquid and paste-like food for one week and then a specific diet with mineral and vitamin supplements. ADO is discontinued. One month after surgery, fasting blood glucose, measured repeatedly, is normal. He is eating according to the diet and does not feel hungry. Three months after surgery, she has lost 13 kg. Her loud snoring has disappeared. She starts a fitness programme, 3x2 hours/week and daily walks of at least 2 km. She is reintegrated professionally with normal working capacity. Her self-esteem has greatly improved, and her anxiety disorder and social phobia have remitted. At 6 months, she has lost 22 kg, representing 55% of her excess weight. Fasting blood sugar, cholesterol and triglycerides are normal. She easily maintains her lifestyle: diet with supplements and exercise programme, has a normal appetite, without compulsive eating. She has completely renewed her wardrobe. She reports moderate hair loss, for which she is undergoing topical treatment with Revalid lotion.

One year after surgery, she weighs 76 kg, corresponding to a 70% reduction in excess weight. The objective is to achieve a marked reduction in abdominal adiposity with the appearance of a skin "abdominal apron". The surgical team is considering performing an abdominoplasty in 3 months.

cases.title: Acute abdominal pain with vomiting, abdominal distension and cessation of bowel movements
cases.dx: Colonic obstruction from left colon cancer
kp: Constipation, blood in stool, then pain, faeculent vomiting, distension
cases.presentation: Patient MN, a 62-year-old retired railway worker, presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain throughout the abdomen, vomiting and absence of bowel movements. He has a history of type II diabetes, treated with diet and oral antidiabetic medication, high blood pressure, chronic ischaemic heart disease and chronic alcoholism. He has a history of appendectomy. He reports recent constipation (for about 6 months), alternating with short episodes of diarrhoea and fatigue; he has sometimes noticed bloody streaks in his stool. The current pain has been present for 3 days and is persistent and intense. Vomiting has accompanied the pain since its onset, but its appearance has changed over time: initially it contained food, but now it is dirty in appearance. The last stool was 3 days ago (a few hours before the onset of pain). Objective findings: overweight patient, sweating, with altered general condition; BP = 110/70 mmHg, pulse 110/min; distended abdomen, sensitive to palpation; a right inguinal hernia approx. 5 cm in diameter, reducible, painless; on rectal examination, empty rectal ampulla, normal prostate. Laboratory tests show: leukocytosis (23,000/mm3 ), anaemia (Hb 10 g/dl), hyponatraemia (135 mEq/l), nitrogen retention (urea 83 mg/dl, creatinine 2.1 mg/dl), hypoalbuminaemia (6.1 g/dl), hyperglycaemia (165 mg/dl), slightly elevated amylase.

steps.q: What diagnoses are possible? / Differential diagnosis
a: A large number of conditions, some surgical, others medical, must be considered. It is important to differentiate between conditions that benefit from surgical treatment and those that benefit from conservative treatment. The provisional diagnosis is acute abdomen. Clinical situation

Characteristics Intestinal obstruction This is suggested by the combination of generalised abdominal pain + lack of bowel movements + abdominal distension + vomiting. The deterioration in general condition, as well as some laboratory changes (hyponatraemia, nitrogen retention) could be explained by this diagnosis. Some causes of intestinal obstruction in this patient could be:

– a history of surgery (appendectomy) could cause a bridle obstruction; – Transit disorders (reported in the medical history) and fatigue could be due to a colonic tumour; this could be the cause of an obstruction.

– the hernia discovered during the physical examination could cause occlusion, but the description indicates an uncomplicated hernia. The empty rectal ampulla may be due to an obstruction in the sigmoid colon or upper rectum (Hocheneg's sign), but it may also be incidental. The dirty (faecal?) appearance of the vomit suggests an old intestinal obstruction, but it could also occur in neglected peritonitis. Blood pressure ("normal" in a hypertensive patient) and tachycardia, as well as electrolyte imbalance and abnormal renal function tests, indicate hydro-electrolytic sequestration (possibly in the digestive lumen).

Generalised peritonitis Generalised peritonitis is most often secondary (perforation of a hollow organ, leading to bacterial contamination ± chemical aggression of the peritoneal cavity). The characteristic sign of generalized peritonitis is muscle guarding (or contracture), which is absent in this patient; however, we must take into account that the patient is examined 3 days after the onset of pain, in which case muscle guarding may be masked by abdominal distension, which gradually develops in peritonitis. Alteration of general condition, cessation of intestinal transit and vomiting also occur in peritonitis and other acute abdominal conditions.

High leukocytosis, sweating, and altered general condition could be due to a septic factor (peritonitis). On the other hand, high leukocytosis could also occur in strangulation occlusion or entero-mesenteric infarction. Dehydration (hypotension, tachycardia), electrolyte imbalance, and increased urea and creatinine levels may be the result of fluid sequestration in the peritoneal cavity.

Acute pancreatitis Abdominal pain and altered general condition (shock?) are characteristic of acute pancreatitis. Alcohol is a trigger for pancreatitis. Physical examination may reveal abdominal distension, and sometimes intraperitoneal amylase spillage causes muscle guarding. Amylase and lipase levels are elevated. The diagnosis is established according to the "minimum 2 out of 3 criteria" rule:
– acute onset of severe and persistent abdominal pain, located in the epigastrium and radiating to the flank, back or entire abdomen,
– serum lipase/amylase levels more than three times higher than the normal maximum value,

– characteristic appearance on imaging (computed tomography or MRI or ultrasound). In the patient presented, amylase is slightly elevated, which is not characteristic of pancreatitis; pancreatic enzymes may also increase slightly in peritonitis.

Enteromesent eric infarction This occurs through embolism or thrombosis. Abdominal pain, vomiting, abdominal distension, and cessation of transit are common symptoms of entero-mesenteric infarction. However, abdominal pain is intense and the general condition is severely altered. During a rectal examination, blood may be observed on the examiner's glove, but this sign may be absent. Leukocytosis is significant. Risk factors for the patient include high blood pressure and ischaemic heart disease.

Inferior myocardial infarction Inferior myocardial infarction can manifest as radiating abdominal pain, deterioration of general condition, and vomiting. Even though it is unlikely for a myocardial infarction to evolve over 3 days without characteristic cardiovascular signs, this diagnosis should not be overlooked. An electrocardiogram and determination of myocardial necrosis markers are necessary.

Diabetic ketoacidosis Acidosis caused by the accumulation of keto acids can cause generalised abdominal pain by irritating the nerve endings in the peritoneal serosa. However, the patient's blood glucose level does not justify these symptoms. The blood glucose level (165 mg/dl) is more likely to be the result of decompensated diabetes in the context of stress due to another condition. However, this diagnosis must be considered in order to be ruled out.
Others For example:

– renal colic; biliary colic – acute pyelonephritis – saturnine colic – acute porphyria – basal pneumonia, basal pleurisy – splenic infarction – ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, dissecting aneurysm – sigmoid volvulus, intestinal volvulus – etc.

steps.q: What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
a: 1. Intestinal obstruction 2. Generalised peritonitis The obstruction is supported by the association between abdominal pain, cessation of intestinal transit (the cardinal sign of obstruction), abdominal distension and vomiting. Intestinal transit disorders and rectal bleeding suggest obstruction by a tumour of the descending/sigmoid colon or rectum. However, the clinical picture could also be that of neglected peritonitis due to colonic tumour perforation. Since the case presentation does not specify imaging investigations, the diagnosis cannot be established with certainty. Even so, it is noteworthy that the most likely conditions require surgery as the main treatment method. Therefore, the provisional diagnosis is acute surgical abdomen.

steps.q: What do you do next?
a: Once the diagnosis of acute abdomen (and implicitly the absolute indication for surgery) has been established, the following will be considered:
– rapid preoperative preparation – completion of investigations (during the time until surgery)
Preoperative preparation consists of:

– peripheral venous access (± central) – nasogastric aspiration; cessation of any food and fluid intake per os – hydro-electrolytic rebalancing treatment – analgesic treatment – antibiotic treatment – oxygen therapy – urinary catheterisation and diuresis monitoring – monitoring of blood pressure, pulse, PVC
At the same time, several investigations will be carried out:

– abdominal ultrasound (quick and easy to perform) – abdominal CT scan with contrast medium (most informative) – chest X-ray – electrocardiogram – laboratory investigations (coagulogram, acid-base balance parameters, etc.)

steps.q: How serious is the patient's condition? / What is the stage of the disease?
a: Even if the preoperative diagnosis is not precisely established, it is clear that there are conditions that threaten the patient's life. Dehydration, electrolyte imbalance and metabolic acidosis lead to the patient's death.

steps.q: What treatment do you recommend?
a: Surgical treatment is absolutely necessary. Only surgery can interrupt the pathophysiological mechanism that would lead to death. Even if the results of imaging tests are known before the operation, surgery is the final stage of diagnosis; surgical exploration of the abdomen will determine the cause of the obstruction/peritonitis and allow staging of the disease that led to this complication. The surgery will be chosen based on intraoperative findings. Most likely, a Hartmann resection will be performed. Subsequent treatment (removal of the colostomy and restoration of the continuity of the digestive tract, chemotherapy, etc.) depends on what is found during the surgery.

stations.scenario: R10-1.1 A 62-year-old female patient presents with abdominal pain, absence of bowel movements, and vomiting. She reports recent constipation (for about 6 months), alternating with short episodes of diarrhoea and fatigue; she has sometimes noticed bloody streaks in her stool. The current pain has been present for 3 days and is persistent and intense. The vomiting has accompanied the pain since its onset, but its appearance has changed over time: initially it contained food, but now it is foul-smelling. The last bowel movement was 3 days ago (a few hours before the onset of pain). You are asked to take this patient's medical history.
items: The patient presents with
Asks the patient how she would like to be addressed
Explains the purpose of the examination to the patient and asks for her permission to examine her
Asks questions in a logical and orderly manner: age, occupation, family, etc.
Ask the patient about the characteristics of the pain:

– how it started – context of onset – whether she has had this type of pain before – the nature of the pain and how it has evolved (intensity, location) – the radiation of the pain – symptoms accompanying the pain Ask the patient about the characteristics of the vomiting:
– time of onset – relationship between pain and vomiting – the initial appearance (content) – how it has evolved Ask the patient about changes in bowel movements:

– characteristics of bowel movements before the first symptoms – when changes in bowel movements occurred – how the changes in bowel movements have evolved – when she last had a bowel movement Ask the patient if she has any fears, concerns, questions, etc.
Thank the patient.

stations.scenario: R10-1.2 A 62-year-old female patient presents with abdominal pain, absence of bowel movements, and vomiting. She reports recent constipation (approximately 6 months), alternating with brief episodes of diarrhoea and fatigue; she has occasionally noticed blood streaks in her stool. The current pain began 3 days ago and is persistent and intense. The vomiting has accompanied the pain since its onset, but its appearance has changed over time: initially it contained food, but now it looks dirty. The last stool was 3 days ago (a few hours before the onset of pain). You are asked to perform a physical examination.
items: Introduces himself to the patient; washes his hands
Asks the patient how she would like to be addressed
Explain the purpose of the examination to the patient and ask for her permission to examine her.

She asks the patient to lie down on the bed in a comfortable position and helps her to expose her abdomen. She sits down to the right of the patient. She warms her hands. She then says aloud what she is doing
Relevant elements from the general physical examination and tests: Observe the patient's facial expression, attitude, blood pressure and pulse, skin (colour, signs of dehydration, etc.); temperature
Observe the amplitude of breathing; measure respiratory rate; percussion and auscultation of the chest bases.
Inspection of the abdomen: Observe the shape of the abdomen and the participation of the abdomen in respiratory movements
Observe hernial points (in clinostatism and orthostatism); presence/absence of postoperative scars
Palpation of the abdomen: Before palpation, ask the patient about the location of the pain; pain when coughing, mobilisation
Start on the opposite side to the maximum location of the pain, observe/test for possible skin hyperesthesia
Perform light percussion or gentle one-handed palpation of the abdomen to see if/where pain occurs (bell sign; Blumberg's sign).
Check the condition of the abdominal muscles (muscle contracture/defence).
Abdominal percussion: Sound obtained by percussion (tympanism, shifting dullness)
Assess prehepatic dullness/its disappearance
Auscultation of the abdomen: Presence and character of bowel sounds
Rectal examination: Presence of faecaloma, rectal tumour and tenderness of the Douglas pouch
Check for traces on the examiner's glove (faeces, pus, blood)
Ask the patient if she has any questions or comments; thank her.
